# PREFACE
## BY LUDWIG DINDORF.

---

Two editions of this Chronicle had appeared before our own: one by Matthäus Rader <note>original Latin: "Matthaei Raderi"</note> in Munich in the year 1615, and the second seventy-three years later by Du Cange <note>Charles du Fresne, sieur du Cange (1610–1688), a massive figure in the study of the Middle Ages and Byzantium</note> in Paris, which was later reprinted in Venice in 1729. Although both were derived from the same "Augustan" manuscript <note>original: "codice Augustano"; named after Augsburg, where it was once held</note>—now located in Munich and written at Lleida <note>original: "Ilerdae", a city in Spain</note> in 1573—that book was quite recent and so defiled by numerous and significant errors and gaps <note>original: "lacunis"</note> (as can be seen by the variety of readings we have noted), yet the Parisian edition was somewhat superior. 

For Du Cange, while he surpassed his predecessor by an infinite degree in his own learning, had also prepared for himself an excellent opportunity to restore missing and corrupted passages by frequently using excerpts from the famous Vatican manuscript. However, since those excerpts were made from passages chosen more by chance than by a clear plan, and were not handled with the diligence we expect today, it was easy to estimate how important it would be to examine such a book entirely anew. 

When the task of editing the Chronicle was offered to me, I saw that this must be done as soon as possible. I immediately convinced Niebuhr <note>Barthold Georg Niebuhr, the historian who founded the "Bonn Corpus" of Byzantine historians</note> of this necessity. Angelo Mai <note>original: "A. Maius"</note>—an illustrious and most celebrated man who, with his fortunate intuition, had himself recovered from the Vatican book small fragments of this writer (along with many others whose names would be too long to list) that had long been counted among the lost—favored our work so much that accurate records of the manuscript’s variations, prepared by a suitable assistant, were soon returned to me. With their help, so much healing has already been brought to this book...

<summary>Ludwig Dindorf discusses the flaws in previous editions of the Chronicon Paschale (1615 and 1688) and describes his efforts to create a more accurate edition using the Vatican manuscript with the help of scholars like Niebuhr and Angelo Mai.</summary>
<keywords>Ludwig Dindorf, Chronicon Paschale, Du Cange, Matthäus Rader, manuscript studies, Vatican manuscript, Angelo Mai, Barthold Georg Niebuhr, philology</keywords>

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page continues Ludwig Dindorf's 1831 preface to the Chronicon Paschale. On the previous page, Dindorf discussed earlier editions by Rader and Du Cange and the necessity of a new edition based on the superior Vatican manuscript. Here, he describes the specific manuscripts used and concludes his introductory remarks.</meta>

# PREFACE.

...it has come to pass that a text once considered extremely corrupt is now, through the correction of scribal errors, held to be purer than the works of many even among the best writers. No one who devotes effort to its improvement in the future need fear being misled by the negligence of the "little Greeks" <note>original Latin: "Graeculorum," a somewhat dismissive term Dindorf uses for later Byzantine scribes</note> of the lowest age.

There is, moreover, a Vatican book, numbered **1941** in the Papal library, remarkable for both its age and its quality. According to the judgment of Angelo Mai <note>A celebrated Italian cardinal and philologist who rediscovered many lost ancient texts</note> in the *New Vatican Collection*, volume I, part II, page 222, it was written quite carefully on parchment around the tenth century. However, the system of vowels is almost entirely reversed in this manner: *they have* <note>original Greek: "ἔχουση" (echousē); a common misspelling for "ἔχουσι" (echousi)</note>, and *spherical sky* <note>original Greek: "σφερῶϊδεῖ οὐρανόν" (spherōidei ouranon)</note>. We have noted very few instances of this kind of error. Some scholarly notes <term>scholia|marginal comments made by ancient or medieval teachers and students</term> were placed in the margin by a later hand, and some corrections were also made in the text itself. Several leaves were lost in the middle of the work, and the beginning and end are not intact. From this book, the Munich manuscript (found in Hardt's catalog, volume V, page 416) was derived, such that it shares all the gaps found in the Vatican manuscript, yet possesses its own large abundance of errors. In a few places, it offers a truer reading, though it has mostly incorporated the marginal notes into the main text. I would not, however, state with certainty that the Munich manuscript was copied directly from the Vatican one, both because of the sheer multitude of errors and because of significant small sections omitted from the beginning and at pages 570, 655, and following. These sections remain easy to read in the Vatican manuscript, but in the book which Andreas Darmarius <note>A prolific 16th-century Greek scribe often criticized by later scholars for his haste and inaccuracies</note> had before his eyes, they seem to have either been absent or illegible.

It was not my task to reshape the Latin translation by Du Cange. Nor did I touch the small treatises which Du Cange added to the end of the Chronicle, except that I have improved the text of Dorotheus <note>referring to a list of Apostles and Disciples attributed to Dorotheus of Tyre</note> with the variations from an ancient Leiden manuscript, thanks to the kindness of the most learned and friendly Jacob Geel <note>A prominent Dutch librarian and scholar (1789–1862)</note>.

->I wrote this in Leipzig on the **24th of November, 1831.**<-

***

# THE PASCHAL CHRONICLE

<term>Paschal Chronicle|A massive 7th-century Byzantine world chronicle that begins with Adam and concludes in the reign of Emperor Heraclius. It is named for its focus on the "Paschal" or Easter cycles used to determine the date of the holiday.</term>

# PREFACE

...it has come to pass that a text once considered extremely corrupt is now, through the correction of scribal errors, held to be purer than the works of many even among the best writers. No one who devotes effort to its improvement in the future need fear being misled by the negligence of the "little Greeks" <note>original Latin: "Graeculorum." Dindorf uses this diminutive term to criticize the perceived sloppiness of later Byzantine copyists compared to earlier classical standards.</note> of the lowest age.

There is, moreover, a Vatican book, numbered **1941** in the Papal library, remarkable for both its age and its quality. According to the judgment of Angelo Mai <note>A famous Italian cardinal and librarian who was a pioneer in using reagents to recover lost texts from palimpsests (reused parchment).</note> in the *New Vatican Collection*, volume I, part II, page 222, it was written quite carefully on parchment around the tenth century. However, the system of vowels is almost entirely reversed in this manner: *they have* <note>original Greek: "ἔχουση" (echousē); a common spelling error where the scribe uses "η" instead of the correct "ι" (ἔχουσι), a phenomenon known as itacism where different Greek vowels began to be pronounced identically.</note>, and *spherical sky* <note>original Greek: "σφερῶϊδεῖ οὐρανόν" (spherōidei ouranon); the scribe has used "ε" and "ω" incorrectly here.</note>. We have noted very few instances of this kind of error. Some <term>scholia|marginal notes or explanatory comments added to a manuscript by later readers or teachers.</term> were placed in the margin by a later hand, and some corrections were also made in the text itself. Several leaves were lost in the middle of the work, and the beginning and end are not intact. PASCHAL CHRONICLE.
<meta>Digitized by Google</meta>

### From Philo, the wise man among the Hebrews ¹)

**M**oses records the beginning of the spring <term>equinox|The time in March when day and night are of equal length, marking the start of the Jewish month of Nisan.</term> as the first month in the cycles of the years. He granted this month the place of honor, not because of the passage of time—as some do—but rather because of the gifts of nature which it brings forth for mankind. For it is during this season that <margin>5</margin> the **seeds** ²) <note>original: "σπέρματα" (spermata). Philo argues that nature's cycle of food production dictates the calendar.</note>, which provide our essential food, are brought to completion. The fruit of the trees, which is currently blooming, is born next, holding the second rank because it ripens later; for in nature, those things that are not strictly necessary always follow after the most essential. Indeed, wheat, barley, and other types of grain are strictly necessary, for without them one cannot live. However, oil, wine, and <margin>10</margin> **orchard-fruits** are not among the absolute necessities, since men can live and reach an extreme **old age** ³) over many years without them. In this month, around the 14th day, when the lunar cycle is about to become full, the "Crossing-Festival" <note>original: "διαβατήρια" (diabateria). Philo uses this Greek term, meaning "sacrifices for crossing," to explain the meaning of the Passover.</note> is celebrated—a festival **publicly manifest** ⁴) which is called *Pascha* in the Chaldean language <note>original: "χαλδαϊστὶ λεγόμενον πάσχα." In this period, authors often used "Chaldean" to refer to Hebrew or Aramaic.</note>.

<margin>15</margin> These are the words of Philo. Furthermore, the fact that the Israelite people unfailingly observed the feast of the Passover on the 14th day of the first lunar month—not only until the Lord's Passion, but even until the capture of Jerusalem which occurred under **Vespasian**, the Roman Emperor—is attested by the God-bearing <margin>20</margin> shepherds and teachers of the Church, of whom I shall set forth a few out of many...

---

¹) From the work *On Moses*, Book III, edited by Mangey, volume II, page 169. — MAI <note>original Latin: "MAIUS." This refers to Cardinal Angelo Mai, the 19th-century editor.</note>.
²) In the manuscript, which has a gap, only ". . mata" is legible. I have preferred to read this as "seeds" [*spermata*] rather than "sown fields" [*sparta*] as found in the printed editions. — MAI.
³) The edition reads "old age" [*gērēs*] with a variant spelling. — MAI.
⁴) The edition reads "publicly manifest" [*dēmophanēs*]. — MAI.

<summary>This page quotes the Jewish philosopher Philo of Alexandria to explain why the Jewish calendar begins with the spring equinox, linking the timing of Passover to the natural harvest cycle. The author of the Chronicle then asserts that this 14th-day tradition was maintained until the Roman destruction of Jerusalem.</summary>

# CHRONICLE

. . . Peter, Bishop of the church of the Alexandrians, will bring forward in his discourse on <term>Pascha|The Greek and Latin term for Passover, used by early Christians to refer to Easter.</term>, which he wrote to a certain **Tricentius** ⁵), which discourse also the great **Athanasius** <note>Archbishop of Alexandria (c. 296–373 AD), a central figure in early Christian theology.</note>, who became Archbishop of the same church . . . . . . . in his [letter] to Bishop **Epiphanius** ⁶) . . . . . . . speaks somewhat as follows:

<margin>5</margin>
<margin>P 1 V 1</margin> Since . . . great is the mercy of God; in . . . all . . . we give thanks to him, and that he sent down the **Spirit of Truth** to us, guiding us into all truth. For because of this, the legislated **Month of New Things** <note>original: "μὴν τῶν νέων" (mēn tōn neōn). This refers to the month of Abib or Nisan, the first month of the Hebrew calendar, associated with ripening grain.</note>, the beginning of months and the first <margin>10</margin> among the months of the year, was made known to us. It was shown to have a most pure and manifest boundary both by the ancient writers who lived before the capture of Jerusalem and by the newer ones after the capture, especially because sometimes the **new crops** <note>original: "τὰ νέα" (ta nea)</note> in certain places come early, and sometimes they are late by being <margin>15</margin> either early-ripening or late-ripening, just as it happened at the very beginning of the law before the Passover, as . . .

6. Before "Since," P places the title: **Of Peter, Bishop of Alexandria and Martyr, that the Hebrews correctly fixed the 14th day of the 1st month of the moon until the capture of Jerusalem.** 15. *by the*] *the* in P.

->From Peter, Bishop of Alexandria and Martyr, regarding the fact that the<-

<note>The following is a translation of the Latin parallel text provided by the 19th-century editor.</note>

Since the mercy of God is great everywhere, let us bless him, and because he sent the spirit of truth to us, leading us into all truth. For indeed the month of new things introduced by the law, the beginning of months, and the first among the months of the year, was made known to us: and it was shown to have a most sincere and evident boundary both by the ancient Scriptoribus [Writers] who lived before, and by the later ones who lived after the destruction of Jerusalem: especially because the new crops are sometimes anticipated in certain places: and sometimes it happens that early crops are lacking or occur later, just as it was in the very beginning before the Passover . . .

---

⁵) Let us take note of this man [Tricentius], of whom there is nothing in either Du Cange's or Petavius's edition of Peter's fragments. — **MAI**. <note>Angelo Mai (1782–1854) was the editor of this volume.</note>
⁶) This is why Du Cange (p. 4) says "in the aforementioned letter"; because the author of the Chronicle had already praised that letter in this place, which is missing in Du Cange's version. Furthermore, those gaps that appear in Du Cange (p. 2) cannot be filled from the decayed parchment of the manuscript, except that at D. line 3, it is read in the manuscript as "into a clear [sign]." — **MAI**.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the timing of Pascha (Easter), moving from the general introduction of the "Month of New Things" into a specific argument based on the Old Testament and the natural cycle of the spring season. ### CONCERNING EASTER

-> [H E A D E R : O N  P A S C H A] <-

It is written, "but the wheat and the spelt were not struck; for they were late-ripening." <note>original: "ὁ δὲ πυρὸς καὶ ἡ ὄλυρα οὐκ ἐπλήγη· ὄψιμα γὰρ ἦν." Quote from Exodus 9:32, referring to the crops that survived the plague of hail in Egypt.</note> For this reason, it has been rightly legislated that from the <term>vernal equinox|The point in spring (around March 21) when day and night are of equal length, marking the start of the new solar year.</term>, in whichever week the fourteenth day of the first month falls, on that week the <term>Pascha|The term for Passover, which early Christians used to refer to Easter.</term> should be celebrated, after having also included the most fitting and harmonious praises for this purpose. "For this," he says, "is your first month... and the beginning of months <margin>B</margin> among the months of the year it is written," <note>Exodus 12:2. The ellipsis indicates a gap (lacuna) in the manuscript which the editor notes can be filled with the word "is."</note> at the time when the sun, moving toward summer, gives forth lights that are more numerous and brighter; the day, extending itself, grows larger while the night withdraws and diminishes; and the new seeds, having blossomed, are purified and gathered into the threshing floors. Furthermore, all the fruit-bearing trees sprout and blossom... [bringing forth]. Immediately they are overtaken in a succession of various and diverse fruits, so that even a cluster of grapes is sometimes found at that very time, just as the <term>Legislator|A traditional title for Moses, who delivered the Law to Israel.</term> says, "and the days were the days of spring, the precursors of the grape," <note>Numbers 13:21 (or 13:20 in modern bibles).</note> when he sent those who were to spy out the land, and they brought the great cluster <margin>C</margin> on carrying-poles, along with pomegranates and figs. For at that time, as they say, even our eternal God, the Founder and <term>Demiurge|From the Greek 'demiourgos', meaning a craftsman or creator who fashioned the physical universe.</term> of all things, established the universe, according to what he recounted: "Let the earth sprout the herb of grass, sowing seed according to its kind..." <note>Genesis 1:11.</note>

---

1. **the — ripening** ] Exodus 9:32. **3. fourteenth [V]** constantly, **fourteenth [P].** <note>V and P refer to the Vatican and Parisian manuscripts; the note highlights a spelling variation in the Greek word for 'fourteenth'.</note> **6. first — written** ] Exodus 12:2. The gap can be filled by adding "is." **15. and — grape** ] Numbers 13:21. I have added a second "days." **19. the Demiurge [P].** **21. let the earth sprout — rightly** ] Genesis 1:11.

---

At the beginning of the Legislation: according to what is written, *The wheat and the emmer <note>A type of hulled wheat, similar to spelt.</note> were not harmed, because they were late-ripening.* For which reason it is rightly prescribed by the law that from the vernal equinox, into whichever week the fourteenth of the first month falls, in that week the Pascha is to be celebrated, with the appropriate and fitting praises first having been taken up for its celebration. *For this month, he says, is the first, the beginning of months, written among the months of the year:* namely, when the sun in the summer season sends out much more and clearer light: the day is truly lengthened and becomes greater, while the night is contracted and diminished: furthermore, when the new seeds have flowered, they are thoroughly cleaned and brought to the threshing floors. Nor however [is it] only those, but even all the trees sprout and turn into flowers. Immediately, therefore, they are found to send out various and different fruits in turn, so that sometimes a cluster [of grapes], sometimes another fruit is found at one and the same time, just as the Legislator says: *And the days of spring were the precursors of the grape-cluster,* when he sent those who would scout the land, and they brought a huge cluster on poles, along with pomegranates and figs. For then, as the founder and craftsman of all things, our eternal God, brings together all things according to what he chose: *Let the earth germinate green herb, both making seed according to its kind and its likeness, and the fruit-bearing tree making fruit, whose...*

<summary>This page explains the theological and natural reasoning for the date of Easter, linking the "fourteenth day of the first month" to the vernal equinox and the agricultural renewal of spring. It cites the books of Exodus, Numbers, and Genesis to show that God established the world and the Law during this season of increasing light.</summary>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the technical and theological defense of the Christian timing of Easter (Pascha). It transitions from the natural cycle of the spring equinox to the biblical authority of Genesis and the Gospel of John, arguing that the Jewish community lost the correct method of calculation following the destruction of Jerusalem.</meta>

### CHRONICLE

-> [C H R O N I C O N] <-

"...and according to its likeness, and fruit trees bearing fruit, whose seed is in itself according to its kind upon the earth." <note>A quotation of Genesis 1:11–12, linking the creation of the world to the "month of new things."</note> And it added that "it was so, and it was very good and just." This revealed the first month established by law among the Hebrews, which we know was preserved among the Jews until the capture of Jerusalem, because it had been handed down especially to the Hebrews in this way. However, after the capture, this month was treated as a matter of nonsense by some, and in this, a <term>hardening|Greek: porosis. A theological term used to describe a spiritual blindness or a "callousness" of the heart, here referring to the loss of the correct calendar calculation.</term> occurred; this is the month which we, observing lawfully and sincerely, have received. And in this, according to the [missing] word, saying [missing]... leads into the <margin>D</margin> auspicious day of our holy feast, which the "chosen" attained, but the rest were hardened, just as the Scripture said. <note>Original: "ἡ ἐκλογὴ ἐπέτυχεν, οἱ δὲ λοιποὶ ἐπωρώθησαν" — a reference to Romans 11:7, contrasting those who found the truth with those who were blinded.</note>

And after other matters, he says: "For all these things they will do to you, because they did not know the one who sent me." <note>John 15:21.</note> If they were ignorant of both the Sender and the One sent, there is no doubt that they also possessed an ignorance of the legislation regarding the Pascha. Thus, they did not only fall away from the proper <margin>P 3</margin> timing according to the "chosen," but also from the very beginning of the months—the first among the months of the year. In ancient times, those who sincerely observed the fourteenth day of this month after the <term>equinox|The moment when the sun crosses the celestial equator, making night and day equal. The author argues that Easter must always fall after this event.</term> sacrificed the Pascha according to the divine command. But those who do it now before the equinox do so with great neglect and error...

***

**Notes on the text:**
2. **"it added"**: The Vatican manuscript reads *epēnegken*, while the Paris manuscript reads *epenēgken*. 
7. **"hardening"**: Found in both manuscripts. I note once that I have cited the Vatican codex as compared to the Paris edition; where I saw no difference noted, I have treated them as in agreement.

Furthermore, he ordered that those who acted to the contrary should be expelled from communion and remain exiles from the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church of God. All those who were blamelessly set over the holy Churches of Christ agreed to these terms.

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the Council of Nicaea. Having addressed the Arian controversy, the text now details the Council's technical solution for the uniform celebration of Easter, focusing on the mathematical 19-year cycle.</meta>

-># THE PASCHAL RECKONING<-

The ecclesiastical rule for the festival of Easter is the 19-year cycle <note>original: "ἐννεακαιδεκαετηρὶς" (enneadecaeteris). This is the "Metonic cycle," a period of 19 years after which the phases of the moon fall on the same dates of the solar year.</note> of the moon set forth by the God-bearing fathers. This cycle revolves back into itself perpetually and indicates, in each year, on what day <margin>C</margin> of March or April the 14th day of the first <margin>5</margin> lunar month is found. This is the day on which the legal Passover <note>original: "νομικὸν... πάσχα" (nomikon pascha). This refers to the Old Testament requirement for the Jewish Passover on 14 Nisan.</note> is commanded to be performed. By knowing this, any person can perceive on which day of the week it falls in any given year. And by knowing the established boundary—that if this day is found to be a Sunday, one must celebrate the holy Easter on the following Sunday; but if it falls on any <margin>10</margin> other of the six days of the week, it is celebrated on the next coming Sunday—one will be able to know clearly and very easily in each year on what day of March or April the Church of God will celebrate the saving Easter.

But some, acting out of a greater desire for distinction <note>original: "φιλοτιμότερον φερόμενοι" (philotimoteron pheromenoi). This implies an ambitious attempt to improve upon the established rule.</note>, <margin>D V 8</margin> established a cycle of five 19-year periods <note>A 95-year cycle (19 x 5 = 95).</note>. <margin>15</margin> They rashly claimed that this cycle, as it perpetually returns to itself, would bring the 14th day of the first lunar month not only on the same days of the solar months (March or April) but also on the same days of the week. Some of the simpler folk, having found this and suspecting it to be true, <margin>20</margin> not only recorded it in books but even set it up on display tables in many of the churches. Consequently, Pagans <note>original: "Ἕλληνας" (Hellenas), literally "Greeks," used here to mean non-Christian practitioners of traditional religion.</note>, Jews, and the leaders of heresies, seeing this displayed...

<note>Textual variants: In line 2, one manuscript (V) uses a different grammatical case for "19-year cycle." In line 12, "of God" is omitted or altered in manuscript P. In line 22, the word "both" is omitted in manuscript P.</note>

<column-break/>

The 19-year Lunar Cycle proposed by the God-bearing Fathers suffices as a rule; it always recurs into itself and indicates in which year, and on which day of March or April, the fourteenth day of the first lunar month is found—the day on which the legal precept commands the Passover to be celebrated. Once this is known, anyone will perceive on which day of the week it occurs in individual years. Thus, if it is found on a Sunday, the holy Easter must be celebrated on the following Sunday. If, however, it falls on any other of the six days, anyone can easily figure out that the holy Easter must be celebrated on the following Sunday, and on what day of March or April the Church will celebrate the saving Easter in individual years.

Furthermore, some others, led by I know not what ambition, established a cycle of five 19-year periods. They rashly asserted that this returns into itself, claiming it would bring the fourteenth day of the first lunar month not only according to the lunar days of the months of March and April, but also according to the same days of the week. Certain simpler people, having found this cycle and believing it to be consistent with the truth, described it not only in books but even on tablets which they hung in many churches. The result was that when the Pagans <note>original: "Gentiles."</note>, Jews, and [leaders] of heresies noticed this display...

Therefore, when this occurred, certain members of the Catholic Church were moved by necessary reasoning to refute such a strange and unlearned opinion of those who had composed the aforementioned cycle of ninety-five years. They instead demonstrated the true cycle, which is consistent with the facts: the cycle of twenty-eight 19-year periods <note>28 x 19 = 532</note>, or nineteen 28-year periods <note>19 x 28 = 532</note>, which brings together <margin>5</margin> a total of 532 years. For this cycle—I mean that of 532 years—always revolving back into itself, shows the 14th day of the first lunar month falling not only on the same <margin>10</margin> days of the two solar months (I mean March and April), but also on the <margin>B</margin> same days of the week, in the same year of the four-year leap year cycle <note>original: "βισέξτου" (bisextou), from the Latin "bissextus," referring to the leap day</note>, in the same year of the 19-year cycle, and even in the same year of the 28-year cycle. <margin>15</margin> For the aforementioned cycle of 532 years is completed and is divisible by 19, by 28, by 4, and by 7.

Once this was known, many people wrote out festive cycles of 532 years; however, by mixing falsehood with the truth, they provided <margin>20</margin> occasions of scandal and confusion to the simpler folk. For some [incorrectly] considered the fourteenth days of the first lunar month to be immovable...

# PASCHAL [CHRONICLE]

...finding the churches to be discordant and contradictory, and those festal cycles recorded by some to be causing disturbances and scandals among the children of piety, we have deemed it necessary to record a festal cycle of 532 years <note>original Greek: "φλβ΄" (532). <margin>15</margin> We shall set forth, before the festal cycle of 532 years, the <margin>P 12</margin> natural twenty-eight-year cycle of the sun. This cycle also began at the creation of the luminaries and, always recurring into itself, indicates in each year the [lunar data] according to the ecclesiastical [rule]...

# CHRONICLE

It should be understood that at the creation of the luminaries <note>The sun and the moon, created on the fourth day in Genesis.</note>, that is, at the beginning of the world’s constitution, the first year of the natural <term>28-year solar cycle<span>A period of 28 years after which the days of the week return to the same calendar dates.</span></term> has no <term>epacts<span>In this context, "epacts" (from the Greek 'epaktai', meaning 'added days') refer to the extra days beyond a 52-week year (364 days) that accumulate to keep the calendar in sync with the solar year of 365.25 days.</span></term>. For the epacts are taken from the one and a <margin>5</margin> quarter days remaining after the completion of the 52 weeks of each leading year, and they are added to each following year. How then is it possible to have epacts at the very beginning of the world’s creation? For that would be ridiculous; I mean, to have epacts, or a single epact, or even fractions of epacts <note>original: "lepta epakton" — literally 'minutes' or small portions of the extra day.</note> at the start of the world’s constitution. But after the completion <margin>10</margin> of the first 28-year solar cycle that began with the creation of the world, the first year of the second 28-year solar cycle has 7 epacts. If they exceed 7, they are no longer called 8 or 9; rather, by subtracting the 7 <note>The 7 days of the week.</note>, they are called 1 or 2, and so on again up to 7. The second and third years of the <margin>15</margin> 28-year cycle and its remaining years behave the same way in the first 28-year cycle, the second, and in all the others likewise.

Here it must also be noted that each year of the natural 28-year solar cycle begins on the 21st <margin>20</margin> of the Roman month of March, on which the spring equinox <note>The day when day and night are of equal length; the anchor point for calculating Easter.</note>...

Furthermore, it should be noted that at the rising of the luminaries, or at the beginning of the world's composition, the first year of the natural 28-year Solar Cycle has no Epacts. Indeed, Epacts are taken from the day and a quarter remaining after the completion of the 52 weeks of each first year, and are brought into each following year. How then could it happen that Epacts occurred at the beginning of the created world? For it is quite ridiculous that, as I say, Epacts, or a single Epact, or even the minutes of Epacts should occur at the beginning of the world's composition. However, after the first 28-year Solar Cycle has been completed—that is, the one which began at the world's birth—the first year of the second 28-year Solar Cycle has 60 Epacts. <note>The Latin translator here reads "LX" (60), likely misinterpreting a Greek numeral or a variant manuscript; the Greek text and logic suggest 7 (VII), representing the days of the week.</note> If indeed they exceed 60...

This must also be observed in this place: that each year of the natural 28-year solar cycle begins on the 21st day of the month of March according to the Romans, on which day the spring equinox occurs, as the God-bearing Fathers <note>The Bishops and theologians of the early Church Councils, such as Nicaea.</note> have taught...

The Law clearly prescribes the holy and blessed Passover of God, simultaneously indicating the month in which this must be done, and commanding that the day be observed with great precision. For the voice of God is carried within that Law, [commanding us]

### **A brief resolution with demonstration concerning the holy and saving Legal Passover of any year, and the questions regarding it.**
<note>This section is the Latin translation of the Greek text above, provided in the original manuscript for scholarly comparison.</note>

The Law prescribes the holy and blessed Passover of God quite clearly, and at the same time indicates the month in which it ought to occur, and on which day it is ordered to be observed, and this with the utmost accuracy. Indeed, the voice of God has entered into the Law, by which it is commanded to observe the month of New Fruits: *And you shall perform the Passover to the Lord your God on the fourteenth day of the first month.* Now, He calls it the "New Month," which He also calls the first, in which the budding fruits announce the cessation of the old. Moreover, He commands the Passover to be observed on the fourteenth of the first month for no other reason than that, just like the light of the Moon when it has its full circle, we likewise, having the luminary of the mind full, should not remain in the shadows of sin; but rather, blooming with virtues of every kind, and covered by their leaves like pleasant plants, we may remain beautiful like the crops. Indeed, He says the fourteenth of the month, not according to the solar cycle, but according to the lunar. For the sons of the Hebrews [reckon] not from the solar...

...for the children <note>Referring to the Israelites/Jews</note> were taught to determine the month not from the solar course, but from the cycle of the moon, since the month is also named after the moon; for she is called *Mene* <note>original: μήνη (mēnē). The author is noting the linguistic link between the Greek word for moon and the word for month, "mēn."</note> in the Greek tongue. The *Egyptians*, at least, were the first—because the course of the moon is the most erratic <note>original: ἐξώτατον (exōtaton), literally "outermost," but here referring to the moon's high variability compared to the sun.</note> and because this results in a "wandering" of the days among some people—to devise the method of calculating the days of the month by the sun. This is because the sun moves more slowly in its own course than the moon, which allows its position to be more easily grasped. Since things are thus, many people also designate the first 
month of the year—which is the conclusion of the winter solstice <note>The author uses "solstice" (τροπή) generally for a seasonal turning point; here it refers to the end of the winter season.</note>—as being the absolute first month. But they do this in ignorance, not knowing that <margin>D</margin>
the beginning of the spring equinox <note>original: ἐαρινῆς τροπῆς (earinēs tropēs). This is the crucial turning point for calculating Easter.</note> occurs on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April <note>term: "Kalends of April" — The first of April. Twelve days before this is March 21, the traditional date of the Vernal Equinox.</note>, which is the 25th of Phamenoth <note>Phamenoth: The seventh month of the Egyptian calendar.</note>. According to the *Syrians of Antioch*
and the *Macedonians*, this is the twenty-first of *Dystros* <note>Dystros: A month in the Macedonian calendar corresponding roughly to March.</note> according to the solar course. 
It is most necessary to observe this date, lest anyone, having wandered below it and having mistakenly set the fourteenth day of the moon <note>The Paschal Full Moon.</note> there, should fail in the calculation of the Passover by thinking that this [earlier date] belongs to the first month.

for the divine Law established this as the primary sign of the first month. But since it happens that, under the pretext of the fourteenth day of the moon of this same first month, people fall into error...

# CHRONICON
<note>Latin: "Chronicle"</note>

...some people, when it <note>The Fourteenth day of the moon</note> falls on a Sunday or a Saturday, break the fasts when the moon is only on its thirteenth day, acting as if they are strangers to the Law. It is proper to consider this: if it happens that the fourteenth day of the moon is found to be on a Sunday, it is better to postpone the celebration to the following week for two reasons. 

<margin>V 15 B</margin> First, so that we do not break the fasts on a Saturday when the moon is on its thirteenth day. This would be inconsistent, as the Law does not command it, and because the luminary of the moon is still incomplete in its own cycle <note>The author considers the moon "imperfect" until the full 14th day</note>. Second, so that we are not forced to fast while it is both Sunday and the fourteenth day of the moon, which would be an unseemly thing to do; for such a thing is a characteristic practice of the **Manichaeans** <note>A dualist religious group that Christians criticized for fasting on Sundays, which was traditionally a day of joy and feast</note>. Therefore, since one must not fast when the fourteenth of the moon falls on a Sunday, nor is it consistent to break the fasts when the thirteenth falls on a Saturday, a postponement to the following week is necessary, as was said a little while ago. This postponement does not result in a violation of the **Passover** <note>original: πάσχα (pascha)</note>; rather, just as the number ten includes the number nine, so if the fourteenth of the moon is <margin>C</margin> found on a Sunday—since one must not fast on that day—the postponement to the following week should occur. This postponement does not cause a reduction of the Passover, as the six days <note>The six days of Holy Week</note> encompass the others as well. Furthermore, since our Savior on the thirteenth—

...certain people are led, when that day occurs on a Sunday or Saturday, to break their fasts; and since the moon is then found to be on its thirteenth day, they act against the Law. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; And first, indeed, so that we do not break the fasts when the thirteenth moon occurs on a Saturday, since that is by no means in accordance with the Law, which does not prescribe it, while the luminary of the moon is still imperfect in its cycle. Second, so that if Sunday should coincide with the fourteenth moon, we are not forced to fast and perform an unseemly act, since that is a practice peculiar to the **Manichaeans**. Therefore, since one must not fast when the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, just as the fasts are not to be broken when the thirteenth falls on a Saturday, it is necessary that it be delayed until the following Sunday, as was said shortly before. The fast of the Passover is not broken because it has been delayed; but just as the number ten encompasses nine, so when the fourteenth moon falls on a Sunday, because one must not fast on that day, it must necessarily be delayed until the following week. # PASCHAL CHRONICLE
<note>original: PASCHALE; this refers to the "Chronicon Paschale," a massive 7th-century Byzantine work that calculates time from Creation to the author's present day.</note>

...[thir]teenth He was betrayed, that is, on the fifth day of the week <note>Thursday</note>, and on the fourteenth He was crucified, rising within three days, that is, on the sixteenth day of the moon, which at that time fell on a Sunday, as the record of the Gospels maintains. Let us take this as a source of comfort for performing the **Passover** <note>original: πάσχα (pascha); here referring to the Christian Easter celebration</note> correctly, even if a postponement happens due to a prevailing necessity. If, then, the fourteenth day of the Holy Passover falls on a Saturday or before Saturday—that is, on the other days of the week—it is appropriate to celebrate it fixedly. But if the fourteenth day of the moon of the first month should occur on a Sunday, it must certainly be postponed to the following week; for **Sunday** <note>original: κυριακὴ (kyriake), the Lord's Day</note> is the first day of the week, as was stated previously. **D**

He was betrayed on the thirteenth, that is, on the fifth day of the Sabbath <note>Thursday</note>, and crucified on the fourteenth, rising after three days, that is, on the sixteenth day of the Moon, which was found to be on the Lord's Day <note>Sunday</note>, as the observation of the Gospels puts forward; in performing the Passover correctly, even if it is necessarily delayed, let us be allowed to console ourselves. But even if the fourteenth of the holy Passover falls on a Saturday, or the day before Saturday, and on the other days of the week, it is fitting to observe it firmly. If, however, the fourteenth day of the Moon of the first month occurs on the Lord's Day, it must be postponed entirely to the following week; for the Lord's Day is indeed the first day of the week, as was said above.

From here on, it is necessary for a brief history to be made of the years from Adam, the first of men formed by God, or from the beginning of the world's foundation, which harmonize with the Scripture that God inspired, and even with the festivals blamelessly handed down by the Holy and God-bearing Fathers, and duly celebrated in the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church of God.

## On Abel.

<margin>C</margin> This is Abel the righteous, who, by being the first of all humans to die unjustly, showed that the foundations of death are unstable. Because of this, even though he is dead he still speaks, foretelling the resurrection of the dead. The Lord Christ was the first of all to demonstrate this resurrection in Himself, thereby destroying the apparent power of death. ## Concerning the Prophecy of Enoch.

*This man prophesied, saying: "Behold, the Lord comes with His holy thousands to execute judgment against all, and to convict the ungodly of all the evils which those ungodly sinners have spoken against them."*

Noah, being just and perfect in his generation, when he had fallen into drunkenness unintentionally and unwillingly, saw within it certain secret mysteries; for the Scripture says: *But Noah awoke from the wine, and knew whatever his younger son had done to him.* And after he addressed him in the place of a curse, but others in the place of a blessing, he predicts things that will come to pass and happen, when he says, *Blessed be the God of Shem.* For in a certain way, he did not imprecate the first, nor did he bless this one, but he uttered a prediction of mysteries which were fulfilled through the Lord Christ: for the sons of Canaan never served their brothers, but rather those others served them in Egypt. But neither did the Gibeonites serve them, as some have suspected, but rather they served God: for they appointed them as woodcutters and water-carriers for the Temple of God, and not for themselves. What else is this, then, but a pure prediction that those very ones would serve the Lord who was to be born from Shem according to the flesh? Furthermore: *Blessed be the Lord God of Shem.* What are these things to Shem, if it is God who is blessed? But he adds: *May God enlarge Japheth, and may he dwell as God in the tents of Shem.* Then, *Enlarge, O God, Japheth.* For He enlarged both Japheth and Canaan, and again both served Christ, who was born from Shem. For all...

The mothers, first-ranked, and most famous of all heresies are these: **Barbarism**, **Scythism**, **Hellenism**, and **Judaism**. From these "mothers," all other heresies have grown.

<margin>P 24</margin> **Barbarism** is that which, existing by itself, lasted from Adam for ten generations until the Flood of Noah. It is called "barbarism" because men did not have any single leader or a unified agreement, but rather every individual followed their own path, and each became a law unto themselves according to the preference of their own will.

It has been shown from the preceding points why the Flood occurred. Let us now speak of the things that followed the Flood.

Noah lived three hundred and fifty years after the Flood. And all the days of Noah were nine hundred and fifty years, and he died.

God’s dwellings, which He made among men—partially in the Prophets, but perfectly, without distinction, and universally in the Lord Christ according to the flesh—were made for His descendants from Shem: just as it is written of the Lord Christ according to the flesh, *In whom dwells the fullness of the Divinity bodily.* Therefore, by these visions, he [Noah] was also worthy to announce in advance those things which were carried out by Christ for the purpose of securing the salvation of the human race.

Furthermore, the mothers and principal, celebrated sects of all types are these: **Barbarism**, **Scythism**, **Hellenism**, and **Judaism**; from which the rest of the heresies were born.

**Barbarism** is a certain way of living according to one's own will, such as existed from Adam through ten generations until the Flood of Noah. It is called "Barbarism," however, because men had no leader, nor did they come together or agree with one another; rather, each followed whatever pleased him, and his own will was the law for each individual.

...and Persia and the remaining parts of the East. From the first son of Noah <note>referring to Shem</note>, there was born and appeared a man of the giant race named Cronus <note>original: "Kronos"; the Greek equivalent of the Roman Saturn</note>. He was given this name by his own father, Domnus, after the name of the wandering star <note>the planet Saturn</note>. He became a powerful man, who was the first to demonstrate how to rule as a king—that is, to lead and hold power over other men. He himself was the first to rule over Assyria for many years, and he subdued all the land of Persia, beginning from <margin>C</margin> Assyria. He was a source of fear to everyone, acting as a warmonger and destroying all who opposed him. He had a wife named Semiramis, who was also called Rhea by the Assyrians because she was exceedingly proud and arrogant. She, too, was from the tribe of Shem, the son of Noah.

Cronus had a son named Picus, who was also called Zeus <note>Jupiter</note> by his parents after the name of the wandering star <note>the planet Jupiter</note>. This same Cronus also had another son named Ninus, and a daughter named Hera <note>Juno</note>. Picus, also known as Zeus, took his own sister Hera as a wife; some called her "The Joiner" <note>original: "Zygiên", a title for Hera as goddess of marriage</note> and "Nemesis," giving thanks to her as one who was good and desired all things to be just. From her, Picus (also called Zeus) had a son <margin>D</margin> whom he named Belus <note>a Greek form of the Semitic "Bel" or "Baal," meaning Lord</note> because the boy was extremely swift.

The forefather Cronus, leaving his own son Picus in Assyria along with his wife Rhea (also known as Semiramis) with Picus...

...and while he ruled the other regions looking toward the East, a man flourished who was procreated from the lineage of giants. He was called Cronus or Saturn, which name was bestowed upon him by his father Domnus from the nomenclature of the wandering star. This man, since he was quite powerful, was the first to teach the art of reigning and commanding, and of subjecting other men to himself. He himself first reigned for many years in Assyria; then all of Persia was subjected to his empire, beginning from the Assyrians, as he was a terror to all as an enemy and a tyrant. His wife was Semiramis, whom the Assyrians called Rhea on account of her pride and arrogance; she herself was likewise descended from the tribe of Shem, the son of Noah. To Saturn truly there was a son, Picus, who was called Jupiter by his parents, likewise from the name of the wandering star. Saturn also had another son, whose name was Ninus, and a daughter called Juno, whom some called the "conjugal Nemesis" because she was good and because she wished for all things to be just. From her, Picus or Jupiter had a son, whom he named Belus, because he excelled in swiftness of feet. But the grandfather Saturn, having permitted Assyria to Jupiter or Picus his son, and having left his wife Rhea or Semiramis with his son Picus or Jupiter...

<header>PASCHAL CHRONICLE</header>

...gave him the kingdom of the West; for he was old and weary, this same Cronus. And Picus, also called Zeus, ruled the West—that is, Italy—for sixty-two full years. In Assyria, after Belus, Ninus ruled, the other son of Cronus, who even took his own mother, Semiramis, to be his wife. From this came the law among Persians to marry their own mothers and sisters, <margin>C</margin> because Picus also took his own sister Hera as his wife, just as the most wise Homer sets forth, when he addressed Hera <note>original: "Ἥρην προσεῖπε κασιγνήτην ἄλοχόν τε"; a famous line from the Iliad</note> as "sister and wife." And Cronus passed away. Ninus, having become powerful over Assyria, built the city of Nineveh for the Assyrians and was the first to rule in it, having with him Semiramis, also called Rhea, who was both his mother and his wife.

<margin>R 88</margin> From this lineage, then, was born Zoroaster, the famous astronomer of the Persians. When he was about to die, he prayed to be consumed by heavenly fire, saying to the Persians, "If the fire burns me, take what remains of my burned bones and guard them; the kingdom shall not fail from your land for as long as you guard my bones." <margin>D</margin> And having prayed to Orion <note>The constellation or the legendary hunter, here treated as a celestial power</note>, he was consumed by fire from the air. And the Persians did just as he told them; and they still keep his remains, reduced to ashes, until now.

---

The ruler of the West voluntarily yielded to him, as he was burdened by old age and sickness. Picus, therefore, who is also Jupiter, reigned in the West, or in Italy, for a total of sixty-two years. Truly, after Belus, Ninus commanded Assyria; he was another son of Saturn, and he took his mother Semiramis as his wife. From this, it was granted by law to the Persians that it was permitted to take mothers and sisters as spouses, since Picus had likewise joined his sister Juno to himself in marriage. Just as the most learned Homer says, he addressed Juno as both sister and wife. After Saturn was deceased, Ninus gained power over the kingdom of Assyria, and having built the city of Nineveh, he was the first to rule the Assyrians there, together with Semiramis (or Rhea), his mother and also his wife.

From that lineage, therefore, was born Zoroaster, the celebrated astronomer among the Persians. Being near death, he prayed that he might be consumed by celestial fire, addressing the Persians thus: *“When the fire has burned me, take the ashes from my burned bones and keep them; for the kingdom shall not be taken away from your region so long as you preserve my bones.”* Then, having called upon Orion, he was consumed by fire from the air. The Persians, having followed what he commanded, preserve his remains, reduced to ashes, even to this day.

After Ninus, a man named Thurras reigned over the Assyrians. His father Zames, who was the brother of Rhea, renamed him Ares after the name of the wandering star <note>original: "Ἄρεα εἰς ὄνομα τοῦ πλάνητος ἀστέρος"; referring to the planet Mars</note>. This man became a fierce warrior who campaigned in the northern regions. He attacked <margin>P 38</margin> a certain Caucasus, a powerful man of giant-born lineage and <margin>5</margin> warlike nature, who was descended from the tribe of Japheth, the son of Noah. Having fought Caucasus, Thurras killed him and took over his land. Then, coming into Thrace, he died and was buried there. It was to this Ares that the Assyrians first raised a pillar <note>or "statue"</note> and worshipped him as a god; even until now, they call the god "Baal" in the Persian tongue <margin>10</margin>, which is translated as Ares, the God of War. This is the figure mentioned in the prophetic writing of Daniel and the Three Youths <note>The "three children" in the fiery furnace</note>, where it says they were being forced to worship him. And after the death of Ares, Lames reigned. After Lames, <margin>B</margin> Sardanapalus the Great reigned over the Assyrians <margin>15</margin>, whom Perseus, the son of Danae, killed. Perseus took the kingdom away from the Assyrians, and after becoming their king, he called them "Persians" after his own name. These things were recorded by Semeronius the Babylonian Persian. Meanwhile, the brother of Ninus, Picus (who is also called Zeus), remained as the king of Italy <margin>20</margin>.

At those same times, there was neither a city nor any form of organized administration...

After Ninus, one called Thurras reigned in Assyria, to whom his father Zames (the brother of Rhea) gave the surname of Mars <note>the Roman name for Ares</note> after the name of the wandering star. This man was a most sharp warrior, who, having undertaken an expedition toward the regions of the North, attacked Caucasus—who was himself of the tribe or lineage of Japheth, son of Noah. Having killed him in war, Thurras invaded his kingdom and, advancing into Thrace, he lies there deceased. Indeed, it was to this Mars that the Assyrians first erected a statue, and from then on he was worshipped as a god; even to these times they call him the god Baal in the Persian language, which in Greek has the same value as Mars, the God of Wars. Daniel mentions him in the book of Prophecies, when he says the three youths were forced to adore him. After the passing of Mars, Lames reigned; after Lames, the great Sardanapalus commanded the Assyrians, whom Perseus the son of Danae killed. Having taken the kingdom from the Assyrians and being established as King of the Assyrians, Perseus called them Persians after his own name, just as Semeronius the Persian recorded in writing. Truly, the brother of Ninus, Picus (who is also Jupiter), held the kingdom of Italy.

In these times, there was no city, and no province in the West...

...in the west; rather, all that land was simply inhabited by those who had migrated there from the tribe of Japheth, the son of Noah.

Picus, who is also called Zeus <note>original: "Πῖκος ὁ καὶ Ζεὺς"; the text identifies the Roman figure Picus with the Greek king of the gods</note>, lived one hundred and twenty years, holding power over the West <margin>V 32</margin> and reigning as its king. He had many sons and daughters by beautiful women. <margin>C</margin> This same Picus (also known as Zeus) had a son named Faunus, whom he also called Hermes <margin>R 90</margin> after the name of the wandering star <note>The planet Mercury; ancient chronicles often claimed gods were named after planets or vice-versa</note>. This same Picus, or Zeus, also had Hercules after Hermes; and after him, another son, Perseus, born from a beautiful woman named Danae. She was the daughter of Acrisius, who was descended from the land of the Argives <note>Argos in Greece</note>. Regarding her, the most wise Euripides wrote a mythological account in the composition of his play <note>Euripides' lost tragedy *Danae*</note>, saying that Danae was cast into a chest and thrown into the sea, because she had been seduced by Zeus when he transformed himself into gold.

However, the most wise Brutius <note>A historical writer often cited by Byzantine chroniclers for "realistic" versions of myths</note>, the historian and chronographer, explained that while this woman was in a bedchamber <margin>D</margin> situated near the sea, the same Picus (Zeus) persuaded her with a great deal of gold and was able to entice her to come out. Having snatched her because she was so beautiful, he seduced her, and from her he had the aforementioned son named Perseus. They depict Perseus as winged because from childhood the boy was exceptionally swift and energetic. For this reason, his father Picus (Zeus) taught him how to practice and perform the magic of the loathsome bowl <note>original: "μυσαροῦ σκύφου"; possibly referring to a vessel used in scrying or ritual magic</note>, teaching him all the mystical and impious delusions concerning it, saying—

...in the West, but that land was simply inhabited by those who had migrated there from the tribe of Japheth, the son of Noah.
Picus, who was also called Jupiter, lived 120 years. When he had commanded the West and Italy, many children of both sexes were born to him from women of outstanding beauty. To this same Picus, or Jupiter, was born a son, Faunus, whom he named Mercury after the name of the wandering star. Furthermore, the same Picus, or Jupiter, had Hercules after Mercury; and after him another son, Perseus, from a woman of elegant form named Danae, the sister <note>The Greek text says "daughter"</note> of Acrisius who originated from the region of the Argives. The most learned Euripides created a fiction about her in the tragedy he inscribed with her name, saying she was shut in a certain chest and then cast into the sea, because she had been corrupted by Jupiter transformed into gold. But the most learned Brutius, the Historian and Chronographer, relates that Danae, when she was enclosed in a bedchamber that looked out over the sea, was persuaded by Picus (Jupiter) with much gold to be led out from there. He snatched her away as she was most outstanding in beauty and corrupted her, and from her procreated a son named Perseus, whom we have mentioned. Indeed, they commonly depict him as winged because from a boy he was of a sharp and versatile character. Wherefore his father Picus, or Jupiter, instructed him in the magic arts of the detestable shield <note>The Latin translates "skyphos" (bowl) as "clypeus" (shield), likely identifying it with the famous shield Perseus used to fight Medusa</note>, and taught him all its secrets and impious mysteries and deceits, speaking these things to him:

Now, Cepheus was unable to see due to old age. <margin>V 34</margin> When Perseus heard that Cepheus was making war against him, he became very angry and went out against him <margin>P 41</margin> carrying the head <note>The head of the Gorgon Medusa, which turned onlookers to stone</note>, and he displayed it to him. But Cepheus, being unable to see, continued to charge at him on horseback. Perseus, not realizing that Cepheus could not see, thought that the head of the Gorgon which he held was no longer effective; so he turned it toward himself and looked at it. He was blinded, remained as if dead, and was slain. Then Meros, the son of Perseus and Andromeda, became king of the Persians.

...a globe of lightning fire fell from heaven, which immediately calmed the storm and restrained the overflowing waves of the river. <meta>This page continues the narrative of Hercules the Philosopher’s discovery of purple dye. Having observed a dog’s mouth stained by a murex shell, Hercules realizes the potential of the substance for textile production. This page describes the presentation of the first dyed wool to the King of Tyre and the subsequent invention of royal regalia.</meta>

# PASCHALE

Having taken the fleece from the shepherd, he brought it as a great gift to Phoenix, the King of Tyre. The king himself was also struck with amazement at the sight of the strange hue of the dye. Marvelling at the discovery, he ordered that wool be dyed with the liquid of that same murex <note>original: *konchylēs*. A sea snail from which the famous "Tyrian Purple" was extracted.</note> and that a royal robe be made for him from it. <margin>P 44</margin> He was the first to wear a garment of purple, and everyone marveled at this royal clothing as a strange and wondrous sight.

From that time on, King Phoenix ordered that no one living under his rule should dare to wear this same excellent garment—derived from both land and sea—except for himself and the kings of Phoenicia who would come after him. This was so that the king might be clearly recognized by the army and the entire populace by his marvelous and extraordinary clothing. Previously, people did not know how to dye the colors of garments; instead, they made and wore clothes from sheep’s wool exactly as it was. Even kings wore clothes made of the same colors <margin>B</margin> of ordinary wool, and thus the kings were not easily distinguished from the common people they ruled.

Consequently, the local kings—that is, the <term>regents</term> <note>original: *rhēges*. A Greek transliteration of the Latin *reges*, meaning kings or petty rulers.</note> and <term>toparchs</term> <note>A governor of a specific district or "topos."</note>—having heard of this, devised for themselves purple or reddish robes, some using golden <term>fibulae</term> <note>original: *phiblas*. Ornamental brooches or pins used to fasten garments.</note> and mantles, dyeing them with extracts from herbs. They wore these so that they might be recognized by their own people, just as the most wise Palaephatus <note>An ancient Greek author known for explaining the "true" historical origins behind myths.</note> has set forth.

### Concerning the body of Picus.

<margin>C</margin>At the time when Picus, also known as Zeus, passed away, he commanded that his remains be buried on the island of Crete. His children built a temple for him and placed him there, on the island of Crete, in a tomb. This is an accusative form of Zeus used as a name, often associated with the "shining sky."</note> Regarding him, Diodorus, the most learned chronographer, wrote in the exposition of his treatise *On the Gods*, stating that Zeus, the son of Cronus, lies buried in Crete. <margin>10</margin>

### 104 Concerning Faunus, King of Italy, who first discovered gold.

<margin>D</margin>After the death of the same Picus, also known as Zeus, his son Faunus, also called Hermes, reigned over Italy for thirty-five years. He was a man of great cunning and a <term>mathematician</term> <note>original: *mathēmatikos*. In late antiquity, this term referred to someone skilled in astrology, astronomy, and the secret properties of numbers and nature.</note>, who was the first to <margin>15</margin> discover the ore of gold in the West and the art of smelting it. #### Concerning the body of Picus.

When Picus, or Jupiter, was about to die, he ordered his body to be buried on the island of Crete. There, in a temple established in his name by his sons, he lies deposited; his sepulcher is visited there even unto this time, with this very inscription:

> Here lies dead Picus, who is also Jupiter, whom they also call Jove.

Concerning him, Diodorus the most learned Chronographer wrote, who in the context of his book *On the Gods*, says these things: *Jupiter, the son of Saturn, lies in Crete.*

#### Concerning Faunus, King of Italy, who first discovered gold.

Upon the death of the same Picus, who was also called Jupiter, his son Faunus, who was also named Mercury, reigned in Italy for 35 years. He was a clever man and a mathematician, who first discovered gold ore in the West, and the method of its smelting. When he understood that he was burning with the great envy of his brothers—whom Picus, or Jupiter, his father, had fathered by various wives—and that they had entered into a plan to kill him, as they were not few, but approximately 70. (For Jupiter, having held intimacy with many women, had procreated many children.) <margin>C</margin> Hephaestus established a law that Egyptian women should be devoted to only one husband and live chastely, and that those found in adultery should be punished. The Egyptians were grateful to him, for this was the first law of chastity <note>original: *sophrosynē*, a term meaning temperance, self-control, or moral sanity</note> they had received.

### Concerning iron: who first discovered it.

<margin>R 106</margin> This same Hephaestus, through a certain mystic prayer, received the <margin>5</margin> tongs <note>original: *oxylabē*, literally "sharp-taker," used for handling hot iron</note> from the air in order to manufacture weapons from iron. <margin>D</margin> sustenance for men through the manufacture of tools <note>The text suggests iron tools improved both warfare and agriculture</note> and had provided power and safety in wars. ### *Concerning iron, and who first discovered it.*

<margin>1</margin> A certain Egyptian woman, among those of wealth and high status <margin>v 38</margin> in that land, fell in love with a man and committed adultery with him. When Helios <note>original: *ho Hēlios*; here treated as a mortal king</note> heard of this, he sought to seize her in accordance with the legislation of his father Hephaestus <note>referring to the law of chastity mentioned on the previous page</note>, so that it might not be abolished. Taking soldiers from his own <margin>5</margin> army and learning the time of her adultery—that it was to take place at night—he burst in upon her while her husband was away. He found her sleeping with the other man, her lover. <margin>B</margin> He immediately led her away and paraded her through the whole land of Egypt as a punishment. Consequently, a great sense of moral restraint <note>original: *sophrosynē*, meaning chastity or self-control</note> <margin>10</margin> arose in the land of Egypt. He also put that adulterer to death, for which he was held in high regard. The poet Homer records this history poetically, saying that Helios <note>the Sun</note> exposed Aphrodite <note>Venus</note> while she was having relations with Ares <note>Mars</note> at night. However, he called the "desire for fornication" <term>Aphrodite</term>, which was exposed by King Helios. The truth of the matter, as written <margin>15</margin> above, was recorded by the most wise Palaephatus <note>An ancient Greek author known for providing rational, historical explanations for mythical stories</note>.

After the death of King Helios, the son of Hephaestus, Sosis reigned over the Egyptians. After his reign, <margin>C</margin> Osiris reigned; after Osiris, Horus reigned; and after Horus, Thulis reigned. Thulis, with a certain <margin>R 108</margin> <margin>19</margin> military force, took possession of all the land as far as the Ocean. ...the Egyptians excelled, who, captured by the love of a certain man, practiced a wicked custom with him. Having immediately seized her and led her through all of Egypt, he punished her severely. From this, chastity was strictly observed among the Egyptians thereafter, and the adulterer was punished with death, for which he gained favor from his subjects. The poet Homer tells this in a poetic manner when he says that Venus <note>Aphrodite</note>, lying at night with Mars <note>Ares</note>, was caught by the Sun <note>Helios</note>. He called the "lust for adultery" Venus, which King Helios exposed. Furthermore, the truth of this history, just as it was related above, was described by the most learned Palaephatus.

After the passing of King Helios, son of Vulcan, Sosis reigned among the Egyptians, succeeded by Osiris; Osiris by Horus; and Horus by Thulis, who with some troops occupied the entire earth as far as the Ocean. While he was returning, he came into the regions of Africa with a procession to consult the oracle; and having performed a sacrifice, he questioned it thus: "Tell me, O fire-powerful, truth-telling, blessed one..."

"Hellenism" <term>Hellenismos: In early Christian historiography, this refers specifically to the era of pagan polytheism, categorized as a "way of life" that followed "Scythism."</term> began from the times of Serug <note>A biblical ancestor of Abraham (Genesis 11:20). Early Christian writers often attributed the invention of coins and the start of idolatry to his era.</note> through the practice of idolatry. As people at that time followed their own particular superstitions, the various races of humanity began to organize themselves into more political structures, establishing customs and laws regarding idols. Those who followed these ways at that time began by using colors to paint and depict <margin>10</margin> those who had been honored among them in the past—either tyrants, or leaders, or those who had done something in life deemed worthy of memory <margin>C</margin> due to their prowess or physical strength. 

Afterward, from the times of Terah, the father of Abraham, they also established the error of idolatry through statues. They honored their own ancestors <margin>15</margin> with likenesses, and for those who had died before them, they first devised a method of crafting likenesses using the art of pottery <note>original: "keramikes epistémes." The text suggests that the first idols were made of clay before more expensive materials were used.</note>. Later, every other craft imitated this: masons carved stone against stone, <margin>V 40</margin> while silversmiths and goldsmiths worked with their respective materials to craft these images. <margin>20</margin> Bronze-casters and engravers used their skills to decorate them, as did carpenters and all subsequent trades. <margin>D</margin>

The era of Greek paganism began in the time of Serug by means of idolatry, when each person was led by their own particular superstition. The human race began to shape itself toward a more political way of living, adopting customs and the worship of idols. Following these practices, they used paintings to portray leaders, tyrants, or commanders—anyone who seemed to have done something worthy of memory in their age, whether through military combat or physical strength. Later, in the times of Terah, who had Abraham as a son, they propagated the error of idolatry even through statues and images. While they honored their ancestors through these likenesses, they first expressed those who had met their fate through the craft of the potter. Soon, other artisans followed the first: architects and masons cut stone, while silversmiths and goldsmiths fabricated images from their own materials. Bronze-workers and sculptors varied the work of the craft according to their own talents; finally, carpenters and other craftsmen followed in turn.

<summary>This page outlines the biblical chronology from Nahor to Terah and explains the historical origin of idolatry, tracing its evolution from commemorative paintings of leaders to carved statues of ancestors.</summary>

# CHRONICLE

The Egyptians, Babylonians, Phrygians, and Phoenicians were the first to introduce this form of worship, as well as the creation of statues and the rites of the mysteries. Most of these traditions were transferred to the Greeks starting from the time of Cecrops <note>A mythical king of Athens, often depicted as half-man and half-serpent, who was believed to have introduced the first elements of civilization like marriage and writing.</note>. Later on, in successive generations, many people proclaimed Saturn, Rhea, Zeus, Apollo, and the rulers who followed them to be gods.

The Greeks <note>original: *Hellenes*</note> take their name from a certain man named Hellen, one of those who inhabited Greece. Others, however, say they were named after the olive tree <note>original: *elaia*</note> that sprouted in Athens.

<margin>P 49 R 114</margin> The Ionians were the leaders of these people, as the accurate account holds, descending from Javan <note>original: *Iouan*</note>, one of the men who built the Tower when the languages of humanity were divided. For this reason, all people were called *meropes* <note>An ancient poetic term for humans; the author here connects it to the Greek word *merizo*, meaning "to divide," referring to the "divided voices" at the Tower of Babel.</note> because of their divided speech.

->*Scholium*<-

"Scythism" <term>Scythismos: In early Christian world-histories, this term describes the era from the Flood to the Tower of Babel, characterized by a nomadic, lawless, but not yet idolatrous way of life.</term> persisted from the days of Noah after the flood until the building of the Tower and Babylon, and for a few years after the time of the Tower's construction—that is, until the time of Reu <note>A biblical patriarch, the son of Peleg (Genesis 11:18).</note>. Those who turned toward the regions of Europe in the direction of Scythia <margin>B</margin> were categorized by their own customs from the time of Reu and beyond; from these people, the Thracians arose. Later, "Hellenism" <term>Hellenismos: In this context, the era of paganism and polytheistic philosophy that followed the "Scythian" era.</term> was divided into sects in later times—namely, the Pythagoreans, Stoics, and Platonists...

<summary>This page discusses the origins of ancient religions and the naming of ethnic groups like the Greeks and Ionians, linking them to the biblical event of the Tower of Babel. It defines the historical periods of "Scythism" and "Hellenism" as stages in the development of human culture and religious error.</summary>

<margin>P 56</margin> Having left behind his fatherland, kin, and nation, and having believed in God and being justified <note>original: δικαιωθείς; This refers to the theological concept of being declared righteous by God through faith rather than by works.</note>, he therefore also received the promises of God which God made to him. He <note>God</note> established tens of thousands from a body as good as dead and a deadened womb <note>referring to the advanced age of Abraham and Sarah at the time of Isaac's birth</note>; He produced the blessed fruit for the world as if from a root, through whom the world is blessed and recreated. ### PASCHAL CHRONICLE

...in whose place a sheep was slaughtered. And the father heard from God: "You did not spare your beloved son." Thus it is also said regarding Christ, the Son of God, who certainly did not spare his own son, but handed him over for us all. <note>original Greek: οὐκ ἐφείσατο; see Romans 8:32</note> <margin>D</margin>
<margin>5</margin>And it is the flesh alone that is given for the life of the world, since it is impossible for the Divinity to die. Because the flesh was given, the Scripture says that the "own son" has been given—the flesh being an exchange and a <term>representation</term> <note>original: ἀντίδειξιν (antideixin); a showing-forth or substitute representation</note> of the Son, according to the type of the blessed Isaac. For so the Lord said that *Abraham rejoiced to see <margin>10</margin> my day, and he saw it and was glad.* <note>John 8:56</note> This is the same Isaac who unintentionally handed over the blessing—promised to him and to his father by God—to Jacob, saying: "*Let nations serve you and let rulers bow down to you. And become lord over your brother; and your father’s sons shall bow down to <margin>15</margin> you.*" <note>Genesis 27:27–29</note> The one who curses you is cursed; and the one who blesses you is <margin>P 58</margin> blessed. But we do not see all these things happening in the case of Jacob; rather, he himself, falling seven times to the ground, bowed down before Esau. And thirty kings reigned from the line of Esau before a king ever reigned in Israel, so that the blessings point forward to the <margin>20</margin> expected Lord Christ who comes from them, <margin>R 136</margin> toward whom the entire aim of the Holy Scripture is directed.

...nor did he suffer death, and was called back to life by God: in whose place a sheep was killed. And his father heard from God: *Because you did not spare your beloved son.* So also it was said of Christ the Son of God: *Who did not spare his own son, but handed him over for us all.* And indeed the flesh alone is that which was given for the life of the world, since it cannot happen that Divinity should die. Therefore, with the flesh having been offered, the Scripture says the own son was given, so that that victim might be an exchange, and a model of the son, according to the figure of the blessed Isaac: for so the Lord said: *Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; he saw it and was glad.* This is Isaac who, against his will, handed over the blessing promised by God to himself and his father to Jacob, saying: *Let nations serve you, and let princes adore you, and may you become the Lord of your brother, and let the sons of your father adore you. He who shall curse you, let him be cursed himself, and he who shall bless you, let him also be blessed.* We do not see all these things fulfilled in Jacob: rather, he himself, falling down seven times to the ground, adored Esau. And 30 kings reigned from Esau before anyone from Israel reigned, so that those blessings are transmitted to the expected Lord Christ from them, toward whom every aim of sacred Scripture is directed.

### C H R O N I C O N

This Jacob, himself a co-heir of the promises of God, also waited for the city that has foundations, whose architect and builder is God <note>This is a direct reference to Hebrews 11:10, connecting the Old Testament Patriarchs to New Testament theology.</note>—that is, the heavenly Jerusalem, where Christ entered as a forerunner on our behalf. <margin>5</margin> All Christian worship looks toward this state, which our Master Christ first renewed for us as a new and living way. The great Jacob also foretold this when he passed the blessing to his own son, Judah, and blessed him—the one from whom the Lord of the promises, Jesus Christ, was to appear—speaking as <margin>C</margin> <margin>10</margin> follows: *Judah, your brothers shall praise you; your hands shall be on the back of your enemies. Let the sons of your father bow down to you. Judah is a lion’s cub. From the sprout, my son, you have come up. Reclining, you slept as a lion and as a cub; who shall rouse him? A ruler shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, <margin>15</margin> until the things laid up for him come; and he is the expectation of the nations. Binding his foal to a vine, and the foal of his donkey to the branch. He shall wash his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape. His eyes are more cheerful than wine, and his teeth are whiter than milk.* <note>This is the famous "Blessing of Jacob" from Genesis 49:8–12, traditionally interpreted by early Christians as a prophecy of the Messiah.</note>
<margin>D</margin> <margin>20</margin> And yet, his father’s sons did not bow down to him <note>The author points out a historical discrepancy: the literal Judah did not receive this homage from his brothers.</note>; on the contrary, he himself bowed down to Joseph, even after the death of their father. It is therefore clear that this entire prophecy found its fulfillment in the Master Christ, who was born from him according to the flesh...

This Jacob, also a co-heir of the promises of God, himself expecting the city having foundations, whose founder and architect is God—that is, of that heavenly Jerusalem, into which Christ the precursor entered for us. All Christian religion looks back to this constitution, to which indeed the Lord Christ first gave the beginning of a new and living way: which also the great Jacob foretold, while he commends this to his son Judah, and imparts a blessing to him, from whom the promised Lord Jesus Christ appeared, speaking thus: *Judah, your brothers shall praise you: your hands upon the back of your enemies: the sons of your father shall adore you. A prince shall not fail from Judah, nor a leader from his thighs, until the things stored up for him come, and he is the expectation of the nations.
