# THE PASCHAL CHRONICLE

<margin>P 64</margin> Furthermore, because King **Chenebron**, the ruler of the regions beyond **Memphis**, was plotting against **Moses** out of envy, and because **Merrina**—his wife, who had taken Moses from the river and adopted him as her own son—had died and been buried in the regions of Upper Egypt, Moses founded the city of **Hermopolis**. He arranged for it to be named **Merrin** in her honor. <note>original Greek: "Μεῤῥὶν κληθῆναι παρεσκεύασεν." The historian Artapanus is the likely source for this tradition, which links Moses to the foundation of Egyptian cultural centers.</note>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Later, when Moses learned of the plot by Chenebron, he killed **Chanethothes**, the Egyptian who was intended to kill him, <note>In the biblical account (Exodus 2:12), the Egyptian is unnamed. Here, the chronicle provides a specific name, Chanethothes, following extra-biblical traditions.</note> and thus he fled into **Arabia** to **Raguel**, the ruler of those regions. He then took **Sepphora**, the daughter of Raguel, in marriage. **Artapanus** records these events. <margin>B</margin> **Eupolemus**, however, says that Moses was the first wise man and was the first to hand down the art of writing to the Jews; <margin>R 150</margin> the **Phoenicians** then received it from the **Jews**, and the **Greeks** from the Phoenicians. He also states that Moses was the first to write laws for the Jews. <note>This reflects a common theme in Hellenistic Jewish literature: "cultural primacy," the idea that the foundations of Greek and Phoenician civilization were actually derived from Hebrew wisdom.</note>

<margin>15</margin> From **Abraham** and **Keturah** was born **Jezan**; from Jezan was born **Dadan**; from Dadan was born **Raguel**; from Raguel were born **Jothor** <note>Jothor is the Greek form of the biblical Jethro.</note> and **Jacob**; and from Jothor was born **Sepphora**, whom Moses married. Therefore, Moses is counted as the seventh generation from Abraham, while Sepphora is counted as the sixth.

<margin>20 C</margin> <margin>20</margin> 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 37, 38, 39, 40 <note>These numbers represent the passing years of Moses' life, concluding here at age 40, the traditional age of his flight from Egypt.</note>

## The Ten Plagues

Three were brought through Aaron with the staff: blood, frogs, and gnats. <note>original: σκνίψ (sknips) — refers to tiny, biting insects like lice or mosquitoes.</note>
And three were brought by God Himself: dog-flies, death <note>Refers to the pestilence that killed the Egyptian livestock.</note>, and boils.
And one was brought through the hand of Moses, with Aaron assisting him.
<margin>10</margin> And another three were brought through Moses alone: one through the staff, and one through his hand—these were hail, locusts, and darkness.
<margin>B</margin> And one, the death of the firstborn, was brought by God Himself.

In this year 3838 <note>original: ,γωλη' — This is the Greek numeral for 3838. In the Byzantine calendar used by this chronicler, this date represents the year of the world (Annus Mundi) in which the Exodus occurred.</note> from the creation of the world, beginning from the 21st of the month of March, and being the second year of the Exodus, the Lord spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying: "This month is the beginning of months; it is the first for you among the months of the year. Speak to the entire congregation of the children of Israel, saying: 'On the tenth of this month, let each man take a sheep <note>The Greek "πρόβατον" (probaton) can mean sheep or goat, though traditionally translated as lamb.</note> according to the houses of their fathers, a sheep for each household. But if those in the household are too few to be sufficient for a sheep, he shall take with him his neighbor...'"

<note>The Latin text at the bottom of the page provides a parallel translation of the Greek text above: "For other animals command as if in other camps, when they are sent by a single command in an orderly fashion to the destruction of the enemies. IX. Darkness. X. Death of the firstborn, because they were insolent in their hope of a longer life, and equally in power and glory. **The Ten Plagues.** Three through Aaron's staff: Blood, frog, gnat. Three God through Himself: Dog-fly, [death], boils. And one through the hand of Moses, with Aaron helping him. And another three through Moses alone: one through the staff, one through his hand: hail, locust, darkness. One God through Himself: the slaughter of the firstborn. In this year from the founding of the world 3838, which takes its beginning from the 21st of the month of March, and is the second of the Exodus, the Lord said to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt: This month is the beginning of months, it is first for you in the months of the year. Speak to the whole congregation of the sons of Israel, saying: On the tenth of this month, let everyone take a lamb by the houses of their families, a lamb by the house. If however there are few in the house, so that they are not sufficient for a lamb, he shall take with him his nearest neighbor..."</note>

### CHRONICLE

...April 9th, they become 70. Subtract 60, and 10 remain. And <margin>R 178</margin> it is clear that the 10th of the first month—on which the first Passover <note>original: πάσχα (pascha)</note> was celebrated in Egypt, and the sons of Israel were commanded to take the lamb and keep it—fell on the 9th of the month of April. But why did we divide 3,838, and not rather subtract one and divide 3,837? Because in the year 3,838 from the creation of the world, Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh; and from the 21st of that same month of March, the 3,839th year of the world began. And reasonably <margin>D</margin> we divide 3,838 by 19 <note>The number 19 refers to the Metonic cycle, a period of 19 years used to synchronize the lunar and solar calendars to determine feast dates.</note>.

Then, wishing to know also when the 14th <note>The 14th day of the lunar month (Nisan 14) is the traditional day for the Passover sacrifice.</note> occurred, on which the Passover was celebrated: we set down the 30 <term>epacts</term> <note>An epact is the age of the moon in days on a specific date, used here as a foundation for the 19-year cycle.</note> of the natural 19-year cycle, and the 13 before the <term>luminaries</term> <note>original: φωστήρων (phosteron). In chronological texts, this often refers to specific markers or intervals related to the sun and moon.</note>, plus 7 pre-lunar days, and the 11 days from the 21st of March, and the 13th of April; they become 74. Subtract 60, and 14 remain. And so we know that the 14th of the moon in the present year fell on the 13th of the month of April.

Then, wishing to know also what day of the week it was when the first Passover occurred in Egypt, we set down the 3,838 years. <margin>P 76</margin> To these we add the fourth part <note>Adding a "fourth part" (one day for every four years) accounts for leap years in the Julian calendar system.</note>, which makes 4,797. Divide by 7; 600 times 7 is 4,200. 80 times 7 is 560. 5 times 7 is 35. 2 remains. To these add the 3 before the luminaries, which makes 5, and the 11 from the 21st of March, which makes 16. Add also the 13th of April, which makes 29. Divide these by 7; 4 times 7 is 28. There remains—

### Concerning Moses.

<margin>D</margin> This is the great Moses, the performer of miraculous signs and wonders, the <term>cosmographer</term> <note>One who describes or maps the order of the universe; here it refers to Moses writing the account of Creation in Genesis.</note> of creation, who was honored with the <margin>5</margin> shadows of our true shepherd, Christ, and was glorified in his face by God. By his words and his deeds, he foretold the <term>dispensation</term> <note>The divine plan or arrangement of events in salvation history.</note> of the Lord Christ. Through his deeds, he redeemed Israel from the slavery of the Egyptians, instituting the Passover and the pouring out of the blood. By the crossing of the sea, <margin>10</margin> he foretold <term>baptism</term> through the cloud. By the giving of the Law and the journey through the desert, he prefigured the Holy Spirit and the Church. By setting the bronze serpent on high, <margin>P 77</margin> he proclaimed in advance the suffering of the Lord Christ upon the cross. By passing on the entry into the Promised Land through <term>Jesus</term> <note>original: Ἰησοῦ (Iesou). This refers to Joshua son of Nun. In Greek and Latin, the names Joshua and Jesus are identical; the author uses this to show Joshua as a "type" or precursor to Jesus Christ.</note>, he pre-sketched the <margin>15</margin> dwelling place in the heavens. His role as a supernatural mediator is recorded through many miracles. What more needs to be said concerning the <term>Tabernacle</term>, which is a likeness of the entire world, in which he also placed the <term>mercy seat</term> <note>original: ἱλαστήριον (hilasterion). The gold cover of the Ark of the Covenant where God’s presence rested.</note>, occupying the place of the Lord Christ? ### Concerning Moses.

This is that great Moses, the worker of wonderful signs and miracles, who described the creation of the world: who earned the right to foreshadow Christ our true Pastor and to see God: who by words and deeds announced in advance the dispensation of Christ. And indeed by his deeds, as one who liberated the Israelites from the servitude of the Egyptians, he instituted the Passover and the shedding of blood: he expressed baptism through the event of the crossing of the sea: by the cloud foretelling the promulgation of the law and the life in the desert, he designated the form of the Holy Spirit and the Church: through the bronze serpent raised on high, he predicted the passion of Christ the Lord through the cross: by sending ahead the entrance into the land of the Promise through Jesus the son of Nave <note>original: Jesus filium Nave. "Nave" is the Latin form of the Hebrew "Nun." This refers to Joshua.</note>, he described the celestial domicile: whose status as a supernatural Mediator was described through many miracles. Furthermore, what pertains to saying anything of the Tabernacle, which stood as a figure of the whole world, in which he also placed the mercy seat, which obtained the place of Christ the Lord? Truly, lest the sermon [be longer]...

<note>Moses, Christ, Israel, Egypt, Passover, Baptism, Tabernacle, Joshua, Chronicle</note>

<summary>This page presents a theological eulogy of Moses, framing his life and the Exodus as "types" or prophetic symbols that prefigure the life of Christ and the Christian Church. It emphasizes how events like the crossing of the Red Sea and the bronze serpent were symbolic precursors to Baptism and the Crucifixion.</summary>
<keywords>Moses, typology, Jesus Christ, Joshua son of Nun, Passover, Tabernacle, Exodus, Christian symbolism, Bronze Serpent</keywords>

# THE PASCHAL CHRONICLE

...let us come to his prophecy which he delivered through words. He speaks, therefore, as follows:

"The Lord God will raise up for you a **Prophet** from among your brothers <margin>B</margin> just like me. You shall listen to him in everything he says to you. And it shall be, that every soul who does not listen to that prophet shall be **utterly destroyed** from among her people." <note>This is a quotation from Deuteronomy 18:15–19, a passage traditionally viewed by early Christians as a direct prediction of Jesus Christ.</note>

And again, Moses himself writes, as if it were spoken by **Balaam**: <note>The Latin text on this page mistakenly names Abraham here, but the Greek text correctly identifies the speaker as the seer Balaam from the Book of Numbers.</note>

"A **star** shall rise out of Jacob, and a **man** shall rise out of Israel, and he shall crush the princes of Moab and subdue all the sons of Seth." <margin>R 182</margin>

Now, the "sons of Seth" refers to the **entire world**; and this prophecy does not fit anyone except the Lord Christ. For the name **Seth** is interpreted as "foundation." <note>original: θεμέλιος (themelios). The author uses a popular ancient etymology to link Seth to the word for a foundation stone.</note> Since Cain and his whole lineage perished in the Flood, and Abel died younger without children, Seth was born after them <margin>C</margin> and from him both Noah and the entire world are descended, making him a kind of **foundation for all humanity**. For this cause, Adam, being inspired by God, named him Seth to signify the whole world. This prophecy fits Christ and Him alone, toward whom all Holy Scripture looks.

->**Joshua son of Nun** <note>original: Ἰησοῦς Ναυῆ (Iesous Naue). In Greek, the names "Joshua" and "Jesus" are identical. Early Christian writers frequently highlighted Joshua as a "type" or shadow of Jesus Christ.</note>, 27 years; total 3884 years.<- <margin>V 63</margin>

->Year 1, 2, 3, 4, 5.<-

->**Eleazar**, the son of Aaron, was High Priest.<-

# PASCHALE <note>The Paschal Chronicle, a 7th-century Byzantine universal chronicle.</note>

...a complete victory over the foreigners <note>Original: *allophylon*, the standard term in this text for the Philistines.</note> was achieved; for which reason he also named the city Jerusalem, as it was built on a high mountain. Now, "mountain" in the Hebrew language is called **Jebus**, and in the Greek language, **Salem** means "peace." <note>The author provides a creative etymology: Jerusalem as "Mountain of Peace." Historically, Jebus was the name of the Canaanite city prior to David's conquest.</note>

# CHRONICLE

Absalom, the son of David, behaving insolently toward his own father <note>original: *emparoinōn*, meaning to act with drunken-like violence or rebellion</note>, was riding upon a beast of burden while in flight. As he passed through a large, leafy tree, he became entangled by the hair of his head in the branches and was left hanging. When this happened, one would not be wrong to consider it the fulfillment of what was spoken by Moses regarding such a person: "Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree." <note>Deuteronomy 21:23. The author views the manner of Absalom's death as a divine judgment.</note> Moses also prophesied concerning the Savior <margin>C</margin> <note>The Greek text uses "Savior" while the Latin parallel uses "Christ."</note>, saying: "You shall see your life hanging before your eyes night and day, and you shall not believe in your life." <note>Deuteronomy 28:66. In early Christian tradition, this verse was interpreted as a prophecy of Christ (the "Life") hanging on the Cross.</note>

## How the Psalter was composed.

After Moses and his successor Joshua the son of Nun <note>original: *Iēsoun ton tou Nauē*</note>, and after the judges who appeared in Israel, the kingdom was eventually taken up by Saul. After he was rejected, God raised up for them a virtuous and righteous king and prophet <note>David</note>, who <margin>D R 202</margin> composed the book of 150 Psalms. He was moved by the Holy Spirit to write in meter according to the specific measure of the Hebrew language, and he sang them melodiously with rhythm, various musical instruments, dances, and songs; for he himself played the kithara <note>A stringed instrument like a lyre or harp.</note>. He also had various choirs under him composed of "minor prophets"; for so they called those who... <note>The text continues on the next page to describe the guilds of singers and prophets who assisted David.</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins of the Book of Psalms, specifically describing the musical arrangement, the various choirs, and the technical meaning of musical terms like "diapsalma."</meta>

### EASTER CHRONICLE

...remaining with the prophets, and they often called them "sons of the prophets" <note>In the biblical context, "sons of the prophets" refers to disciples or members of a prophetic guild.</note> <margin>2.</margin>; they held various instruments, one having cymbals, another flutes, another drums, another trumpets, another the psaltery and the kithara <note>The kithara was a professional version of the lyre, used in formal performances.</note>, and others were the singers known as vocalists <note>original: *vokalious* / *Vocales*</note> <margin>P 86</margin>.

Each chorus had a leader: one was called Asaph, another Idithum <note>Commonly known as Jeduthun in English Bibles.</note>, others were the sons of Korah, another was Ethan the Israelite, and another was Moses, the man of God. Whenever, therefore, David was moved by the Spirit <note>Some manuscripts and the Latin parallel specify "the Holy Spirit."</note> to prophesy anything—whether regarding the captivity of the people, their return, moral teachings, divine providence, or concerning Christ the Master—he would compose the psalm in meter, with each psalm focused on a single theme. This is the reason why there are both long and short psalms. He would then hand it over to a specific chorus, as he judged best or as was fitting for the delivery, and he would first sing it within <margin>B</margin> that chorus. 

If, however, he decided in the middle of the psalm to hand the remainder over to another chorus, then this succession of rhythm was called a *diapsalma* <note>original: *diapsalma*; this term is usually translated as "Selah" in modern Bibles. The author here explains it as a technical instruction for alternating choirs.</note>. Thus, whenever he wished to hand over the middle of a psalm to those called the singers or "vocalists," it was then called an "ode of the diapsalma," because the singers took their turn in succession to sing the rest of the psalm. Anyone who wishes may learn more about this from what is written in the Books of Chronicles <note>original: *Paraleipomenōn* / *Paralipomenon*, meaning "the things omitted," the traditional Greek and Latin name for the Books of Chronicles.</note> as follows: "And he offered this song of praise by the hand of Asaph the prophet" <margin>V 70 C</margin>.

**Of Asaph the Prophet.** Once the first Psalm was delivered in this manner, the individual choirs in turn—sometimes separately and sometimes together in one voice, with exultation and rhythm—sang the Psalm while dancing for the glory of God, some with instruments and others responding alternately with similar tools. But one may also learn this from David himself, who, when the Ark was recovered from the foreigners, danced before it; and when rebuked by Michal his wife, he added these words: *I will play and be mocked before the Lord.* For he did not merely cease, but commanded those very things to be extended. Some, however, did not follow this order and neglected this accuracy; as people who did not wish to be taught by those they encountered, they fled to allegories, denying that all the Psalms belonged to David. They claimed they belonged only to those who asserted they received them from David. They frequently argued this was established by the promise made to them, which God finally performed for our children when He raised Jesus from the dead, as it is written in the second Psalm: *You are my Son, today I have begotten You*, where he understands "generation" to mean the resurrection. The same second Psalm, spoken concerning Him, confirms this, just as all the Apostles say. And these things indeed concern His humanity: for what is said concerning His divinity in the same Psalm is this: *You shall shepherd them with a rod of iron, and like a potter’s vessel you shall shatter them.* By these words, he indicates the force and power of the Divinity in the same...

<meta>This page continues the theological argument regarding the interpretation of the Psalms. The text begins mid-word with the conclusion of the word "psalms."</meta>

### CHRONICON

...psalms regarding the Master Christ and spoke [of Him] alone. <margin>P 90</margin> For he did not treat the attributes of the Master Christ as common with any others, nor the things of the Master as shared with his servants. Instead, he spoke of the things of the Master specifically as the Master, and the things of the servants as servants. Whatever other passages the Apostles took from the Psalms, they did not take them as being spoken primarily about Him, but rather as being fitting to their subject. Examples include: "*They divided my garments among themselves*" <note>Psalm 22:18, quoted in Matthew 27:35.</note>; and this: "*They gave gall for my food*" <note>Psalm 69:21.</note>; and this: "*I saw the Lord before me always*" <note>Psalm 16:8, quoted in Acts 2:25.</note>; and "*Having ascended on high, he led captivity captive*" <note>Psalm 68:18, quoted in Ephesians 4:8.</note>. These and other similar verses were used because they were appropriate to the occasion. The blessed Paul did the same when he made use of the words of Moses in *Deuteronomy*, adapting them to his own purpose as fitting. <margin>B R 212</margin> He says: "*Do not say in your heart, 'Who will ascend into heaven?'*"—that is, to bring Christ down—or "*Who will descend into the abyss?*"—that is, to bring Christ back from the dead <note>Romans 10:6-7, adapting Deuteronomy 30:12-13.</note>. Paul interpreted the passage as suitable for his own <margin>V 73</margin> argument. For the rest of the content in those Psalms does not apply to the Master Christ, even though the Apostles borrowed specific lines from them. For instance, the line "*They divided my garments among themselves*" is from the twenty-first Psalm <note>This is Psalm 22 in modern English Bibles; the author follows the Septuagint numbering system.</note>. Yet that same Psalm also says: "*Far from my salvation are the words of my transgressions*" <note>Psalm 22:1.</note>. To apply such a statement to Christ would be unfitting and inconsistent with Holy Scripture; indeed, it would be clear madness to understand it that way. Because...

...concluded. For he did not make the things belonging to the Lord Christ common with others, nor the things of the Lord common with his servants. Whatever other things the Apostles took from the Psalms, they did not receive them as things spoken properly of Christ, but as things which suited their purpose, such as: *They divided my garments among themselves*. And that: *They gave gall for my food*. And that: *I always foresaw the Lord in my sight*. And: *Ascending on high, he led captivity captive*. These and similar verses they used as suitable for their argument, just as the blessed Paul used the saying of Moses in Deuteronomy, which he translated into his own argument, saying: *Do not say in your heart, Who shall ascend into heaven?* That is, to bring Christ down; or, *Who shall descend into the Abyss?* That is, to call Christ back from the dead; interpreting that saying as suitable for his argument. For the rest of the Psalms are by no means applicable to the Lord Christ, though some things were taken from them: such as that, *They divided my garments among themselves*, which is from Psalm 21. But it says of himself: *Far from my salvation are the words of my sins*. This is by no means fitting or congruent with sacred Scripture; indeed, it would be open madness if one were to accept such a thing regarding Christ.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the interpretation of the Psalms, specifically contrasting how some psalms refer exclusively to Christ ("the Master"), while others refer to "servants" or historical events. ### PASCHAL CHRONICLE

<margin>C</margin> Of these four psalms spoken regarding the Master Christ, they fit Him entirely and completely. For as we said before, the blessed *David* did not treat as common <note>original: "ἐκοινοποίει" — to make common or shared, here meaning David did not mix attributes of Christ with those of ordinary men.</note> the things spoken regarding the Master Christ with the things spoken regarding certain others. <margin>5</margin> For even the Savior Himself appears to do this when the Jews accused Him, saying, "*Why do you work on the Sabbath?*" He answered, saying, "*My Father is working until now, and I am working.*" <note>John 5:17.</note> But when they accused His disciples, He said, "*Have you not read what David did, when he ate the bread of the presence* <note>original: "τοὺς ἄρτους τῆς προθέσεως" — also known as showbread, twelve loaves set out in the Temple as an offering.</note> *himself, <margin>10</margin> which it is not lawful to eat except for the priests alone?*" <note>Matthew 12:3-4.</note> By this, He was clearly <margin>D</margin> contrasting Himself with the Father, and the disciples with the prophets—or rather the priests—as servants to servants and as a Son to a Father. So also the prophet *David*, moved by the Holy Spirit, did not indiscriminately mix the <margin>15</margin> subjects concerning the Master with the subjects of servants. Instead, he was deemed worthy to foretell and compose these four psalms specifically for the subject of the Master. He set out all the other psalms for the common benefit and instruction of everyone, concerning other persons, matters, or histories. For this reason, he also spoke them melodiously and with rhythm, <margin>20</margin> <margin>P 91</margin> so that they might be easily grasped and easily remembered by everyone because they are pleasant. And this is evident, as we find the works of *David* being sung in all the churches of the world and by nearly all men...

Africanus <note>Sextus Julius Africanus (c. 160 – c. 240 AD) was a Christian traveler and historian whose work is a primary source for early Christian chronography.</note> calculates the first Olympiad <term>Olympiad: A four-year period used by the Greeks to record time, beginning with the first Olympic Games traditionally dated to 776 BC.</term> to coincide with Jotham <note>original: Ἰωαθὰμ / Joatham</note>, king of the Hebrews of the tribe of Judah. Our own canon also places it at this same time. Furthermore, Africanus writes exactly as follows:
*“Aeschylus, the son of Agamestor, ruled the Athenians for 23 years; <note>The Latin text provided in the transcription lists 24 years, while the Greek text specifies 23.</note> it was during his reign that Jotham reigned in Jerusalem.”*
<margin>C</margin> And our own canon says that the first Olympiad includes the reign of Jotham, king of Judah.
In the 51st year of Uzziah <note>original: Ὀζίου / Osiae</note>, who is also called Azariah, king of Judah, the first Olympiad was established by Iphitus <note>Iphitus of Elis was the legendary restorer of the Olympic Games after a period of civil unrest in Greece.</note>. During this time, the following were prophesying: Isaiah son of Amoz, Hosea <note>original: Ὡσηὲ / Osee</note> son of Beeri, Joel son of Pethuel <note>original: Βαθουήλ / Batouel</note>, Oded, and Micah the Morasthite.
The first Olympiad was celebrated among the Greeks, which is a four-year cycle.

They deposited the weapons of Hercules in the city they had founded, Rome, which was formerly called the village of Valentia in the Boarian Forum <note>original: "Βοαρίῳ φόρῳ" — The Forum Boarium was the site of the ancient cattle market in Rome</note>. They also built a great temple to Zeus, which they called the Capitolium in the Roman tongue, which means "the head of the city." Having also brought the Palladium <note>A sacred wooden cult image (xoanon) believed to protect the city that held it</note> from the city of Silve <note>referring to Alba Longa, the city of the Silvii</note>, <margin>P 110</margin> they deposited it in Rome.

But from the time he killed his own brother, the entire city of Rome was shaken, its people were in revolt, and civil wars broke out during his sole reign. It was said to him by the Pythia <note>The priestess of the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi</note>: "Unless your brother sits with you upon the royal throne, your city of Rome shall not stand, nor shall the people or the war be quieted." <margin>B</margin> So, having made an image of his brother—

Furthermore, whenever he issued a decree or a law, he spoke as if on behalf of both himself and his brother, saying: "We have commanded," "We have decreed." This custom has persisted among monarchs from that time until the present—the practice of saying, <margin>V 89</margin> "We have commanded," "We have decreed." <note>This refers to the "Royal We," where a single ruler refers to themselves in the plural to denote collective authority.</note> He also sent golden busts of himself and his brother to every city <margin>C</margin> under Roman rule, to be placed near the local governors.

After King Romulus completed the city walls and beautified the city, he also built a temple to Mars. In that same month, he held a great festival and sacrificed to Mars, naming the month March (it was formerly called *Primus* <note>original: "πρῖμον" — Meaning "First," as March was the first month of the original Roman calendar</note>, but was renamed to what is interpreted as "belonging to Mars"). All Romans perform this festival every year until now, calling the day of the assembly "Mars in the Field" <note>original: "Μάρτις ἐν κάμπῳ" — The Campus Martius, or Field of Mars, in Rome</note>. Immediately afterward, he began building the *Cercesion* <note>original: "Κερκέσιον" — The Circus Maximus</note> in Rome, which he named the Hippodrome. He did this to distract the common people <margin>D</margin> of Rome, because they were rioting and rising up against him on account of his brother's death. ...for that reason the Kings of the Persians conducted their wars successfully, as those who worshipped these four elements. For neither were those four elements worshipped at Rome before, nor was any festival established for them. In this contest, as they say, the earth and sea contended—that is, Ceres and Neptune—and the elements subject to the Sun. 

A lot was cast between King Oenomaus himself and another from whatever region he might have come, who was to contend with him. Thus, if by chance the lot determined that Oenomaus should contend for Neptune, then he would put on a blue garment, because that is the color of the waters; he who was to fight with him, moreover, would use a green one, because that is the color of the earth. Furthermore, if the lot had designated Oenomaus to wear the habit of Ceres, he would be adorned in green attire, and his opponent would be clothed in a blue habit—namely that of Neptune, which is the color of the waters. And indeed, the defeated party would pay the penalty with death. To that royal and annual contest, an infinite multitude of men from individual regions and cities would flock together. Furthermore, the sailors who inhabited the maritime cities, islands, and coastal villages, would pray for victory for him who wore the blue garment, that is, Neptune's, since from there...

But Oenomaus was the first to institute that equestrian contest in which four-horse teams pulled the chariots, which is why he was considered quite famous, as is held in the histories of the most learned Charax...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the historical and symbolic origins of chariot racing, moving from the mythological inventors like Enyalius to a philosophical and cosmic interpretation of the Hippodrome's design as recorded by the historian Charax and the Roman founder Romulus.</meta>

# PASCHAL CHRONICLE

In the histories of the most wise Charax <note>Joannes Charax, a historian likely from the 6th century AD</note>, who also wrote these things, it is stated that the gymnasium of the **Hippodrome** <note>original: Ἱππικοῦ — the arena for horse and chariot racing</note> was conceived to represent the governance of the cosmos—that is, of the heaven, the earth, and the sea. For historians recorded that the twelve houses of the **Zodiac** <note>The circle of twelve constellations through which the sun appears to move</note> <margin>5</margin> govern the earth, the sea, and the transitory life of humans. They say that the floor of the **Hippodrome** represents the entire earth, and the **Euripus** <note>original: εὔριπον — the central barrier or canal in the middle of the racing track</note> represents the sea that lies in the midst of the land. The turning post toward the gates represents the East <note>The rising sun</note>, <margin>R 264</margin> and the **Sphendone** <note>original: σφενδόνα — the curved, semi-circular end of the stadium</note> represents the West. The seven laps <note>original: σπατία — the circuits or "spaces" of the race</note> represent the course <margin>10</margin> <margin>B</margin> and the movement of the stars belonging to the seven planets and the Great Bear <note>The Big Dipper constellation</note>.

The same King **Romus** <note>Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome</note>, also wishing to honor the Sun and the four elements under its control, was the first to invent and perform this contest in Rome, in that same region of the West—that is, Italy. He used four-horse chariots to symbolize the **earth**, the **sea**, **fire**, and **air**. And Romus <margin>15</margin> assigned these names to the four elements: to the earth, the **Green** faction <note>original: Πράσινον — the "Prasina" team</note>, because it is verdant; to the sea (that is, the waters), the **Blue** faction <note>original: Βένετον — the "Veneta" team</note>, as it is dark blue; to fire, the **Red** faction <note>original: Ῥουσαῖον — the "Russata" team</note>, being fiery; and to the air, the **White** faction. From this, the four factions were devised in Rome. <margin>C</margin> He called the Green faction "**Praesentem**," <margin>20</margin> which is a Roman word... <note>original: Πραίσεντον — Romulus is said to have used the Latin *Praesentem* (meaning "present" or "enduring") because the earth is always present and green</note>

---

<note>Critical Apparatus Notes:</note>
4. **the twelve houses**: Malalas <note>John Malalas, a 6th-century chronicler</note> says "the twelve gates represent the twelve houses."
7. **Euripus**: spelled *Eurippon* in manuscript V.
9. **laps**: spelled *spathia* in manuscripts P and V; *spatia* is used by Cedrenus and suggested by scholars Chilmead and Du Cange.
10. **astral**: Malalas uses "astronomy," Du Cange suggests "astral placement," Chilmead suggests "astral revolution." On page 219 D, it says "since this does not happen even in the astral movement."
10. **the**: found in Malalas; manuscripts P and V have "and the."
10. **Great**: omitted in manuscript P.
12. **its**: manuscript P reads "his."

<note>Translation of the Latin summary provided at the bottom of the original page:</note>
And this is added: that the exercise of the equestrian contest was invented to express the governance of the world—namely of heaven, earth, and sea. Indeed, they imagine the twelve houses of the Zodiac circle, by which the earth, the sea, and the fleeting life of men are ruled. For the floor of the Circus designates the entire earth; the **Euripus** the sea which stands in the middle of the land; the turn toward the gates, the East; the one at the turning posts, the West; the seven laps, the course and motion of the seven planets and the Great Bear. Furthermore, the same Romulus, in honor of the Sun itself and the four elements, was the first to celebrate the contest he discovered in Rome, in the same region of the West or Italy, with a four-horse chariot, by which he might designate the earth, sea, fire, and air. To these four elements Romulus imposed their names: to the earth, the Green (Prasina), that is, herbaceous or green; to the sea or waters, the Blue (Veneta) or sea-blue; and finally the White (Alba) faction assigned to the air. Moreover, he called the Green faction "Praesentem," a word derived from Latin which sounds like something "Remaining" or "Abiding," because the earth remains and exists forever green with its forests and glades. He called the Blue (Veneta) from the province called Venetia, subject to Rome...

# PASCHAL CHRONICLE

...[practice], which is interpreted as "remaining constant"; for the word *praesentare* <note>original: πραισεντεύειν — a Greek spelling of the Latin *praesentare*, meaning to present or be present</note> is said to mean "to stay behind," because the grassy earth stands forever with its groves. He called the **Blue** faction <note>original: Βένετον — the Veneti or Blue team</note> after the province under Roman rule called **Venetia**, whose capital is <margin>5</margin> **Aquileia**; it is from there that the dark blue dyes come—that is, the "Venetian" dyes for garments. To the **Green** faction, which represents the **Earth**, he joined the **White**, which he says represents the **Air**, because the air rains upon, serves, and harmonizes with the earth. To the **Blue** faction, which represents the **Water**, he joined and mixed the **Red** <note>original: Ῥουσαῖον — the Russati or Red team</note>, which represents **Fire**, since <margin>10</margin> water extinguishes fire as something subject to it. <margin>D</margin>

Consequently, those living in Rome were divided into these factions and no longer lived in harmony with one another, for each person loved their own victory and championed their own faction as if it were a kind of religion <note>original: θρησκείας — a sacred cult or sect</note>. A great schism arose in Rome, and the factions held great enmity toward one another <margin>15</margin> from the time **Romus** <note>Romulus, the legendary founder of Rome</note> devised the spectacle of the horse races for them.

During the reign of this same Romus, his army became very large and was composed of outsiders, and there was a multitude of wild men in Rome. There were not enough women for the crowds of men, and the young soldiers desired the pleasures of life, <margin>P 113</margin> <margin>20</margin> and they began to accost women in the marketplace, and there was turmoil <margin>V 91</margin> and civil war. Romus was disheartened, being at a loss as to what to do... <margin>R 266</margin>

The army rushed into the **Hippodrome** <note>original: Ἱππικῷ — the Greek term for the Circus Maximus</note>, and from the benches they snatched the virgin girls and those who did not have husbands, taking them for themselves as wives. **Romus** <note>Romulus, the legendary first king of Rome</note> caused this to happen only once, just as the most wise poet **Virgil** wrote, and likewise **Apollonius** the Roman historian, as well as **Silvius**. <note>The author likely refers to the historian Livy; "Silvius" may be a manuscript error or a reference to a source now lost</note>. Other historians have written that the first <margin>D</margin> **chariot race** <note>original: ἱπποδρόμιον</note> performed by the Romans was done using **mules** <note>original: βουρδῶνας (bourdones) — specifically cross-bred equines or pack-mules</note>.

Historians also relate that Romus and **Remus** were nourished by the milk of a **she-wolf**, because King **Amulius**, their grandfather, had ordered them to be cast into the woods as children born out of wedlock. This was because **Ilia** <note>Also known as Rhea Silvia</note>, their mother—who was a priestess of **Mars**—had been corrupted by a certain soldier. Regarding this, the storytellers say mythologically that <margin>R 268</margin> Mars himself impregnated her; she gave birth to twins, and for this reason their grandfather threw them into the woods. A certain countrywoman who was tending sheep found the boys; <margin>P 114</margin> moved by compassion because they were so handsome, she took them and raised them on her own milk. In that region, even to this day, they call the countrywomen who tend sheep "**she-wolves**" <note>original: λυκαίνας (lykainas) — the chronicler is offering a rationalized explanation for the famous myth, suggesting the "wolf" was actually a woman nicknamed for her wild lifestyle</note>, because they spend their entire lives and conduct themselves among the wild beasts and the wolves.

Because of this, Romus devised the festival called the **Brumalia** <note>A winter festival lasting from late November to the winter solstice, celebrated in both Rome and the later Byzantine Empire</note>, stating, it is said, that it was necessary for the king at the proper time to feed—

He rushed into the Circus, and snatching from the steps the virgin girls and women who lacked husbands, he joined them to the soldiers as wives. This Romulus did only once, as the most learned poet Virgil, as well as Apollonius the writer of Roman history, and Silvius have handed down. Other historians indeed wrote that the first Circus games were then first performed by the Romans with mules. They tell that Romulus and Remus were suckled by a she-wolf. For King Amulius, their grandfather, had commanded them to be exposed in the woods as illegitimate, because their mother Silvia, a Priestess of Mars, had been compressed by a certain soldier; from which they feigned that she had been made pregnant by Mars. However, when she had birth to twins, and for that reason they had been exposed in the woods by their grandfather, a certain rural woman who was pasturing flocks found them; moved by pity, as they were very handsome, she took them and nourished them with her own milk. In this region, they call the rural women who pasture flocks "She-wolves" even today, as they lead a life with beasts and wolves, and are constantly engaged with them. # CHRONICLE

...all his entire senate and those in positions of dignity and all the military forces within the Palace, as honored guests during the winter season when military matters are at a lull. He began first to call and feed those whose names began with the letter Alpha, and then <margin>B</margin> subsequently through to Omega <note>original: ἕως τοῦ ω — referring to the Greek alphabet from A to Z</note>, commanding his senate also to provide food <margin>V 92</margin> in the same fashion. They themselves also fed the entire crowd, each one choosing whom they wished. Therefore, the musicians <note>original: πάνδουροι (pandouroi) — players of a three-stringed lute-like instrument</note> of each regiment went to the houses of those being invited at evening time, playing their instruments for the benefit of those being called to the morning meal the next day, so that they would know they were to be fed there tomorrow. And the custom of the **Brumalia** <note>A midwinter festival celebrated in Rome, often associated with the shortest days of the year and the honoring of Bacchus</note> has persisted in the Roman state until the present. 

The same **Romus** <note>The Greek name for Romulus, the legendary first king of Rome</note> did this wishing to wipe away the insult against him, because the Romans—being his enemies and hating him—spoke insults against him, saying <margin>C</margin> that he ought not to rule because the two brothers were fed by strangers until they reached full age and became kings. They were indicating that they were raised by **Faustulus** the farmer and his wife **Lycaina** <note>original: Λυκαίνης — meaning "she-wolf" in Greek, corresponding to the Latin Lupa; here it refers to the woman who raised the twins</note>, eating from the resources of others. For among the Romans and all the ancients, it was a reproach for someone to be fed by others. Hence, even in the banquets called "friendly" <note>original: φιλικοῖς — likely referring to the *Charistia* or *Cara Cognatio* festivals where family and friends settled disputes</note>, each of those coming together for the banquet brings his own food and drink with him, and everything is set out in common, and they eat while maintaining the ancient custom.

...those who were in positions of dignity, and even the Palatine soldiers, as more honored men, in the winter storm—at which time military affairs are naturally vacant—the King received with feasts. The trumpeters of each troop, having set out to the houses of those who were invited to the banquet, so that they might know they were invited for the following day, indicated it by the song of the trumpet on the evening before: and from then on the custom of the **Brumalia** has obtained in the Roman Republic until these times. 

Moreover, Romulus did this so that he might abolish the memory of the stain cast upon him: since the Romans, by whom he was hated, would object with insults that he was not at all worthy to reign, and that those twin brothers, having been educated from what belonged to others until their full age, had seized the kingdom. They indicated by this reasoning that they had been nourished by Faustulus the farmer and his wife **Lupa** <note>Latin for "She-wolf"</note>, and had lived off the property of others. For among the Romans and all the ancients, for anyone to be nourished by others was always held as a disgrace. # THE PASCHAL CHRONICLE

->PASCHAL<-

"And all this land shall be for a desolation and for a vanishing, and they shall serve among these nations the king of Babylon for seventy years. And when the seventy years are fulfilled, I will take vengeance upon the king of Babylon and upon that nation," says the Lord. <note>This is a quotation from the Prophet Jeremiah, chapter 25, predicting the length of the Jewish exile in Babylon.</note>

In the same fourth year of Jehoiakim—also known as Jechonias <note>The text here conflates Jehoiakim with his son Jeconiah/Jehoiachin; historically, these were two different kings</note>—king of Judah, Jeremiah the prophet was commanded by the Lord <margin>P 124</margin> to take a scroll of a book <note>original: κεφαλίδα βιβλίου - literally a 'header' or 'roll' of a book</note> and to write in it all the words of the Lord which had been proclaimed against Jerusalem from the days of Josiah, king of Judah, until the fourth year of Jehoiakim. The Lord said, "Perhaps they will turn back because of the things I am planning against them," but you did not turn back. 

After Baruch, son of Neriah, read these words into the ears of all the people, Jehoiakim sent Jehudi to take the book; and Jehudi, having taken the book, read it. ### XII.

## ***On the captivity of the Jews, and the destruction of the temple of Jerusalem.***

The first year of the beginning of the destruction of the temple, and the captivity of the Jewish race, with the exception of a few who set out into Egypt to Vaphres King of Egypt, after another part had been led away into captivity, when the King of the Chaldeans and Babylonians, Nebuchadnezzar, ended the siege of Jerusalem, and, after Zedekiah was blinded, led him away as a captive. Nabuzardan, the Prince of the Cooks <note>A literal translation of the Greek 'archimageiros,' meaning the captain of the guard.</note>, burned the temple on the 10th day of the 5th month, which had stood for 442 years from the first building by Solomon. Clement himself harmonizes with us in the 1st book of the *Stromata*, writing that in the forty-fourth Olympiad the Jewish race was led away into the city of Babylon into captivity, during the reign of Vaphres among the Egyptians, and while Philip was Archon at Athens: and further, that the 70 years of the devastation of the place were completed in the 2nd year of Darius son of Hystaspes. Thus far the above-mentioned man.

### I.

Cyrus released the Jewish nation from their captivity, allowing them to travel to Jerusalem. At that time, approximately fifty thousand Jews returned from Babylon and raised the altar and laid the foundations of the temple. <margin>5</margin> However, because the surrounding nations hindered them, the work remained incomplete until the second year of Darius, son of Hystaspes, the King of the Persians; only the altar stood during this time, since the Prophecy mentions Darius and the three prophets—Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi (who was also called an "Angel") <note>The name Malachi literally translates to "my messenger" or "my angel" in Hebrew, which is why the text refers to him as "the angel."</note>—as they were prophesying. <margin>10</margin>

<margin>D</margin>
Daniel and Ezekiel prophesied in Persia, while Habakkuk, Haggai, and Zechariah prophesied in Judea. During their time in Persia, Joshua <note>original: Ἰησοῦς (Iesous). This refers to Joshua son of Jozadak, the High Priest.</note> son of Jozadak the priest was well known, along with Zerubbabel son of Shealtiel, who was of royal descent; these were the leaders of the return from Babylon. In that year, Daniel fell asleep <note>A common historical and biblical idiom for death.</note> after <margin>20</margin> prophesying for fifty years.

### I.

Cyrus gave power to all the captives of the Jewish race to return to Jerusalem: at which time about 50,000 departed from Babylon, restored the sanctuary, and laid the foundations of the temple. But with the neighboring nations attacking the Jews, the work remained unfinished until the second year of Darius, son of Hystaspes, King of the Persians, with only the sanctuary standing: for indeed the Prophecy mentions Darius, and the three Prophets, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, who was also called an Angel, prophesying the same.

Daniel and Ezekiel prophesied in Persia: in Judea, Habakkuk, Haggai, and Zechariah: in whose time Joshua son of Jozadak the Priest was famous, and Zerubbabel, son of Shealtiel, who was of royal descent, and who were the leaders of the return from Babylon.

To Daniel, in this very first year of Cyrus, a word was revealed on the 24th day of the first month, when he was at the Tigris river, concerning the five Kings yet to follow, and concerning the total destruction of Jerusalem, and of the incense and the anointing in it, and concerning the calling of the nations: in which year indeed Daniel fell asleep, when he had prophesied for 50 years.

<note>The following section contains scholarly notes by the editor regarding variations found in different ancient manuscripts.</note>

5. **Cheilon** in manuscript V. *In the same place*, regarding the phrase **"first in Lacedaemon"** (Lacedaimoni alpha): manuscript V reads *Lacedaimonia* (Spartan things), while manuscript P reads *Lacedaimonia* (in the region of Lacedaemon). Scaliger repeated this error when compiling these words into his edition of Eusebius on page 162. However, in his *Notes* on that author (page 72, note 1257), he correctly understood a passage from Diogenes Laertius regarding Chilon: "He became an Ephor during the 56th (Casaubon restored this to '55th' based on two manuscripts) Olympiad; but Pamphila says it was during the 6th, and that he was the first Ephor during the time of Euthydemus." As Sosicrates says, this should be understood to mean Chilon was the first person ever to be made an Ephor, not, as Menagius thought, the leader of the college of Ephors. Furthermore, since the number '1' (alpha) is missing in both Jerome's and the Armenian translations of Eusebius, and since the *Paschal Chronicle* sought these facts from no other source than Eusebius, I believe it is credible that the faulty reading *Lacedaimonia* already appeared in Eusebius's own work. 

As an example, one and the same error was imposed upon Jerome (page 76), the Armenian translator (page 283), and Syncellus (page 153): the first two state: "Hercules in Phoenicia, surnamed Desanaus, was considered famous in Phoenicia," and "Hercules was known in Phoenicia, called Desandas." Syncellus reveals the origin of this error when he says: "Some say a certain Hercules was known in Phoenicia, being called Disandan," which is to say "known as Sandan" (gnorizesthai Sandan). Regarding this surname of Hercules, Wesseling collected the surviving evidence in his notes on Hierocles (page 710), in addition to the recently published work of John Laurentius *On the Roman Magistrates* (page 268), where it is written as "Sandon."

6. Note regarding years 41, 42, 43, 44, and 45 of the captivity in manuscript R.
7. In manuscript P, the number 9 is placed before 10 in verse 9.
10. **Xenophon** in manuscript V: manuscript R notes "otherwise Xenophon." *In the same place*, **Colophonos** in manuscript V, which usually writes the name with the same accent as Solomon; manuscript P reads "the Colophonian." Compare our preface to John of Antioch, pages 7 and 8.

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 287 regarding how the prophetic and historical books of the Bible were compiled and preserved in the Temple archives.</meta>

# CHRONICON

<margin>R 360</margin>On the day he prophesied, they would write down in the account of that prophet what he proclaimed concerning a single matter. And again, after some time, if he proclaimed concerning another matter, they would again write it down, placing it after his previous discourse, as if making the beginning of a new chapter. And in this way, they compiled his entire book. For this reason, one can find in their books a chapter suited to the **Babylonian captivity** or to the **return**, and immediately another concerning **Christ**, and then again something speaking of the captivity and the return. And to put it simply, unless you read with close attention, you will find everything jumbled together. Not only these, but also the **Books of Kingdoms** <note>These are the books known today as 1 and 2 Samuel and 1 and 2 Kings.</note> were written in this manner in the Temple, part by part: in the time of Saul, those things up to Saul; and in the time of David, those things up to David. Similarly, the deeds of each king were written during his own time. Likewise, they also wrote in the royal <term>archives<note>original: "σκρινίοις" (skriniois), referring to the chests or cases where scrolls were kept.</note></term> those things which we call **Paralipomena** <note>original: "Παραλειπομένας" (Paraleipomenas). This is the Greek name for the Books of Chronicles, meaning "Things Omitted" or "Passed Over," implying they contain details left out of the Books of Kingdoms.</note>. **Moses** wrote the **Pentateuch**, a history of things past, present, and future. **Joshua** <note>original: "Ἰησοῦς" (Iesous). In Greek, the names of Joshua and Jesus are identical.</note> in turn wrote his own book; the **Judges** and likewise **Ruth** were recorded in the Temple, that is, in the **Tabernacle**. **Solomon**, for his part, wrote his own works: the **Proverbs**, the **Song of Songs**, and **Ecclesiastes**. For having received the gift of wisdom from God, he admonished every man to conduct himself wisely in this life; however, he had not received the gift of **prophecy**. Therefore, as many prophets as we have found who were deemed worthy to speak concerning our Master **Christ**...

***

<note>Critical notes on the Greek text: 1. "They prophesied" (plural) in Manuscript P. 2. "Or" instead of "If" in Manuscripts P and V. 10. "You will find" (singular) in Manuscript V. 10. "The" is omitted in Manuscript P. 11. "The" is omitted in Manuscript P. 13. "The things until David" is omitted in Manuscript P; manuscript P reads "until David." 14. Manuscript P adds "and." 18. Manuscript P reads "in the Tabernacle." 20 or 22. Delete the word "for."</note>

***

<note>The following is a Latin translation of the Greek text above: On the day he had announced something. Again, if after some time he had predicted something about another matter, they then subjected it to his previous discourse, making a beginning of a chapter. And by this method they composed his whole book. Wherefore it is possible to find in their books a chapter which fits the Babylonian captivity, or the return, and immediately another which treats of Christ, and again of the captivity or the return. And to say it in one word, unless you read these things attentively, you will find all things confused. Nor were the Prophecies alone, but also the books of Kingdoms written in the temple part by part in the same way, such as during Saul's reign, the things concerning Saul, and in David's time, the things which looked to David. And in the same way the acts of each King were written, each in his own time. But they likewise wrote in the royal archives what we call Paralipomena. Moses however wrote the Pentateuch, a history of things past, present, and future. Joshua also composed a particular book; Judges again in the temple, or Tabernacle, and similarly the book of Ruth. Solomon likewise wrote his books, Proverbs, and Songs, and Ecclesiastes. For gifted by God with the grace of wisdom, he exhorted all men to behave themselves wisely in this life, yet he did not obtain the grace of Prophecy. As many therefore as we have found...</note>

It attributes specific authorship to Moses, Joshua, and Solomon, while distinguishing Solomon’s wisdom from prophetic revelation.</summary>

# THE PASCHAL [CHRONICLE]

<sig>19</sig>

...we have set in order. Furthermore, let us also write concerning the other four prophets, who were deemed worthy to speak about the <term>dispensation<note>original: "οἰκονομίας" (oikonomias). In early Christian theology, this refers to God's plan for the salvation of humanity, specifically through the incarnation and life of Jesus.</note></term> of Christ the Master, toward which the entire aim of Divine Scripture is directed. Let us, therefore, first bring forward the most "loud-voiced" Isaiah, who was deemed worthy to see and to foretell, both through symbols and through words, the mystery concerning Christ.

### Concerning Isaiah.

<margin>R 362 D</margin>
This is the great Isaiah, the son of Amoz, who saw in a symbolic form the things concerning the mystery of Christ, when he beheld the Lord sitting upon a throne, high and lifted up; and <term>seraphim<note>A type of celestial or heavenly being described in the Bible as having six wings.</note></term> stood in a circle around Him. Each one had six wings; with two they covered their faces, with two they covered their feet, and with two they flew <note>The transcription notes "six wings for the one and six wings for the one," describing the symmetry of the beings.</note>. And they cried out to one another: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of <term>Sabaoth<note>A Hebrew word meaning "Hosts" or "Armies," referring to God's command over the heavenly powers.</note></term>; the whole earth is full of His glory!" Following this, one of the seraphim was sent, and he took a coal from the altar with <term>tongs<note>original: "λαβίδι" (labidi). In later Christian tradition, this term was also used for the spoon used in the Eucharist.</note></term>, and he touched his lips, saying: "This shall take away your sins." Clearly, through this vision shown to him, and through the hymn and the symbolic form, he was taught to announce beforehand the mystery concerning Christ.

### On Daniel.

This Daniel, while prophesying in Babylon and being himself deemed worthy to foretell concerning Christ the Lord, speaks in this way: "**And you shall know and understand from the going forth of the word that you may be answered and that Jerusalem may be built until Christ the leader—seven weeks and sixty-two weeks**," and so forth. <note>This is a quotation from the "Seventy Weeks" prophecy in Daniel 9:25, which Christian chroniclers interpreted as a precise timeline for the coming of Jesus.</margin>5</margin> And again: "**A stone was cut without hands, and it struck the image, and the stone became a great mountain, and it filled the entire earth.**" <note>Referencing Daniel 2:34-35, the vision of the statue representing world empires destroyed by the Kingdom of God.</note> And again: "**And behold, coming with the clouds of heaven as a Son of Man, and he reached even unto the Ancient of Days, and to him was given the honor and the authority,**" <margin>10</margin> <margin>V 128 C</margin> and the rest of what was spoken.

This Daniel was from the tribe of Judah, from among the prominent men of the royal service; but while still a young child, he was led into captivity from Judea into the land of the Chaldeans <note>The Babylonians.</note>. <margin>15</margin> He was born in Upper Beth-horon <note>original: "Βεθωρὼμ" (Bethōrōm). Indeed, those who possess power are often infected by such vices while they are young, but towards the end of their lives, they turn into wild beasts, as they snatch, devastate, strike, and kill in the manner of tyrants and live impiously, for which they finally receive punishment from God the judge. <margin>15</margin> From this point, therefore, Africanus <note>Julius Africanus (c. 160 – c. 240 AD) was a Christian traveler and historian whose work was foundational for later Christian chronographies.</note> reckons the number of the seventy weeks in this same prophecy, extending not only to the appearance of the saving preaching <note>The ministry of Jesus.</note>, but indeed to 490 years. *...seven weeks until the leader, and sixty-two weeks; and it shall return, and the square and the wall shall be built, and the times shall be emptied. *From this point, Africanus considers the number of 70 weeks in this very prophecy in such a way that he extends it not only to the beginning of Christ’s preaching, but even to the 490 years from which the 70 weeks of years predicted by Daniel took their beginning, and which are completed in the 22nd year of the Empire of Tiberius Caesar, or in the 4th year of the 201st Olympiad: so that 69 weeks are fulfilled in the 14th year of the Empire of Caesar: and the first of the 202nd Olympiad...*

# PASCHAL CHRONICLE

<margin>D</margin> Alexander captured Babylon, and the kingdom of the Persians was overthrown, having endured for 266 years from the first year of Cyrus until the present sixth year of Darius, son of Arsames. <note>Darius III, the last King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire, was defeated by Alexander at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE.</note> This kingdom was the likeness of the statue <note>This refers to the biblical prophecy in Daniel 2:31-45, where a giant statue represents successive world empires. The silver chest and arms were traditionally interpreted as the Medo-Persian Empire.</note> whose hands, chest, and arms were of silver.

Alexander founded 12 cities, whose names are as follows:

**I.** Alexandria near Pentapolis, <note>original: "παρὰ Πεντάπολιν"</note> previously called Tettous, which served as a trading center for Memphis.

<margin>V 137</margin> **II.** Alexandria near Egypt. <note>The most famous Alexandria, founded in 331 BCE on the Mediterranean coast.</note>

**III.** Alexandria near Harpa.

**IV.** Alexandria Cabiosa.

**V.** Alexandria, which is also called Scythia, in the Aegean region. <note>Possibly Alexandria Eschate, or "Alexandria the Furthest," in modern Tajikistan, though the text places it "in the Aegean."</note>

**VI.** Alexandria at Porus. <note>Founded in India to commemorate Alexander's victory over King Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes.</note>

<margin>P 171</margin> **VII.** Alexandria near the river Cypris. <note>original: "περὶ Κυπρίδος ποταμόν"</note>

**VIII.** Alexandria in the Troad.

**IX.** Alexandria in Babylon.

**X.** Alexandria at Mesargages.

**XI.** Alexandria in Persia. <note>The list ends at eleven despite the introductory text claiming twelve cities; such discrepancies are common in ancient manuscript transmissions.</note>

<note>The following section provides philological variants from different manuscript traditions (P, V, and R) and scholarly corrections regarding the names of these cities.</note>

1. Babylon: Manuscript P alone reads *Babylona*. 4. "Whose": omitted in manuscripts R and V. 7. Alexandria: Manuscript P numbers each Alexandria from 1 to 12. ib. *Tettoun*: Manuscript P. 10. *Harpan*: Corrected to *Harpasa* by the historian Rochette. 11. *Cabioson*: Manuscript V; *Cabiosum* in Scaliger’s Excerpts. 12. *And Scythia*: Corrected to *Near Cilicia* by Rochette. 17. *Mesargaphes*: Manuscript P; *Mesasgiges* in Scaliger’s Excerpts.

<meta>This page continues the chronology of the Ptolemaic dynasty, specifically focusing on the early years of the reign of Ptolemy II Philadelphus. It transitions from the list of consuls into a detailed account of the translation of the Hebrew Bible into Greek (the Septuagint), a pivotal moment in both Jewish and Christian history.</meta>

<page-num>326</page-num>
# CHRONICLE

1. Under the consulship of Lepidus and Caecina.
2. Under the consulship of Tacitus and Denton.

Ptolemy Philadelphus released the Jewish <margin>P 173</margin> captives in Egypt who had been taken by his father Ptolemy. He sent royal offerings to Jerusalem to Onias <margin>5</margin> Simon the high priest, the brother of Eleazar, and he took great care that the Jewish scriptures be translated from the Hebrew tongue into Greek. This was done by seventy-two <term>wise men</term> <note>These are the famous scholars who produced the Septuagint; the name "Septuagint" comes from the Latin word for seventy.</note> among the Hebrews, whom he shut away on the island of Pharos—the island of Proteus—in seventy-two separate houses. He then deposited these translations in the <margin>10</margin> libraries he had established in Alexandria, along with a vast number of other books of every kind which he had collected from every city. When he saw the books brought from Jerusalem written in letters of gold, <margin>B</margin> he was filled with wonder. After arranging for them to be transcribed, he sent them back with gifts. The books were translated on the island of Pharos in seventy-two <margin>15</margin> days. It was considered a miracle that these seventy-two men, though separated from one another while translating the scriptures, produced texts that were found to be identical when they came together and compared them before Ptolemy. Thus, God was glorified, and <margin>V 139</margin> the scriptures were recognized as truly divine, since everyone had translated them in the same way, so that even the surrounding nations might know that they were written by divine inspiration <margin>20</margin>...

---

### 2. Under Tacitus, 5th year.

| Year of the World | Year of Rome | | [Olympiad] |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| | [Ptolemy Philadelphus], son of Ptolemy Soter, for 38 years. | Total years: 5,259. | |
| 6222. | 469. | 1. Consulship of Lepidus and Caecina. | 4th year of the 123rd. |
| | 470. | 2. Consulship of Tacitus and Denton. | 1st year of the 124th. |

Ptolemy Philadelphus released the Jewish captives in Egypt who had been taken by his father Ptolemy, and sent royal gifts, which had formerly been in Jerusalem, to Onias Simon the High Priest, the brother of Eleazar. He arranged for the Jewish scriptures to be translated from the Hebrew language into Greek by <term>seventy-two</term> men who were considered wise among the Hebrews. He confined them in <term>Pharos</term> <note>The island famous for its great lighthouse, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World.</note>, the island of <term>Proteus</term> <note>A shape-shifting sea god in Greek mythology said to live on Pharos.</note>, in <term>seventy-two</term> separate buildings. These books he placed in the libraries he had furnished at Alexandria, along with very many other volumes of every kind gathered from individual cities. Having looked upon the books brought from Jerusalem, which were written in letters of gold, he was amazed; and when he had seen to it that they were transcribed, he sent them back with gifts. The books were indeed translated on the island of Pharos in a space of <term>seventy</term> days. The matter was a source of wonder because those <term>seventy-two</term> men, though separated from one another, translated the scriptures in such a way that when they returned and their individual translations were compared before Ptolemy, they were found to agree perfectly <note>original: "ad amussim convenire," meaning to fit a carpenter's rule or to be perfectly exact.</note>. Then indeed glory was given to God, and those scriptures were thereafter held to be truly divine, because in them...

<margin>R 412</margin> 1. Under the consulship of **Paulus** and **Salinator**. <note>original: ὑπ. Παύλου καὶ Σαλινάτωρος. Lucius Aemilius Paullus and Marcus Livius Salinator, 219 BCE.</note> <margin>10</margin>
When the Jews were captured by this Ptolemy, and after they had lost forty <insert>thousand</insert> armed men <note>original: τεσσαράκοντα. The chronicler likely meant 40,000, as noted by the scholar Ducange.</note> and captives were led away to Jerusalem, by the order of this same Ptolemy, five hundred elephants—which they kept ready for use—were given wine mixed with frankincense to drink for three days. This was done so that they might destroy all the Jews in a shared fate. <margin>15</margin>
<margin>B</margin> But when the fourth day arrived and the Jews had prayed, the elephants instead charged at the king's own armed soldiers and the crowds. In the madness that gripped them, the beasts destroyed a great multitude of people. Having been saved in this way, the Jews returned to their own homes with thanksgiving. <note>This account is a summary of the events described in the apocryphal Third Book of Maccabees, which places the event in Alexandria rather than Jerusalem.</note> <margin>20</margin>

<margin>D</margin> ### **21. Under the Consulship of Pamphilus and Paulus.**

A certain Simon, a protector <note>The Greek term "prostates" suggests an administrative official or governor of the Temple</note> of the temple in Jerusalem, came into political opposition with Onias the high priest. Having slandered the Jewish nation in every way to King Seleucus Nicator <note>Though the text says Nicator (Seleucus I), the historical context refers to Seleucus IV Philopator, who reigned 187–175 BCE</note>, and being unable to personally harm Onias, he became a fugitive and resolved to betray their fatherland. He went to Apollonius, <margin>5</margin> the general of Syria, Phoenicia, and Cilicia, and promised him wealth, claiming that the treasuries in Jerusalem were filled with vast amounts of private funds and that these did not belong to the temple, but rather to the King. <margin>10</margin>

<margin>P 178</margin> Apollonius reported these matters to King Seleucus, and having received authority from the King, Apollonius arrived in Jerusalem with Simon and a very heavy <note>meaning large or formidable</note> army. When the people and the temple priests protested, Apollonius entered the temple with threats. After the people had entreated <margin>15</margin> God to shield the temple, suddenly angels appearing as horsemen became visible from heaven and struck Apollonius with terror. He fell half-dead to the ground in the *pamphylon* <note>original: πάμφυλον; likely referring to the "Court of the Gentiles" or a common outer precinct accessible to all tribes</note> of the temple enclosure. Stretching out his hands, he begged the people to pray for him and to entreat God. Onias the high priest, being persuaded by his words... <margin>20</margin>

<margin>772 years from the founding of Rome.</margin> <margin>3rd year of the 148th Olympiad.</margin> ### **21. In the Consulship of Pamphilus and Paulus.**

A certain Simon, set over the Jerusalem temple, who was an adversary to Onias the High Priest, slandered the Jewish race to King Seleucus Nicator in every way. When he could not harm him, he became an exile and decided to betray his own country. Therefore, setting out to Apollonius, the Governor of Syria, Phoenicia, and Cilicia, he promised him money, saying that many riches were stored in the Jerusalem treasuries <note>original: Gazophylaciis</note> which belonged to private individuals and did not concern the temple, but rather the King.

Apollonius reported these things to King Seleucus, and having received power from the King, Apollonius came to Jerusalem together with Simon and a strong army. While the people and the priests of the temple were resisting, Apollonius, making threats, entered the temple. When the people poured out in prayers to God that He might protect the temple, immediately angels sitting upon horses appeared from heaven, who struck Apollonius. He indeed collapsed half-dead upon the ground within the temple precinct full of people; stretching out his hands, he as a suppliant asked the people to pray to God for him. Onias the High Priest, persuaded by his words, especially lest [the King should suspect] men...

17th year. Under the consulship of **Ahenobarbus** and **Longinus**. <margin>10</margin> <note>96 BCE: Gnaeus Domitius Ahenobarbus and Gaius Cassius Longinus.</note>
**John**, being at once priest and general, having campaigned against the **Hyrcanians**, was renamed **Hyrcanus**; he also sent an embassy to the **Romans** and, by a decree of the Senate, established a treaty of friendship with them. <note>The author provides a folk etymology for the name "Hyrcanus," though modern historians suggest it may have been a family name or acquired differently.</note>

...his mother having died in the ninth month, they cut her open and removed the infant; for this reason he was called Caesar, for in the Roman language <note>original: "romaisti" (in Latin)</note> an incision is called "caesar." <note>The author provides a popular folk etymology: that "Caesar" derives from the Latin "caesus," meaning "cut." This is the historical origin of the term "Caesarean section."</note> Having been raised and proving himself a man of courage,
<margin>R 438</margin> he was appointed Triumvir <term>Triumvir: one of a group of three men sharing power</term> alongside Pompey and Crassus, who had served as consuls, during the first year of the aforementioned 180th Olympiad <note>Approximately 60 BCE.</note>. For Roman affairs were administered by these three men.
But Julius Caesar the Dictator, after Crassus was killed in the Persian regions <note>The author refers to the Parthians as Persians; Crassus was defeated at the Battle of Carrhae in 53 BCE.</note> having been captured during the war, remained alone, waging war with his own forces in the
<margin>D</margin> regions of the West. When the consulship, or rather the Triumvirate, was ended following a decision of the common assembly of the Roman Senate and Pompey the Great—his own son-in-law—the said Julius Caesar, being aggrieved, seized power as a tyrant <note>In this context, "tyrant" refers to an extralegal or absolute ruler rather than just a cruel one.</note> over the Romans. Having incited enemies against the Romans, he marched against the Senate of Rome and Pompey the Great. Upon arriving in Rome and taking possession of it, he put its senators to death.
This Gaius Julius the Dictator—which is to say, "sole ruler"—held power over all things in pride and tyranny for 4 years and
<margin>P 187</margin> 6 months, until the 4th day before the Ides of May <note>May 12th</note> of the first indiction <term>Indiction: a 15-year tax cycle used for dating in the later Roman and Byzantine periods.</term>. At that time, the "freedom" of Antioch the Great was publicly proclaimed, when also under—

Julius Caesar the Dictator was not born [normally], but his mother having died in the ninth month, she was cut open and the infant was led out: whence he was named Caesar, because for the Latins this is the same as a cutting. Having been educated, and as he excelled in remarkable strength, he was created Triumvir with Pompey and Crassus, men of consular rank, in the 1st year of the aforementioned 180th Olympiad; the Consulship and Triumvirate were not, however, abolished by decree of the whole Senate. For by these three, Roman affairs were administered.
But Julius Caesar the Dictator, after the killing of Crassus—who had been captured by the Persians in battle in Persia itself—remained alone, carrying out war with his troops in the West. Then, the Consulship or the dignity of Dictator having been abolished by decree of the whole Senate, and even at the instance of Pompey the Great himself, his father-in-law Julius Caesar, being offended, seized tyranny over the Romans, and having stirred up wars against the Romans, he moved arms against the Roman Senate and Pompey the Great, and having occupied Rome, he killed the Senators.
This Gaius Julius the Dictator, that is, Monarch, exercised a proud and tyrannical command over all for 4 years and 7 months from the 4th day before the Ides of May. And there was proposed and published in the great city of Antioch...

->*During the consulship of Lepidus and Plancus.*<-

Gaius Julius Caesar was the first of the Romans to be chosen as monarch <margin>B</margin>, under whom Roman affairs reached their peak; and those who followed after him were also addressed by his name <note>The name "Caesar" became a permanent title for all subsequent Roman Emperors.</note>. He was the first to come forward as a "consul-king" <note>The Greek "hypatos basileus" refers to Caesar’s unique position, combining the Republican office of Consul with the absolute power of a monarch or Dictator.</note>.
He was trained to the highest degree in rhetoric.

### The Beginning of the Indictions.

From the first year of Gaius Julius Caesar and the aforementioned consuls Lepidus and Plancus <note>Marcus Aemilius Lepidus and Lucius Munatius Plancus were consuls in 42 BCE.</note>—specifically from the 12th of the month Artemisios—the people of Antioch began to number their own years <margin>R 448</margin>. # CHRONICLE

->7th year [of the Indiction]. Under the consulship of Antony and Isauricus.<-
->2nd year of Gaius Julius Caesar.<-

The people of Laodicea <note>A prominent city in Asia Minor, modern-day Turkey.</note> reckon their own era of time from this point.
During the term of the aforementioned consuls, the Isaurian war <margin>5</margin> was fought.
<margin>D</margin> Antony the consul decreed that the month of Quintilis <note>original Latin: "Quintilis", meaning the "fifth" month in the old Roman calendar which began in March.</note> be renamed July, because Caesar himself had been born in it.
The same Caesar also added 11 days to the year <note>This refers to the transition from a lunar-based calendar to the solar Julian calendar, correcting the drift between the seasons and the months.</note>, having calculated the course of the sun and the moon.

->8th year [of the Indiction]. Under the consulship of Albinus and Pollio.<- <margin>10</margin>

<margin>P 188</margin> These are the High Priests who led the Hebrews <margin>15</margin> after the return from the 70-year captivity <note>The Babylonian Captivity.</note>, specifically from the 8th year of Darius the son of Hystaspes <note>The Persian King Darius I.</note> and the 2nd year of the 63rd Olympiad <note>Olympiads were four-year periods used for dating in the Greek world; the 63rd Olympiad began around 528 BCE.</note>, as follows:
