# THE PASCHAL CHRONICLE

### THE MARTYRDOM OF POLYCARP

...When persecutions were stirred up throughout Asia, many suffered martyrdom. Among these was Polycarp, the Bishop of Smyrna, who was a disciple of the Apostle John <note>John the Apostle is traditionally identified as the author of the Fourth Gospel; Polycarp serves as a vital "living link" to the apostolic generation.</note> and had been appointed bishop by him. He was arrested under the Proconsul <term>Tatius Quadratus</term> <note>The Roman governor of the province of Asia.</note> by Herod the <term>eirenarch</term> <note>A local magistrate or "justice of the peace" responsible for maintaining order and apprehending suspects.</note>,
<margin>5</margin> who was the son of Nicetas. After enduring much for his faith in Christ, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April <note>original: "πρὸ ζ' καλανδῶν ἀπριλίων" — This corresponds to March 26.</note>, on Great Saturday <note>The Saturday before Easter Sunday, also known as Holy Saturday.</note>, 
<margin>P 258</margin> at the eighth hour <note>Approximately 2:00 PM.</note>, a centurion witnessed the persistence of the gathered Jews and 
Gentiles <note>original: "ἐθνικῶν" (ethnikon) — referring to the non-Jewish, pagan Roman population.</note>. Polycarp was placed in their midst 
<margin>10</margin> and burned alive, being eighty-six years old. Indeed, it had been revealed to him that he would reach 
his end by being burned alive. Regarding his age, he spoke to the Proconsul who told him, "Blaspheme Christ!"
But he replied: "Eighty-six years I have served Christ, and He has done me no wrong.
How then can I blaspheme my King who saved me?" As he was entering the stadium of Smyrna, 
a voice from heaven was given to him: 
<margin>15</margin> <margin>B</margin> "Be strong, Polycarp, and act like a man" <note>original: "Ἴσχυε, Πολύκαρπε, καὶ ἀνδρίζου" — A phrase echoing biblical exhortations to courage.</note>. No one else saw the speaker, but many of our people heard the voice. 
Along with the holy Polycarp, nine others from Philadelphia also suffered martyrdom in Smyrna. 
Others died in Pergamum, among whom was Papias <note>Another early Christian author and associate of Polycarp.</note> and many others whose 
<margin>20</margin> martyrdoms are preserved in writing. Most of their struggles remain recorded even now; 
through all their intercessions, may it be our lot to become fellow-partakers and disciples with them.

Having suffered much for his faith in Christ, on March 26, on Great Saturday, at the 8th hour, while the Centurion watched the stubbornness of the gathered Jews and Gentiles, he was placed in the middle of them and burned alive, being in his 87th year <note>The Latin text here cites 87 years, whereas the Greek above said 86.</note>. It had been revealed to him that he would be consumed by fire while alive. Regarding his years, when the Proconsul said to him, "Curse Christ," he responded: "Eighty and six years I serve Christ, nor has He ever affected me with any injury. How therefore can I curse the King to whom I owe my salvation?" Furthermore, as he went into the stadium at Smyrna, a voice was sent from heaven in these words: "Strengthen your soul, Polycarp, and act virilly." No one else saw who said this, but many of our own heard the voice. Along with Saint Polycarp, nine others from Philadelphia underwent martyrdom at Smyrna; and others at Pergamum, among whom was Papias and many others whose martyrdoms remain commended to writing. Very many...

## 236th Olympiad
<note>An Olympiad is a four-year period used by ancient Greeks for dating; the 236th Olympiad began around 165 AD.</note>

<margin>C</margin> **Indiction 2. 5th year of the reign. Under the consulship of Macrinus and Celsus.** <note>Indictions were 15-year tax cycles used for dating; Macrinus and Celsus were the Roman consuls for the year 164 AD.</note>
**Indiction 3. 6th year. Under the consulship of Orphitus and Pudens.** <note>Consuls for the year 165 AD.</note>

**Justin, a philosopher of our doctrine, presented a second book in defense of our dogmas to the Emperors Marcus Aurelius and Antoninus Verus.** <note>original: "Ἰουστῖνος φιλόσοφος" — Justin Martyr was one of the first "Apologists" who used Greek philosophy to explain Christian beliefs.</note> **Not long afterward, he was adorned with the divine crown of martyrdom, after being denounced by Crescens.** <note>Crescens was a Cynic philosopher and a bitter rival of Justin.</note> **Furthermore, Melito of Asia, the Bishop of Sardis, also gave a book of apology to the aforementioned emperors, as did many others. Among them, the previously mentioned Justin, after other things he had written, included this:** <margin>D</margin> **"I also expect to be plotted against and perhaps even thrust onto the wooden beam** <note>original: "ξύλῳ ἐντιναχθῆναι" — likely referring to the instrument of execution or the stocks.</note> **by someone like those named before, or even by Crescens, that man who is no lover of wisdom but a lover of empty boast. For it is not worthy to call that man a philosopher who publicly testifies against us, claiming that we Christians are atheists and impious.** <note>Early Christians were often accused of "atheism" because they rejected the traditional Roman pantheon of gods.</note> **He does this to win the favor and pleasure of the many who have been led astray." And after a few more words:** <margin>V 207</margin> **"For I want you to know that when I proposed certain questions to him and interrogated him, I discovered and proved that he truly knows nothing. If these discussions of ours have not been reported to you, I am ready to be questioned again in your presence."**

<margin>P 260</margin>
Indiction 9, Year 12. Under the consulship of Severus and Herennianus. <note>This corresponds to the year 171 AD.</note>

<margin>C</margin> The heresy of the **Encratites** <note>The name comes from the Greek word "enkrateia," meaning "self-control" or "abstinence." They were a radical ascetic group.</note>, which was just then springing up and introducing a strange and destructive false belief into the world, had **Tatian** as its leader. He had been a disciple of **Justin** <note>Justin Martyr, the famous Christian philosopher.</note>; and as long as Justin lived, Tatian did not dare to show any corruption of the healthy faith <margin>5</margin> in Christ. But after Justin’s death, Tatian began—swallowed up by empty words—to teach the doctrine of celibacy <note>Greek: "agamia" (refusal to marry).</note>, just as **Saturninus** and **Marcion** had done before him. Along with them, he quietly set aside the ancient handiwork of God, finding fault with the one who created male and female for the generation of human beings. He also <margin>10</margin> introduced abstinence from what they call "living things" <note>This refers to a strictly vegetarian diet, refusing to eat any meat (animal "souls").</note>, showing ingratitude toward the God who created all things. Furthermore, they argue against the salvation of the first-formed man <note>Adam; Tatian famously argued that the first man could not be saved.</note>, a new idea discovered among them. Tatian was the first to introduce this blasphemy. He also introduced certain "infinite aeons" <note>Spiritual emanations or divine powers in Gnostic theology.</note>, telling myths <margin>15</margin> similar to those of the followers of **Valentinus**. He declared marriage to be nothing but corruption and sexual immorality, much like Marcion and Saturninus. Many others wrote against these people, but **Musanus** wrote quite enough.

**Antoninus the Emperor** <note>Marcus Aurelius.</note> frequently pressed hard upon his enemies, <margin>P 261</margin> being present in person as well as sending out his generals. And **Pertinax**... <margin>20</margin>

<margin>[Olympiad 237, Year 3]</margin>
171 AD. Year 12. Indiction 9. Under the Consulship of Severus and Herennianus.

The heresy of the Encratites, which brought a foreign and deadly opinion into the world, had Tatian as its author. As one of Justin’s listeners, he did not venture to betray the corruption of the untainted faith of Christ so long as Justin lived. But once Justin was dead, Tatian—as if seized by madness or drunk on empty talk—began to preach celibacy, just as Saturninus and Marcion had done before him. Their followers set aside and condemned the ancient work of God, who created male and female for the reproduction of mankind. He also introduced abstinence from those things called "possessed of soul" <note>Original Latin: "Anima praedita" — referring to animals/meat.</note>, being ungrateful mortals toward God, the creator of all. Moreover, they deny the salvation of the first man, Adam, a claim first devised by them: for Tatian was the first to think up this impiety. He also introduces certain undefined "Aeons," mixing in fables like those produced by Valentinus. Claiming that marriage was nearly the same as corruption and debauchery—following the views of Valentinus and Marcion—he was written against by many others, but most effectively by Musanus.

The Emperor Antoninus himself often attacked the enemies...

When **Pertinax** <note>Publius Helvius Pertinax, a high-ranking commander who would later briefly become Emperor.</note> and those with him were being hard-pressed by thirst, a rain from God came upon them; but upon their opponents, the **Germans** and **Sarmatians** <note>Nomadic tribes from the Iranian steppes who frequently clashed with Rome.</note>, a thunderbolt fell, destroying many of them. It is said that letters of the Emperor **Marcus** <note>Marcus Aurelius.</note> are in circulation in which he testifies that his army, which was about to be destroyed, was saved by the prayers of the Christians.

<margin>B</margin> Following the aforementioned Tatian, a certain **Severus** gained power and became the namesake of the **Severian** sect. These people make use of the Law, the Prophets, and the Gospels, but they interpret the meaning of the Holy Scriptures according to their own private views. They blaspheme the Apostle **Paul**, rejecting his letters and refusing to accept the **Acts of the Apostles**.

<margin>V 209</margin> However, their predecessor **Tatian** composed a certain "harmony" <note>original: συνάφειαν (synapheian), a joining together.</note> and collection of the Gospels—I know not how—and titled it the ***Diatessaron*** <note>term: Diatessaron (Through the Four). This was the first major attempt to weave the four separate Gospels into a single, continuous narrative.</note>, which is still in circulation among some even to this day. <margin>C</margin> They say that he even dared to paraphrase certain phrases of the Apostle <note>Paul</note>, as if he were "correcting" the arrangement of his style.

Second after Tatian, whom we mentioned above, was **Severus**, who, being infected by the same heresy, was the author of the name of the **Severians**. They indeed admit the Old Law and the Prophets, and even the Gospels, but they interpret the Holy Scriptures according to their own pleasure. They condemn the Apostle **Paul**, proscribing his letters and even rejecting the **Acts of the Apostles**. They also say that he intended to change the words of the Apostle to others, wishing to "improve" his double meaning and composition. Many of his [writings] are circulated...

# CHRONICON

<margin>P 265</margin> During her father’s lifetime, she <note>Phedalia, daughter of Barbysius</note> built many things in that very trading post <term>emporion</term>, and she also established a statue of Fortune <term>tyche</term> within it, which she named Ceroe. And when her father Barbysius was about to die, he instructed her to build a wall in that place from sea to sea—
<margin>5</margin> which is now the old wall of Constantinople—that is, from the place called Petrion to the Gate of Saint Aemilianus, near the place called the Rhabdos <note>literally "The Rod" or "The Staff"</note>. After the death of her father, the aforementioned Phedalia was married to Byzas, the King of Thrace, and he named the place—that is, the trading post—Byzantium after his own name. This is where the statues of the Victories <note>original: "αἱ Νῖκαι" (the Nikae)</note> now stand,
<margin>R 620</margin> <margin>10</margin> near the district of the Cilicians, and he granted the place the legal rights of a city. After many years, Severus <note>Emperor Septimius Severus</note> came from Rome to Byzantium during this year of his reign, and having seen the beautiful location of the city, he restored the "City of Byzas" and built within it the public bath called the
<margin>V 212</margin>
<margin>15</margin> Zeuxippus. Because a bronze statue of the Sun <note>Helios</note> stood there in the middle of the Four-Sided Portico <term>Tetrastōon</term>, and beneath it was inscribed the name of the Sun, "Zeuxippus." The Thracians used to call the place "Helios" <note>Sun</note>, but the citizens of Byzantium themselves also named that same public bath Zeuxippus according to the name the place formerly held;
<margin>20</margin> they no longer called it "Severium" after the emperor’s own name, as he had ordered. Thus the Four-Sided Portico of the Zeuxippus was established.

# P A S C H A L E.

...where the column of the Sun <note>Helios</note> stood in the middle; and in its place, on the acropolis of this same city of Byzas, he built a temple or shrine to Apollo. He also replaced the other two shrines that had been built previously—one by Byzas to Artemis with the Deer, and the other by Phedalia to Aphrodite. After moving the statue of the Sun from the Four-Sided Portico <term>Tetrastōon</term>, the Emperor Severus placed it high up in the shrine. Opposite the shrine of Artemis, this same emperor built a very large hunting theater <term>kynegiōn</term>, and opposite the shrine of Aphrodite, he built a theater. The aforementioned Severus also built the Hippodrome <term>hippikon</term> in Byzantium, having purchased houses <margin>D</margin> and a garden from certain orphaned brothers; after tearing down the houses and clearing the trees from the garden, he created the Hippodrome for the people of Byzantium. This same Severus also renewed the place called the Strategion <note>The General's Headquarters or Muster-Ground</note>, which had originally been built by Alexander of Macedon when he campaigned against Darius. He called the place "Strategion" because it was there that Alexander of Macedon mustered his army <term>stratologēsas</term> before setting out for the war against the Persians.

...the Four-Sided Portico <term>Quadriporticus</term>, where the statue of the Sun stood in the middle, in place of which he raised a sacred temple to Apollo on the Acropolis of the city of Byzas. He also replaced two other shrines built earlier: one to Diana of the Deer <note>Artemis Elaphaea</note> by Byzas, and one to Venus <note>Aphrodite</note> by Phedalia. The Emperor established the statue of the Sun, moved from the Four-Sided Portico, at the top of the temple; he built a very large hunting arena <term>Cynegium</term> facing the shrine of Diana, and a Theater facing the temple of Venus. Furthermore, the same Severus founded the Circus <note>the Hippodrome</note>, buying buildings and gardens from certain orphaned brothers; having demolished the buildings and uprooted the trees from the gardens, he built the Circus for the Byzantines. That same Severus also restored the Strategion or Headquarters <term>Praetorium</term>, which had long ago been built by Alexander the Macedonian when he undertook the expedition against Darius. He gave the place the name "Strategium" because, after the army had been organized there, Alexander the Macedonian moved his forces against the Persians.

In these times, a certain **Symmachus**, a **Samaritan** and one of the wise men among them, found himself unhonored by his own nation. Stricken by an "infirmity of ambition" <note>original: *philarchian* — a craving for power or status</note> and being resentful toward his own tribe, he went to the **Jews**, became a proselyte, and underwent a second circumcision. To subvert the interpretations held by the **Samaritans**, he translated and published a third version <note>of the Hebrew Scriptures into Greek</note>. **Epiphanius of Cyprus** recorded these matters concerning the three translators: **Aquila**, **Symmachus**, and **Theodotion**. <note>These three figures are famous for producing the Greek versions of the Old Testament that Origen later compiled in his Hexapla.</note>

### CHRONICON

...[to bar him from] entering the church, because Philip had acted lawlessly. 
The lawlessness was of this sort: That Philip the Junior <note>original: "Φίλιππος ἐκεῖνος ὁ Ἰουνίωρ". <margin>R 632 D</margin>
And in Smyrna, in Asia, Pionius was martyred along with many others. He was a learned man and well known as one of those distinguished in the study of Christian doctrine. This occurred under Proclus Quintillianus, the Proconsul of Asia, four days before the Ides of March <note>March 12th</note>, which according to the Asian calendar <margin>10</margin> is the 12th day of the 6th month, on a Saturday at the 10th hour.

Likewise, the bishop of the church of Jerusalem, Alexander, was brought before the provincial courts in Caesarea of Palestine. Having distinguished himself in a second confession <note>original: "ὁμολογίᾳ". A public declaration of faith during trial; Alexander had previously confessed his faith during the persecution of Septimius Severus</note>, he finished his life in a ripe old age and a venerable career, completing the course <margin>15</margin> of martyrdom.

<margin>P 271</margin>
The same Emperor Decius brought fearsome lions and lionesses from Africa and released them into the eastern frontier <term>limiton; the fortified border zone of the Empire</term>, from Arabia and Palestine as far as the fortress of Circesium, so that they might breed a population there as a defense against the barbarian Saracens. Similarly, <margin>20</margin> from the dry regions of Libya, he brought venomous and fearsome male [and female] <note>The Greek text ends abruptly at "male-", but the parallel Latin text completes the thought with "serpents of both sexes" and "sent them to the borders of Egypt"</note>...

# CHRONICLE

...the presbyter <note>original: "σίας πρεσβύτερος" — the start of the name Novatian is missing from the top of the page</note> was saying that they should not be received, as there was no longer any hope of salvation for them, even if they performed every act of genuine conversion. He established himself as the leader of a private heresy of those who were puffed up in their own reasoning and declared themselves "the Pure" <term>Cathari; from the Greek 'katharoi', a group that took a hardline stance against Christians who had lapsed during persecution</term>. <margin>D</margin> For this reason, a very great synod was assembled in Rome, <margin>5</margin> sixty in number of bishops, and even more of presbyters and deacons. After specifically investigating what ought to be done in the other provinces as well, a decree was issued by everyone: that Novatian, along with those who were pridefully raised up with him, and those who chose to agree with his most inhumane opinion toward the brothers, should be considered as strangers to the Church. <margin>10</margin> <margin>P 272</margin> However, they decided to heal and treat those of the brothers who had fallen into the calamity <note>This refers to the 'lapsi', Christians who had renounced their faith or performed pagan sacrifices to avoid execution during Emperor Decius's reign</note> with the medicines of repentance. Concerning these matters, Cornelius, Bishop of the Romans, wrote to Fabius, the Bishop of the Church of the Antiochians, <margin>15</margin> explaining to him the acts of the Roman synod and what had been decided by those in Italy, Africa, and the surrounding regions. Many others also wrote to many people regarding the madness of Novatian and the repentance of those who had fallen during the persecution.

<margin>B</margin> **259th Olympiad.**
**4th Indiction. 2nd Year. Under the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.** <margin>20</margin>

<margin>[Olympiad of Iphitus]</margin>
<margin>Years from the creation of the world / Year of Christ</margin> ...having been warned that they should make God propitious, he <note>Bishop Cornelius</note> gave letters to many bishops concerning them. In these letters, Novatian, a presbyter of the Roman Church, swollen with pride, said they were not to be admitted because no hope of salvation remained for them, even if they performed everything suitable for conversion. He is established as the prince of a private heresy of those who, inflated in mind, call themselves "the Pure" <note>original: "Catharos"</note>. For this reason, a very great council was gathered at Rome of 60 bishops, but many more presbyters and deacons. After an inquiry was made in the remaining provinces about what should be defined, it was finally decreed by all that Novatian, together with his followers and those who embraced that man’s utterly inhumane sentence against the brothers, should be banished from the thresholds of the Church. But those of the brothers who had fallen into this calamity should be healed and cared for with the remedies of penance. Regarding these matters, Cornelius, the Roman Pontiff <note>Bishop of Rome</note>, gave letters to Fabius, the Bishop of the Church of Antioch, in which he explained the decrees of the Roman Synod and the opinion of the bishops of Italy and Africa. But many others also wrote much to several people about the madness of Novatian and the penance of those who had lapsed in the persecution.

<margin>5764. 258 AD. 2nd Year. 4th Indiction.</margin> Under the consulship of Tuscus and Bassus.

# CHRONICLE

Indiction 3. Under the consulship of Carinus for the 2nd time and Numerian.

<margin>B</margin> In the 255th year from the Ascension of the Lord into heaven, a persecution of Christians took place, and many were martyred; among whom were the holy George <note>St. George the Trophy-bearer, though tradition often places his martyrdom slightly later under Diocletian</note> and the holy Babylas. This Babylas was the bishop of Great Antioch. Carinus the emperor reached that city while departing to wage war against the Persians with his uncle Carus; this Carus was struck by lightning in Mesopotamia. Carinus, having been defeated, fled to the city of Carrhae <note>modern Harran, Turkey; a site of several famous Roman military disasters</note>, and the Persians, having surrounded the city, took him prisoner and immediately killed him. After flaying him, they made his skin into 

<margin>C</margin> a sack, and having treated it with myrrh, they kept it for their own glory <note>original: "ἰδίαν δόξαν" — a trophy of their victory</note>. This Carinus died at the age of 36. After his death, his brother Numerian campaigned against the Persians to avenge his own brother Carinus, and he prevailed over them powerfully.

<margin>R 640</margin> Afterward, Numerian was slaughtered in Perinthus of Thrace—the city now called Heraclea <note>modern Marmara Ereğlisi, Turkey</note>—by Aper the prefect.

<margin>D</margin> The 33rd ruler of the Romans, Diocletian, reigned for 20 years. Total years from creation: 5,814. Diocletian, having been proclaimed emperor 15 days before the Kalends of October <note>September 17</note> in Chalcedon, entered Nicomedia 5 days before the Kalends of October <note>September 27</note>.

<margin>284. III. Indiction 3.</margin> Under the consulship of Carinus (II) and Numerian.

> In the year 255 from the Lord's Ascension into heaven, a persecution of Christians was carried out, in which many ended their lives through martyrdom: and among them Saint George and Saint Babylas. The latter was Bishop of Great Antioch, where the Emperor Carinus arrived with his paternal uncle Carus, intending to bring war upon the Persians: indeed, Carus perished in Mesopotamia, having been struck by lightning from heaven. Carinus, however, having been defeated, fled to Carrhae, where he was made a prisoner by the Persians—who had placed their camp at the city—and was immediately killed by them. Having stripped off his skin, they fashioned a sack from it, which they preserved thereafter, rubbed with ointments, as a monument of their victory. Moreover, Carinus died when he was 36 years old. After his death, his brother Numerian, having undertaken an expedition against the Persians, went to avenge his brother, reporting a distinguished victory over them.
> Afterward, Numerian was killed at Perinthus, a city of Thrace which they now call Heraclea, by Aper the Praetorian Prefect.

### PASCHAL CHRONICLE

In the 269th year from the Ascension of the Lord into heaven, and during the aforementioned consulships <note>referring to the previous entry for 297 AD</note>, the holy Gelasinus suffered martyrdom in the city of the Heliopolitans <note>Heliopolis, modern-day Baalbek, Lebanon</note> in the province of Libanensia. This man was a "second mime" <note>a supporting actor in a theatrical troupe</note>; while a public festival was being held in the theater and a great crowd was watching,
<margin>5</margin> <margin>P 276</margin> the other mimes threw him into a large vat <note>original: "βοῦττιν" (bouttin), a large tub or vessel</note> of a bathhouse filled with warm water, mocking the teachings of the Christians and the holy rite of baptism. But this Gelasinus, the second mime, having been baptized and having emerged from the vat, put on white garments <note>the traditional dress of the newly baptized</note> and refused to continue his theatrical performance. He declared: "I am a
<margin>10</margin> Christian; for I saw a terrifying glory in the vat, and as a Christian I shall die." When the people watching in the theater of the city of the Heliopolitans heard these words, they were filled with a great rage; rushing from the tiered benches onto the stage <note>original: "θυμέλη" (thymele), the platform or altar-space in the theater</note>, they seized the holy Gelasinus and dragged him outside the theater while he was still wearing his white garments.
<margin>15</margin> <margin>B</margin> They killed him by stoning, and thus the righteous man reached his perfection <note>a common early Christian term for completing a life of faith through martyrdom</note>. His relatives took up his remains and brought them to the village called Mariamme <note>modern Maryamin, Syria</note>, which was his place of origin outside Heliopolis, and there they built a house of prayer <note>an oratory or chapel</note> for him.
In the time of these same consuls, the Persians were defeated by Maximian
<margin>20</margin> Herculius Augustus <note>Though the victory was won by Caesar Galerius, it is here credited to the senior Emperor Maximian</note>.

---

<note>Critical notes on the Greek text: 3. Libanensia: R. identifies this location. / "This man": P. reads "outos" instead of "ostis". / After "second mime", Malalas adds: "and he entered into the play." 5, 10. "Vat": P. uses the spelling "bouttion". 5. "Bathhouse": PV read "balaniou". 8. "The": omitted by P. 12. "Heliopolitans": P. spells it "Heliopolitōn". 16. "The": omitted by P. 17. "Was": P. uses the verb form "ypērxen".</note>

<margin>Year of Christ</margin> <margin>[Olympiad of Iphitus]</margin>
In the 269th year from the Ascension of the Lord into heaven, and under the same consuls named above, Saint Gelasinus ended his life in martyrdom in the city of the Heliopolitans in Lebanon. Since he was a second-rank Mime, and public games were being celebrated in the theater with the people watching, he was thrown into a large bath-tub full of warm water by the other Mimes, who were mocking the Christian religion and holy baptism. But Gelasinus himself, the second Mime, having been baptized and having come out of the bath-tub, clothed in white garments, refused to proceed into the theater thereafter, saying: "I am a Christian, for I saw a fearsome glory in the tub, and as a Christian I die." When the people watching in the theater of the city of the Heliopolitans saw this, they were set on fire with fury, and rushing from the steps onto the stage, they seized Gelasinus and cast him out of the theater with the very white clothes he was wearing, and overwhelmed him with stones and killed him. His kinsmen carried his body to a village called Mariamme, from which he had originated, outside of Heliopolis, and there they erected an oratory for him.
Under these same consuls, the Persians were defeated in battle by Maximian Herculius Augustus.
<margin>Year 1, 269.</margin>
298 AD. 14th year <note>likely of the Emperor's reign</note>. 2nd Indiction. In the consulship of Anicio Fausto and Severo Gallo.

# CHRONICLE OF EASTER

In the 19th year of the reign of Diocletian, in the month [of August, the 7th day—<note>The scholar Henri Valois (Valesius) suggested this date be deleted as it contradicts the later mention of March.</note>], on the 25th of Dystros <note>original: "δύστρῳ" (dystrō); a Macedonian month corresponding to March.</note>, though this would be called March according to the Romans, <margin>P 277</margin> on the day of the feast of Easter, imperial edicts were spread everywhere. These ordered that the churches be leveled to the ground and that the divine scriptures be destroyed by fire. They further proclaimed that those held in positions of honor and rank should be stripped of their status, and those in domestic service, if they persisted in their commitment to Christianity, were to be deprived of their freedom. Not long after, other letters arrived, commanding that the leaders of the churches and all others in every place should first be delivered into bonds, and then later be forced to sacrifice <note>This refers to the Roman requirement to offer incense or libations to the pagan gods or the Emperor as a test of loyalty.</note> by every possible means. As a result, <margin>B</margin> many struggled through various trials and were perfected <note>original: "τελειωθῆναι" (teleiōthēnai); a term used by early Christians to describe martyrdom as the "perfection" or "completion" of their spiritual journey.</note>, while many others, weakened by fear, grew numb in their souls and fell away.

<margin>R 648</margin> In the same year, many everywhere, as we have said, were perfected through their struggles. Nevertheless, in the city of Nicomedia <note>The capital of the Eastern Roman Empire at the time, located in modern-day Turkey.</note> where the Emperor was residing, Dorotheus and Gorgonius, along with many others from the imperial household service, were perfected. At that time, a great choir of martyrs was revealed. Not long after, Anthimus, the bishop of the church in Nicomedia, was also perfected by being beheaded. Others were cast into fire, and even more were thrown into the sea.

1. August 7th deleted by Valesius. 4. "into" omitted in manuscript R. 5. "on the one hand" omitted in R. 7. "commitment" in manuscript P. 13. "from" in manuscripts P and V. 15. "and" omitted in P. 16. "the" omitted in P. 19. "Not after long" instead of "After not long" in P. See what we said on page 128 C.

---

In the 19th year of Diocletian Augustus, the 7th Indiction, in the month of Dystros, on the 25th day (the month which for the Romans is March), on the festive day of Easter, imperial edicts were set forth everywhere, by which it was ordered that churches be destroyed from their foundations and the sacred Scriptures be burned with fire. It was also ordered that those who held magistracies and honors should be deprived of them and held in disgrace; while other private individuals, if they persisted in the profession of Christianity, should have their liberty taken away. Not much later, other edicts followed, in which it was commanded that the overseers of the churches, and all others wherever they might be, should first be handed over to chains, and then be forced to sacrifice by every kind of punishment applied. By this it happened that thereafter many, after various tortures were endured, died. Many also, who at first with a certain self-confidence openly professed the faith of Christ, afterwards failed in spirit out of fear of the torments and fell away.

In the same year, many everywhere, as we have said, met death by enduring punishments with no less constancy. Also in the city of Nicomedia, while the Emperor was staying there, Dorotheus and Gorgonius, with not a few others from the Emperor's service, ended their lives, and at the same time a huge choir of martyrs appeared. Not long after, Anthimus, the Bishop of the Church of Nicomedia himself, died having been struck in the head; others were condemned to fire, many others were thrown into the sea, since they reached such a great and almost infinite number...

In the current 20th year of his reign, on the 19th day of the month of Daisios <note>The Macedonian month corresponding to June; the date is June 19, 325 AD.</note>, he arranged for a council of 318 holy fathers to meet in Nicaea and for the symbol <note>original: "σύμβολον" (symbolon). # PASCHAL CHRONICLE

From the 16th year of Tiberius <note>The Roman Emperor Tiberius (reigned 14–37 AD); the chronicle uses his reign to anchor the timeline of the Life of Christ.</note>, which is the 2nd year of the 202nd Olympiad <note>A four-year period used by the Greeks for dating; the 202nd Olympiad began in 29 AD.</note>, until the twentieth anniversary of the reign of the great emperor Constantine, and the 2nd year of the 276th and 277th Olympiads.

# CHRONICLE

<margin>B</margin> In Byzantium, he renewed the first wall of the city of Byzas <note>Byzas was the legendary founder of the city in the 7th century BC.</note>, making many additions to that same wall and joining them to the old wall of the city. He named the city Constantinople and also completed the *Hippikon* <term>Hippikon: The Hippodrome, the massive stadium used for chariot racing and public ceremonies.</term>, decorating it with bronze <margin>5</margin> works and every excellence. In it, he constructed a *kathisma* <term>Kathisma: The imperial box or throne room within the Hippodrome, where the emperor appeared before the people.</term> for royal viewing, modeled after the one in Rome. He also built a great palace near this same *Hippikon*, creating an ascent from the palace to the *kathisma* of the *Hippikon* by means of the so-called *Kochlias* <term>Kochlias: Literally "The Snail," a famous spiral staircase that allowed the emperor to move securely from his private quarters to the public arena.</term>. 
<margin>V 227</margin> He also built a great and very beautiful Forum, and he set in the center <margin>R 664</margin> <margin>10</margin> a great porphyry column of wonderful Theban stone. At the top of this same column, he set a great statue of himself, having rays upon its head; this bronze work he had brought from Phrygia. The same Emperor Constantine, having secretly taken from Rome the so-called Palladium <note>The Palladium was an ancient wooden statue of Athena, believed to provide divine protection to whatever city possessed it. Moving it to Constantinople symbolized the city's status as the "New Rome."</note>, placed it in the <margin>15</margin> Forum he had built, beneath the column of his monument, <margin>C</margin> as some of the Byzantines say, having heard it by tradition. After performing an unbloody sacrifice, he named the Fortune of the city—which he had renewed—*Anthousa* <note>original: "Ἀνθοῦσαν." This name means "Flowering" and served as the Greek equivalent of the Roman name "Flora."</note>.

The same emperor also built two grand porticoes <note>original: "ἐμβόλους" (emboloi), referring to covered colonnaded walkways.</note> from the entrance <margin>20</margin> of the palace as far as the Forum; these were quite beautiful and decorated with statues and marbles. He named the area of the porticoes the *Regia* <note>meaning "The Royal Way."</note>. Nearby, he also built a Basilica <note>A public building for legal and civic business.</note> containing a conch <note>An apse or semi-circular niche.</note>, and on the outside, he placed great columns and statues...

-> 2. not a few [additions] to the same wall [Manuscript] P. <-

He restored the wall of the city of Byzantium, with no small additions, which he joined to the wall of the old city, the city itself being called Constantinople. He furthermore finished the Circus <note>The Latin translation of "Hippikon."</note>, which he decorated with bronze statues and other ornaments: he also completed the Tribunal <note>The Latin translation of "Kathisma."</note>, from which the Emperor might watch the Circus games, after the likeness of that which was in Rome. A great Palace having been built additionally next to the Circus, he created an ascent through the *Cochlea* from the same palace into the Tribunal of the Circus. He also built a Great and altogether splendid Forum, in the middle of which he placed a huge and marvelous Porphyry Column of Theban stone, upon which he placed his own very large statue, having rays on its head: which bronze work, indeed, he saw to being brought from Phrygia. The same Emperor Constantine, having secretly removed from Rome the Palladium, as it is called, hidden it in the Forum built by him, under the Column upon which his statue was placed, as some of the Byzantines assert, who received this by tradition. The Fortune of the City restored by him, after an unbloody sacrifice was made, he called *Florentia* <note>The Latin equivalent of "Anthousa."</note>.

The same Emperor built twin Porticoes from the entrance of the Palace all the way to the Forum, very elegant, adorned with statues and marbles, giving the name *Regia* to the place of the Porticoes: next to which he raised a Basilica with a Conch, and with huge columns and statues outside the building, which [is called] the Senate...

In the 301st year after the Lord’s ascension into the heavens, and the 25th year of his own reign, Constantine the most pious—father of Constantine the Younger Augustus and of Constantius and Constans <margin>P 285</margin> Caesars—having built a most great, brilliant, and prosperous city, and having honored it with a Senate, named it Constantinople on the fifth day before the Ides of May <note>The Roman method of dating; this corresponds to May 11th.</note>, on the second day of the week <note>Monday, May 11, 330 AD.</note>, during the third indiction. He was the first to celebrate a chariot racing contest [to mark the inauguration], and he was the first to wear a diadem <term>Diadem: A headband made of pearls and precious silk, marking the transition from the Roman "principate" (where the emperor was "first citizen") to the more formal, jewel-encrusted "dominate" style of monarchy.</term> made of pearls and other precious stones. He held a great festival, commanding by his divine decree <note>original: *theiou typou*. A formal imperial edict.</note> that the city's birthday be celebrated on that same day every year, and that the public bath be opened on the 11th of the same month of Artemisios <note>The Greek name for the month of May.</note>.

# CHRONICON

<margin>B R 666</margin> ...the Zeuxippus <note>The grand public baths of Constantinople.</note>, being near the Hippodrome and the Royal Palace <note>original: *Regia*. The main imperial residence.</note>, he made for himself another gilded wooden statue <note>original: *xoanon*. While usually referring to ancient wooden cult images, here it describes a ceremonial imperial statue.</note> carrying in its right hand the Fortune <note>original: *tyche*. The personification of a city's prosperity and protective spirit.</note> of the city, which was also gilded. He commanded that on the day of the city’s birthday games, this same wooden statue should be brought in, escorted by the troops wearing military cloaks and ceremonial boots <note>original: *chlanidion* and *kampagion*. These garments signified the formal, festive dress of the imperial guard.</note>, all of them carrying white candles. The chariot carrying the statue was to circle the upper turn of the track and proceed to the mark <note>original: *skamma*. This likely refers to a specific line on the Hippodrome floor located directly in front of the emperor's viewing box.</note> opposite the imperial seat. Then the emperor of the time would rise and <margin>C</margin> pay homage <note>original: *proskynein*. A formal act of bowing or prostration.</note> to the statue of the same Emperor Constantine and to the Fortune of the city itself.

The same most divine Emperor Constantine remained ruling in Constantinople, having detached it from the province of Europe—that is, from its metropolis, Heraclea—and having <margin>V 228</margin> appointed for this same Constantinople a Praetorian Prefect <note>One of the highest administrative officials in the Empire.</note>, a City Prefect, and other great officials.

From the founding of Rome until the dedication of Constantinople, there are 1,080 years.

<margin>D</margin> In this year, Alexander, Bishop of Alexandria, passed away on the 14th day before the Kalends of May <note>April 18.</note>, the 22nd of Pharmuthi <note>A month in the Egyptian/Coptic calendar.</note>. In his place, Athanasius, the great father, was ordained as bishop.

...the Zeuxippus, which lies adjacent to the Circus and the Royal Palace, was opened. And when he had fashioned for himself another gilded statue of carved work, which carried the Fortune of the City in its right hand—and this too was gilded—he commanded that on the day the games were held for the City’s Birthday, that same statue should enter, escorted by soldiers dressed in cloaks and boots, all carrying white candles. The chariot on which the statue was carried was to circle the upper Turn, and proceed to the Mark directly opposite the Imperial Box. The Emperor reigning at that time, rising from his throne, would adore the statue of the same Emperor Constantine and the Fortune of the City itself.

From the founding of Rome to the year in which Constantinople was dedicated, 1,080 years are reckoned.

# P A S C H A L [CHRONICLE]

Sixteenth day before the Kalends of June <note>original: *prò 16 kalandōn Iouniōn*. In the Roman calendar, this corresponds to May 17th. There is some chronological tension here, as the text links it to Pentecost, which fell on May 22nd in 337 AD.</note>, on the very day of Holy Pentecost, while the body <note>original: *skēnōmatos*. Literally "tabernacle" or "tent," a respectful way to refer to the remains of the deceased emperor.</note> of the pious Constantine was still lying
<margin>V 229</margin> unburied in the palace of Constantinople, guarded until his sons could be notified.

<margin>P 287</margin> Constantius, hearing the news while in the East in Mesopotamia—where the Persian war was still a pressing threat—immediately set out for Constantinople. Upon his arrival, he escorted his father, the celebrated Constantine, in such a grand procession and imperial glory that it cannot be worthily described. The army was present, standing in armor as if the Emperor were still alive. The entire city,
<margin>R 670</margin> which he himself had proclaimed as "Rome" <note>Constantinople was often referred to as "New Rome" or simply "Rome" to signify its status as the new capital.</note>, turned out. Amidst all the glorious events and the distributions of the granted grain rations <term>annonae</term> <note>original: *annōnōn*. These were the state-sponsored food distributions essential to the city's welfare and a key privilege of its citizens.</note>, everyone was in such deep mourning. Never before had an emperor been so glorified both in life and after death.
<margin>B</margin> He was laid to rest in the Church of the Holy Apostles, where the relics of the holy apostles Andrew, Luke the Evangelist, and Timothy (the disciple of the apostle Paul) are kept.

Sapor, King of the Persians, invaded Mesopotamia with the intent of plundering Nisibis <note>Nisibis was a vital Roman frontier fortress in modern-day Turkey/Syria.</note>. After besieging it for sixty-three days and failing to capture it, he withdrew.

The 35th reign of the Romans began after the death of their father Constantine: Constantine the Younger, Constans, and Constantius reigned together for 24 years. Total: 5,870 years <note>This refers to the Byzantine "Era of the World" (Anno Mundi), counting from a calculated date of creation.</note>.

...separated by a distance; the name of the village was **Thraucun**. A Jew joined them as a companion on the journey. Immediately the Jew turned to them and said, *"If you eat this dead snake and do not die, I shall become a Christian."* And immediately Eugenius, having picked up the snake, divided it into three parts, and having reserved one for himself and given the other two to his companions, they devoured these in the presence of the Jew, receiving no harm from it. In this, that Gospel and saving saying was fulfilled: *In their hands they shall take up snakes, and if they drink anything deadly, it will not harm them.* Therefore the Jew, having returned with them to the Inn and remaining in it, later became famous after being made a Christian.

**Constantius Augustus**, while he was occupied in the parts of the East on account of the **Persian war**, and having received news of what had been carried out by **Magnentius**, set out from **Antioch** into **Italy**.

He, when he understood the cause of the danger, struck with fear, commanded the war machines to be burned and whatever he had prepared for the war apparatus to be destroyed, and taking flight with his men, with no one pursuing, he returned to his own country.

<margin>P 292</margin> ...with all honor, an escort, and many gifts, Constantius sent him to live in the city of **Prusias** in **Bithynia** <note>original: "Προυσιάδι τῆς Βιθυνίας" — Prusias ad Mare (modern Gemlik, Turkey) was a prosperous city in the Roman province of Bithynia.</note>, where he received rations and abundant provisions. Being a Christian, **Vetranio** attended the church assemblies, gave alms to the poor, and honored the leaders of the church until the end of his life.

**9th Indiction.** **14th Year.** In the consulship of **Sergius** and **Nigrinianus** <note>original: "Σεργίου καὶ Νιγρινιανοῦ" — This corresponds to the year 351 AD.</note>.

**Constantius Augustus**, now reigning as sole emperor, proclaimed his cousin **Gallus** as **Caesar** <note>original: "Καίσαρα" — A Caesar was a junior emperor or heir-apparent to the senior Augustus.</note> and partner in his rule, 
<margin>B</margin> renaming him **Constantius** <note>It was common for members of this dynasty to adopt the name of the reigning emperor or his father to emphasize legitimacy.</note>. This took place on the **Ides of March** <note>March 15th.</note>. He then sent him to **Antioch** in the East, as the **Persians** were launching attacks.

The **sign of the Cross of Christ** was seen in **Jerusalem** during this time. It was about the **third hour** <note>Approximately 9:00 AM.</note> on the day of **Pentecost**, appearing like light stretched across the sky on the **Nones of May** <note>original: "νώναις μαΐαις" — May 7th, 351 AD.</note>. It extended from the **Mount of Olives** to **Golgotha**, the place where the Lord was crucified toward the east, and from where the Lord ascended. Around the visible holy cross was a crown, like a **rainbow** in appearance. At the same hour, it was also seen in **Pannonia** <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans.</note> by **Constantius Augustus** and the army that was with him during the war against **Magnentius** <note>Magnentius was a Western usurper who had killed Constantius's brother, Constans.</note>. 
<margin>C</margin> Once Constantius began to prevail, Magnentius engaged him near the city called **Mursa** <note>Modern-day Osijek, Croatia. The Battle of Mursa Major was one of the bloodiest in Roman history.</note>. Having been defeated, Magnentius fled to **Gaul** with only a few men.

<summary>This page records the honorable retirement of Vetranio in Bithynia, the appointment of Gallus as Caesar to defend the Eastern frontier, and the miraculous appearance of a celestial Cross over Jerusalem, which coincided with Constantius II's victory over the usurper Magnentius.</summary>

Julian, having learned of the death of Constantius Augustus, openly professed his apostasy and impiety. Having sent an edict against Christianity throughout the whole world, he commanded all the idols to be restored. Inflated by this, the Gentiles <note>Latin: "Gentiles" — pagans</note> who were in the East immediately seized and killed George, the Bishop of the city of Alexandria in Egypt. Mocking his corpse impiously, they placed it on a camel and carried it through the whole city. Then, having collected the carcasses of various animals along with their bones, they mixed them with his remains, burned them, and dispersed the ashes.

In Palestine also, they dug up and scattered the relics of Saint John the Baptist, which had been deposited at Sebaste.

Having also opened the tomb of Patrophilus, Bishop of the Church of Scythopolis, they scattered some parts of the body, but his skull they mockingly fixed and hung for use as a lamp.

In Gaza and Ascalon, they killed priests and virgins, and having then opened their bodies and filled them with barley, they exposed them to pigs.

In Phoenicia, moreover, having killed Cyril the Deacon of Heliopolis, they tasted his liver, because he had overturned their idols while Constantine of blessed memory was reigning. But in what manner the one who had dissected the Deacon...

In Emesa, they entered the great church and set up an idol of Dionysus <note>original: "Διονύσου" — the Greek god of wine and ecstasy, often associated by Christians with pagan excess</note>.

...and had tasted the liver, it is worth setting forth how he finished his life. He lost his rotting tongue; he spat out his broken teeth; his eyes, after immense tortures, were seized; finally, having been most dreadfully tortured in his whole body, he laid down his life.

In Emesa, moreover, they entered the great church and erected an idol of Bacchus <note>original: "Bacchi" — the Latin name for Dionysus</note> within it.

Similarly also in Epiphania, a city of Syria, the Gentiles brought an idol into the church with pipes and drums. Furthermore, the blessed Eustathius, Bishop of the same church, a pious and religious man, having heard the pipes, asked where these things were being done; and having understood that it was done in the church, fired with zeal for the faith, as soon as he heard these things, he prayed to God that he might not be forced to behold such things with his eyes, and gave up his spirit.

Moreover, when Julian had come to Constantinople, and Eudoxius was then Bishop of the city, having constructed snares against the Church by various arts, he busied himself with bringing confusion into it, commanding that all who before this time had been removed from office on account of various absurd opinions should be restored to the churches, having seized an opportunity for harassing the churches of God from the disturbances stirred up in this manner.

So therefore Meletius, who because of impiety and other crimes had been deposed...

...without the men who inhabited it. And once this was confirmed and a written peace treaty was established, the Emperor **Jovian** <note>Jovian was a Christian emperor who ruled for only eight months; his primary legacy was this peace treaty which ended the Roman-Persian war at a high territorial cost</note> took with him one of the Persian satraps <note>original: "σατραπῶν" - a high-ranking governor or official in the Persian Empire</note> who was with the envoy, a man named **Junius**, to take over the province and its capital city. And when the same Emperor Jovian reached the city of **Nisibis** <note>A vital Roman frontier fortress in Mesopotamia, now Nusaybin in modern Turkey</note>, he did not enter it, but stayed outside the walls. Then **Junius**, the Persian satrap, having entered the city at the Emperor's command, placed a Persian standard <note>A flag or military symbol indicating Persian ownership</note> upon one of the towers, while the Emperor of the Romans ordered all the citizens, with all their possessions, down to the last person, to depart immediately. 

<margin>P 300</margin> <margin>10</margin> And **Silvanus**, a man of the rank of Count <term>comes</term> <note>A high-ranking Roman title, here indicating a provincial official</note> and a leader of the same city, came out to him and fell before the Emperor, pleading with him not to hand the city over to the Persians. But when he could not persuade him—for the Emperor claimed he had sworn an oath and did not wish to have the reputation of a perjurer among all men—
<margin>15</margin> [Jovian] fortified a village that was outside the walls of the city of **Amida** <note>Modern Diyarbakır, Turkey</note> and joined its wall to the wall of the city of Amida, calling the village **Nisibis** <note>This was a symbolic act to relocate the "spirit" and population of the lost city to Roman territory</note>. There he made all the people from the region of **Mygdonia** live; and he immediately brought **Silvanus** the leader out of Mesopotamia, along with every Christian.

...at the city of **Nisibis**, with only the walls remaining, stripped of all its citizens. These things having been כך confirmed, and the conditions of peace recorded on tablets, Emperor **Jovian** took with him one of the Persian Satraps, who had come with the envoy, named **Junius**, so that he might receive the province and its capital, the city of the **Nisibenes**. The Emperor, however, did not enter it, but halted outside the walls. **Junius**, the Persian Satrap, entered the city by the Emperor's command and fixed the Persian standard upon one of the towers, while the Emperor ordered all citizens to a man to depart with all their goods. But **Silvanus**, a Count <term>Comes</term> by rank and a Senator <term>Decurio</term> <note>A member of the local city council responsible for administration</note> of the same city, came out and prostrated himself at the Emperor's feet, earnestly praying that he would not surrender the city to the Persians. Yet he did not persuade the Emperor, who said he was bound by a sacred oath and did not wish to incur the guilt of perjury at all. He fortified a village that was outside the walls of the city of **Amida**, and joined the walls of the village with the walls of the city of Amida, bestowing the name of the "Nisibene Village" upon it. There he settled everyone summoned from the region of **Mygdonia**; he also immediately brought back **Silvanus** the Count from Mesopotamia, along with all the Christians, and handed over the high offices and Prefectures to Christians.

With the peace with the Persians concluded, and leaving the East, Emperor Jovian within a short time hurried toward **Constantinople** because of the winter, which had set in severely.

<margin>P 301</margin>
As soon as **Valentinian** began his reign, he succeeded the Praetorian Prefect **Sallustius**. After placing Sallustius under bond <note>original: "ὑπὸ ἐγγύας" (hypo engyas); a legal requirement for an official to provide security or stay under surveillance while their conduct in office is audited</note>, Valentinian issued public proclamations against him, stating that if anyone had been wronged by him, they should approach the Emperor Valentinian. However, no one came forward against Sallustius, for he was a man of the greatest integrity <note>original: "ἁγνότατος" (hagnotatos); literally "most pure" or "most holy," referring here to his incorruptibility in civil service</note>.

# CHRONICLE

<header>CHRONICLE</header>

...those who were doing wrong, stealing, and giving false judgments. <margin>P 302</margin> And the chamberlain <term>praepositus; the high-ranking official in charge of the imperial household</term> of his palace, named **Rhodanus**, a powerful and wealthy man who managed the palace—being the Grand Chamberlain <note>original: "ἀρχιευνοῦχον" (archieunouchon); the chief eunuch</note> and held in great honor—the Emperor had him burned alive <margin>5</margin> in the *sphendone* <note>The "sling" or curved U-shaped end of the Hippodrome</note> of the Hippodrome with brushwood, while the crowds at the Hippodrome watched.

This same chamberlain, **Rhodanus**, had seized the property of a certain widow named **Berenice**, weaving a plot against her because of his great power. She approached the Emperor **Valentinian** to complain against the chamberlain. The Emperor appointed the patrician **Salustius** as judge for them, who then condemned this same chamberlain <margin>10</margin> <margin>R 702</margin> **Rhodanus**. When the Emperor learned of the verdict from the patrician Salustius, he ordered the chamberlain to return to the widow what he had stolen from her. But Rhodanus could not be persuaded to return <margin>B</margin> what he had stolen; instead, he challenged the authority of the patrician Salustius. Indignant at this, Salustius <margin>15</margin> instructed the woman to approach the Emperor while the Hippodrome games were in progress. The woman approached the Emperor Valentinian on the morning of the fourth race <note>original: "δ’ βαΐῳ" (d’ baio); referring to the fourth heat or prize-round of the games</note>, while the chamberlain was standing near him. The Emperor gave the order, and the chamberlain was dragged down from the *kathisma* <note>The imperial box or throne-seat in the Hippodrome</note> in the sight of everyone; he was taken to the *sphendone* and burned. <margin>20</margin> The Emperor then granted the widow **Berenice** all the property of the chamberlain Rhodanus, and he was cheered by the people.

<note>Translation of the Latin Parallel Text:</note>

...he put to death. He also ordered the Chamberlain of the Palace, Rhodanus by name, a powerful and wealthy man—as he was the first among the Eunuchs and held in great veneration—to be burned alive in the *Funda* <note>The Latin term for the sphendone or "sling" of the circus</note> of the Circus with dry brushwood while the people were attending the spectacles.

This same Chamberlain Rhodanus, relying on his power, had snatched the goods of a certain widow, Berenice, through false accusation. She, however, went to the Emperor Valentinian to act against the Chamberlain; the Emperor gave them the Patrician Salustius as judge, by whom Rhodanus was condemned. When the Emperor understood the decree of the Patrician Salustius, he commanded the Chamberlain Rhodanus to restore to the widow what he had snatched. But Rhodanus could not be brought to return what he had taken from the widow, but instead appealed against the Patrician Salustius. Salustius, truly indignant, instructed the woman to approach the Emperor when the Circus spectacles were being watched. The woman approached the Emperor Valentinian around the time of the first prize-heat <note>Latin: "primi Bravii"</note>, while the Chamberlain was standing near him. Then, by the Emperor’s mandate, the Chamberlain was cast down from the Tribunal in the sight of all, taken into the *Funda*, and burned. Immediately, the Emperor assigned all the property of the Chamberlain Rhodanus to the woman Berenice, [praising him] with the whole people and the Senate itself, on account of his justice and severity...

# CHRONICLE

<header>PASCHALE</header>

**Theodosius Augustus** was elevated to the rank of Emperor in **Sirmium** <note>A major Roman city in modern-day Serbia</note> by **Gratian Augustus**, who was his brother-in-law, in the month of Audynaeus, fourteen days before the Kalends of February <note>January 19, 379 AD. The "Audynaeus" is a month in the Macedonian calendar often used in Byzantine records.</note>. He entered **Constantinople** in the month of Dios, eight days before the Kalends of December <note>November 24, 380 AD; however, the chronicle places this within the context of the year 379</note>.

**7th Indiction. Year 1. In the consulship of Ausonius and Olybrius.** <note>379 AD</note>

<margin>D</margin> Under these consuls, Emperor **Theodosius** handed over the churches to the **Orthodox** <note>referring to those who followed the Nicene Creed</note>, after issuing sacred edicts everywhere and driving out those called the **Arian Exokionitai** <note><term>Exokionitai</term>: A sect of Arians who were forced to meet outside the city walls of Constantinople at a district called the Exokionion (the "Outer Column").</note>. He also destroyed the temples of the Greeks <note>original: "Ἑλλήνων"—here meaning Pagans</note> to the very foundations.

**Constantine** of blessed memory, during his reign, only closed the sacred sites and temples of the Greeks; but this **Theodosius** also demolished them. He destroyed the great and world-renowned temple of **Baal-Helios** <note>original: "Βαλανίου", likely referring to Baal in Heliopolis</note> at **Heliopolis** <note>Modern-day Baalbek, Lebanon</note>, famous for its <term>trilithon</term> <note>A group of three massive stone blocks forming part of the temple podium, among the largest stones ever moved by humans.</note>, and he turned it into a Christian church. In the same way, he also made the temple of **Damascus** into a Christian church. Thus, the affairs of the Christians flourished greatly during his reign.

<margin>P 304</margin> ->290th Olympiad<-

**8th Indiction. Year 2. In the consulship of Gratian Augustus for the 6th time and Theodosius Augustus.** <note>380 AD</note>

379. 1. 7th Indiction. In the consulship of **Ausonius** and **Olybrius**.
<margin>3.</margin> Under these consuls, Emperor **Theodosius** delivered the churches to the orthodox, having sent out sacred commands everywhere, and he expelled the **Arians**, called **Exokionitai**. Indeed, he destroyed the temples of the Pagans from their foundations.

The renowned **Constantine**, while he ruled, merely closed the shrines of the Pagans; but this **Theodosius** even overthrew them. He made the huge and most celebrated temple of **Balanius** in the city of **Heliopolis**, constructed with the three-stone masonry <note>original Latin: "marmore trilitho"</note>, into a Church of the Christians; and in like manner he handed over the shrine of **Damascus** to the Christians. The Christian name was greatly increased under the rule of **Theodosius**.

<margin>R 706</margin> Under these consuls, **Gratian Augustus**, the son of **Valentinian the Great**, suffered from a disease of the spleen and remained ill for a long time. While he was going up into the **Hippodrome** of **Constantinople** to view the games, passing through the **Cochlea** <note>original: "Κοχλίου" (Koxliou) — a spiral staircase leading from the Great Palace directly into the imperial box of the Hippodrome</note> near the gate of the so-called **Decimus**, his stepmother **Justina** arranged for him to be assassinated because he was a Christian <note>meaning a follower of the Nicene/Orthodox faith; the chronicle highlights the sectarian divide</note>; for she herself was an **Arian** <note>a follower of Arius, who believed Jesus was a created being rather than equal to God the Father</note>.

<margin>B</margin> **9th Indiction. Year 3. In the consulship of Syagrius and Eucherius.** <note>381 AD</note>
In the three hundred and fifty-first year from the Ascension of the Lord into heaven, a synod of 150 holy and blessed fathers was assembled in **Constantinople** <note>This is the Second Ecumenical Council</note>. They strengthened the Creed of Orthodoxy and struck down **Macedonius**, whose mind was likewise muddled by Arianism. This impious man did not shrink from asserting that the incomprehensible and invisible **Holy Spirit**—who is co-eternal with the Father and the Son—was a created being subject to time.

# CHRONICLE

<margin>B</margin> In this same year <note>395 AD</note>, the body of **Theodosius the Great** entered **Constantinople** in the month of **Dios** <note>The Macedonian month corresponding to November</note>, five days before the Ides of November <note>November 9</note>, and was laid to rest on that same day.
And **Rufinus**, the **Praetorian Prefect** <note>One of the highest administrative officials in the Empire</note>, was killed at the **Hebdomon** <note>A military parade ground and suburb seven miles from the city center of Constantinople</note> by the army.

->**294th Olympiad**<-

**9th Indiction. Year 2. In the consulship of Arcadius Augustus [for the 4th time] and Honorius Augustus [for the 3rd time].** <note>396 AD</note>
This **Arcadius**, the son of **Theodosius the Great**, had **Eudoxia** as his wife, from whom **Theodosius the Younger** was born. He also had 
<margin>C</margin> daughters named **Pulcheria**, **Arcadia**, and **Marina**. Of these, two were notable builders: **Arcadia** built the public baths known as the **Arcadianas**, and **Marina** built the palace known as the **House of Marina**. Later, **Pulcheria** married **Marcian** <note>Who eventually became Emperor from 450–457 AD</note>. **Arcadia** also built the sacred church of **Saint Andrew**, which is called the **Arcadia district**.
There are 335 full years from the time the holy apostles **Peter** and **Paul** reached their perfection <note>original: "ἐτελειώθησαν" – a term for martyrdom, implying they completed their earthly race</note> until the aforementioned consuls, specifically up to the 28th of the month of **June**.

**396 AD. Year 2. 9th Indiction. In the consulship of Arcadius Augustus [IV] and Honorius Augustus [III].** <margin>4.</margin>
This **Arcadius**, son of **Theodosius the Great**, had as his spouse **Eudoxia**, from whom was born **Theodosius the Younger**. He also had daughters: **Pulcheria**, **Arcadia**, and **Marina**. <margin>B</margin> **13th Indiction. Year 7. In the 10th consulship of Honorius and the 6th of Theodosius the Younger Augustus.** <note>415 AD</note>

Under these consuls, the young Emperor **Theodosius II** celebrated his **Quinquennalia** <note>a major festival held every five years to celebrate the continuation of the Emperor's reign</note> in Constantinople in the month of **Audynaios**, on the third day before the Ides of January <note>January 11, 415 AD</note>. Also, the death of **Thermantia** <note>daughter of the general Stilicho and second wife of the Western Emperor Honorius</note>, the wife of the Lord Emperor Honorius, was announced in the month of **Panemos**, on the third day before the Kalends of August, a Friday <note>July 30, 415 AD</note>.

In the same year, in the month of **Gorpiaios**, on the eighth day before the Kalends of October, a Friday <note>September 24, 415 AD</note>, news arrived that the barbarian **Ataulf** <note>the King of the Visigoths and successor to Alaric</note> had been killed in the upper regions <note>likely referring to Gaul or Hispania</note> by the Lord Honorius. On the following day, after the lighting of the lamps <note>the evening ceremony</note>, **chariot races** were held, and a triumphal procession entered the city.

<margin>V 247 C</margin> In the same year, the dedication of the **Great Church** <note>the first Hagia Sophia, which had been rebuilt after being destroyed by fire in 404 AD</note> of Constantinople was performed in the month of **Gorpiaios**, on the sixth day before the Ides of October, a Sunday <note>October 10, 415 AD</note>.

<margin>R 718</margin> Also, the **relics** of **Joseph**, the son of Jacob, and **Zechariah**, the father of Saint John the Baptist, were brought into Constantinople via the **Chalcedon Landing** <note>a major pier on the Golden Horn for travelers arriving from across the Bosporus</note> in the month of **Gorpiaios**, on the sixth day before the Nones of September, a Saturday <note>September 4, 415 AD</note>. **Atticus**, the Patriarch of Constantinople, and **Moses**, the Bishop of Antaradus in Phoenicia, carried these relics in two **caskets** <note>original: γλωσσοκόμοις (glossokomois); literally "tongue-boxes," a term used for reliquaries</note> while seated in **ceremonial carriages** <note>original: βουριχαλλίοις (bourichalliois); light, four-wheeled carriages used by high-ranking clergy or officials</note>. These relics were deposited in the Great [Church]...

## 300th Olympiad.

<margin>D</margin> **3rd Indiction. 12th year [of the reign of Theodosius]. Under the consulship of Theodosius the Younger Augustus (for the 9th time) and Constantius (for the 3rd time).** <note>420 AD. An "Indiction" was a 15-year tax cycle used by the Romans and Byzantines for dating.</note>

<margin>5</margin> <margin>V 248</margin>
As **Theodosius the Younger Augustus** advanced in age, he used to read and study in the palace during the lifetime of his father <note>Emperor Arcadius, who died in 408 AD</note>. After the death of his father, a certain youth named **Paulinus** used to study with him; he was the son of a certain **Count of the Domestics** <note>term: *comes domesticorum*; the commander of the elite corps of the imperial guard</note>. 
<margin>10</margin> <margin>P 311</margin>
Theodosius was very fond of him. When the same Theodosius the Younger Augustus reached manhood, he sought to take a lady <note>original Greek: *despoina*</note> in marriage. He importuned his sister, the lady **Pulcheria**, who was a virgin <note>Pulcheria had taken a vow of perpetual virginity and acted as regent for her brother</note>. She, in turn, because she loved her own brother, had chosen not to be married to anyone. 
<margin>15</margin>
She made inquiries concerning many young virgins—the daughters of patricians and those of royal blood—wishing for someone who would live with her brother in the palace. But Theodosius said to her: 
"I wish to find a young woman who is very beautiful, such that no other woman in **Constantinople** possesses such beauty; she should also be of royal blood. But if she is not beautiful to an extreme degree, I have no need <margin>B</margin> of high rank, nor royal blood, nor wealth. Rather, even if she is the daughter of anyone at all, let her only be very lovely..."

<margin>C</margin> Her father, the philosopher Heraclitus, who also had two sons, made a will as he was about to die. In that same will, he stated: "To Athenais, my most beloved daughter, I wish only one hundred coins <note>term: *nomismata*; the standard gold currency of the Roman and Byzantine Empire</note> to be given; for her own fortune <note>original: "tyche"; this refers to her natural gifts of beauty and intellect, which the father believed would ensure her success without money</note>, which surpasses all womanly fortune, is sufficient for her." And so her father, Heraclitus the wise Athenian, died. 

<margin>D</margin> After his death and the terms of the will were revealed, this same Athenais entreated her brothers—as they were older than her—falling at their feet and begging them not to follow the will strictly, but to let her receive a third part of their father's property. She argued she had done nothing wrong, saying, "Even you know how I conducted myself toward our common <gloss>parent</gloss>..."

### PASCHAL [CHRONICLE]

Having brought them forward, she placed them under consideration for rank, and she made them dignitaries, with the Emperor **Theodosius** promoting them. She appointed the one called **Gesius** as Praetorian Prefect <term>Praetorian Prefect: one of the highest administrative officials in the Empire</term> of the Illyrian nation, and **Valerian** as Master <note>original: "magistron"; specifically the Master of Offices, a senior administrative role</note>. ...summoned them and promoted them to honors, with Emperor Theodosius advancing them. He made Gesius the Praetorian Prefect of Illyricum, and Valerian the Master, while Eudocia Augusta repeatedly said to her brothers: *“Unless you had treated me badly, I would never have been compelled to come to Constantinople, nor would I have ruled. Therefore, the Empire which my birth portended, you have conceded; for my good fortune rendered you harsher toward me, not your own will.”*

The Emperor Theodosius, moreover, advanced Paulinus as his friend and the mediator of the marriage, and his frequent guest, through all grades of honor to high dignities, and finally named him Master; he was increased in honor so that whenever he pleased, he was permitted to meet with Theodosius Augustus and the Augusta, as their Bridal Attendant.

In this year was dedicated the statue of Arcadius, which stands above the spiral of the column in the Forum of Arcadius, in the place called Xerolophus, in the month of Panemos, on the 6th day before the Ides of July, on the Sabbath day.

In this same year, a victory won over the Persians was reported, in the month of Gorpiaeus, on the 8th day before the Ides of September, on the third day of the week.

### 306th Olympiad

| | | | |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|

<margin>P 316</margin>

<margin>R 732</margin>
In this year, as Emperor Theodosius was proceeding to the church for the feast of the Holy Epiphany <term>Epiphany: a major Christian feast day commemorating the manifestation of Christ, often associated with his baptism in the Eastern tradition</term>, it happened that Paulinus the Master <term>Master: refers to the *Magister Officiorum*, the "Master of Offices," one of the most powerful administrative roles in the late Roman Empire</term> fell ill with a foot ailment and remained behind, unable to join the procession, having excused himself. 

A certain poor man brought to Emperor Theodosius a Phrygian apple <note>Phrygia was a region in modern-day Turkey known for its agriculture</note> that was extraordinarily large, exceeding all measure. Both the Emperor and the entire Senate were marveled by it. Immediately, the Emperor gave the poor man 150 gold coins <note>original Greek: "nomismata"</note> and sent the apple to the Augusta <term>Augusta: the title for the Empress</term> Eudocia. 

The Empress then sent it to Paulinus, the Master and friend of the Emperor. However, that same Master, being unaware that the Emperor had sent it to the Empress, sent it back again to Emperor Theodosius as he was leaving the church. The Emperor accepted it without the Empress's knowledge, and having hidden it, he summoned the Empress and asked her, "Where is the apple that I sent to you?" 

She replied, "I ate it." Then he made her swear an oath by his own safety <note>A formal and solemn Roman oath</note> whether she had eaten it or sent it to someone. She swore that she had sent it to no one, but had eaten it herself. Then the Emperor commanded the apple to be brought in, and he showed it to her.

### 306th Olympias.

444 AD. 36th year. 12th Indiction. During the 18th consulship of Theodosius and the consulship of Albinus.

In this year, while Emperor Theodosius was going to the Church on the feast day of the holy Epiphany, it happened that Paulinus the Master lay ill with a foot disease, and did not take part in the procession, having excused himself. Meanwhile, a certain poor man offered a Phrygian apple of a size beyond what is usual, at which the Emperor and the entire Senate were amazed. He immediately ordered 150 gold coins to be paid to the poor man, and sent the apple to the Empress Eudocia; the Empress, in turn, sent it to Paulinus the Master and friend of the Emperor. 

But this same Paulinus the Master, since he did not know that it had been sent by the Emperor to the Empress, sent that very same apple back to Emperor Theodosius as he was departing from the Church. The Emperor received it without the Empress knowing and hid it. Having called for the Empress, he asked: *“Where is the apple that I sent to you?”* She truly replied, *“I ate it.”* Then the Emperor, having demanded a sacred oath from her by his own safety, asked again whether she had eaten it or sent it to another? She swore that she had eaten it. Then the Emperor ordered the apple to be produced, and he showed it to her when it was brought. From this event, a divorce and separation came between them; he held Paulinus under suspicion from then on, and at last, he ordered him to be put to death. Wherefore...

<summary>This page narrates the famous anecdote of the "Apple of Eudocia," a legendary cause for the falling out between Emperor Theodosius II and his wife, Eudocia. The story involves a giant apple, a misinterpreted gift, and a lie that led to accusations of infidelity and the eventual execution of the court official Paulinus.</summary>

Some said that fire had been seen in the sky: because of this, the memory of that Litany is celebrated every year for the sake of the goodness and patience of the merciful God in the Triconchos, starting from the 6th of November. Indeed, in the midst of such great terrors, He gave no one over to death.

During the reign of the Augusti Theodosius and Valentinian, Attila—sprung from the Gepid Huns—set out on an expedition against Rome and Constantinople together with an infinite multitude of troops. He announced this to Valentinian, who was ruling in Rome, through a certain Goth, his legate:
