<margin>R 746</margin> ...he was brought from **Chalcedon** to the **Zeuxippus** <note>The Baths of Zeuxippus, a prominent public building and judicial site near the Hippodrome in Constantinople.</note>, where he was examined by the **Praetorian Prefect** and Consul, **Pusaeus**. The same Pusaeus delivered a statement against **Isocasius**, who had entered before the curtain <note>original: "πρὸ βηλοῦ"; the "velum" or curtain separated the magistrate from the public during high-level legal proceedings.</note> stripped of his robes and with his hands bound behind his back.

<margin>D</margin> Pusaeus spoke these words: *"Do you see yourself, Isocasius? In what a state do you now stand?"*

And Isocasius answered, saying: *"I see it, and I am not surprised; for being a man, I have fallen into human misfortunes. But judge me with the same justice you used when you used to sit in judgment alongside me."* <note>Isocasius is reminding the judge of his own former high status and their previous professional equality.</note>

When the people of **Byzantium** <note>Constantinople</note> who were standing there and watching heard this, they cheered **Emperor Leo** many times. Then, seizing Isocasius, they led him away from the Zeuxippus to the **Great Church** <note>The Magna Ecclesia, or Hagia Sophia.</note>. There, he was instructed in the faith, baptized <note>original: "ἐφωτίσθη"; literally 'enlightened,' the standard term for the rite of Christian baptism.</note>, and sent back to his own country.

The same most divine Emperor also commanded that **Sundays** be days of rest <note>original: "ἀπράκτους"; days without business or legal activity.</note>. He issued his own divine law concerning this, decreeing that neither flute, nor lyre, nor any other musical instrument should be played on Sunday, but that all such things must cease. And every person complied.

<margin>P 323</margin> In this year, because the Patrician **Aspar**—who was the first of the Senate—had plotted to seize the throne <note>original: "τυραννίδα μελετήσαντα"; meaning he planned a 'tyranny' or usurpation.</note>, the Emperor had him killed inside the palace. This caused a great riot in **Constantinople**, for they had a great multitude of **Goths**, counts, and other attendants...

This **Anthemius** built the house of **Saint Thomas the Apostle**, which is called the **Anthemian**, near the property of the **Borraides** <note>original: "τὰ λεγόμενα Ἀνθημίου, πλησίον τῶν Βορῥαΐδου"; likely an estate or church named after Anthemius, who served as Emperor of the West from 467 to 472 AD.</note>.

<margin>469 AD. Year 12. 7th Indiction. Consulship of Zeno and Marcianus.</margin>

In this year, it rained **ash** in **Constantinople** instead of rain; the ash settled on the roof tiles to the height of a palm <note>original: "παλαιστήν" (palaisten); an ancient measurement roughly equal to four fingers or the width of a hand.</note>. Frightened by the destruction, **Emperor Leo** retreated across the water to the district of **Saint Mamas**, where he remained for a stay of six months. He built a small harbor and a portico there, and for this reason, the place is called the **New Portico** <note>original: "Νέος ἔμβολος" (Neos embolos).</note>.

### 314th Olympiad

14th Indiction. 2nd year. In the consulship of **Basiliscus** and **Armatus**.
15th Indiction. 3rd year. In the consulship of **Basiliscus** and **Armatus**.

<margin>P 325</margin>
The Emperor **Zeno**, having been asked for a certain favor by his mother-in-law **Verina** and having refused to grant it, became the target of her plotting. Fearing that he might be assassinated by someone in the palace—for his mother-in-law **Verina** lived in the palace with him—he made a public procession to **Chalcedon** <note>A city directly across the Bosphorus from Constantinople.</note>. From there, he fled using fast horses <note>original: "βερέδοις" (beredois) / "veredis"; the *veredus* was a fast postal horse used in the Roman imperial courier system.</note> and went to **Isauria**, as he was Emperor. The Empress **Ariadne** secretly fled from her own mother and caught up with him in **Isauria**, where she remained with her own husband.

<margin>B</margin>
After the Emperor **Zeno** and the Augusta **Ariadne** had fled, the Lady **Verina** immediately appointed an emperor, crowning **Basiliscus**, her own brother. This **Basiliscus** reigned for two years, which are counted together with the earlier and later years of **Zeno's** reign <note>Basiliscus is treated as a usurper; therefore, official chronologies often fold his years into Zeno's total reign length.</note>.

As soon as **Basiliscus** became emperor, he crowned his own son **Marcus** as emperor, and the two reigned together.

The Emperor **Zeno**, when a certain matter was requested of him by his mother-in-law **Verina** and was denied, was sought after by her with snares. Emperor Zeno, reflecting on the perjury of Armatus, Master of Soldiers of the Presence and father of the Caesar—as one who had sworn by Holy Baptism to Basiliscus that he would not betray him: *“yet,” he said, “urged by me, he betrayed him, and he is dead; how shall he keep faith with my Majesty? I, however, kept faith with him, for I saw to it that he remained as Master of Soldiers, and I named his son Caesar.”* Therefore, Emperor Zeno commanded that Armatus, the ex-consul and Master of Soldiers, be killed as a perjurer. He was killed in the Snail-staircase of the Palace, toward the Decimum, while he was ascending to watch the games of the Circus. After the slaughter of Armatus, he took care that the son Basiliscus the Caesar, still a youth, be ordained Bishop of Cyzicus, the Metropolis of Hellespont—as he had worn the Royal purple as Caesar—and all of Armatus’s goods were confiscated into the treasury.

In these times, seized by I know not what occasion, the Samaritans in Palestine stirred up a rebellion, a certain Justusa, a leader of bandits and a Samaritan, having been crowned. He thereafter entered Caesarea, exhibited games in the Circus, and killed many, ruling over Palestine. But he also burned the Church...

<margin>B</margin> It is said that the Emperor **Zeno** questioned the most wise Count **Maurianus**—who had previously predicted many things for him, for this **Maurianus** was known to be knowledgeable in certain mystical matters—as to who would reign after **Zeno**. He learned from him that a certain man from the <term>silentiaries<note>original: "σιλεντιαρίων" (silentiariōn). A high-ranking class of court officials who maintained order and silence around the Emperor's person.</note></term> would succeed to both his empire and his wife. Upon hearing this, the Emperor **Zeno** arrested the <term>patrician<note>original: "πατρίκιον" (patrikion). One of the highest honorary titles in the Byzantine court.</note></term> **Pelagius**, a wise man who had served as a silentiary and had reached the dignity of a patrician. After confiscating his property, Zeno ordered him to be kept under guard. The <term>excubitors<note>original: "ἐξκουβίτωρες" (exkoubitōres). The elite imperial palace guards.</note></term> who were guarding him then strangled him with a rope by order of the Emperor **Zeno**. When the <term>Praetorian Prefect<note>original: "ἔπαρχος τῶν πραιτωρίων" (eparchos tōn praitōriōn). One of the most powerful administrative and judicial officials in the empire.</note></term> **Arcadius** heard that the patrician **Pelagius** had been murdered, he reviled the Emperor **Zeno**. This reached the ears <margin>C</margin> of the Emperor **Zeno**, and he ordered that **Arcadius** be slaughtered the moment he entered the palace. However, the Praetorian Prefect **Arcadius** learned of this, and knowing he had been summoned by the emperor, as he was passing by the Great Church <note>The "Great Church" refers to the precursor of the Hagia Sophia in Constantinople.</note>, he pretended he wished to pray. Stepping down from his carriage, he entered the Great Church of Constantinople and remained inside, and thus was delivered from a bitter death.

<note>original: "Cum rogasset Imperator Zeno..." The following section is a Latin translation of the Greek narrative provided above for the benefit of Western scholars.</note>

When the Emperor **Zeno** had asked **Maurianus** the Count, a most learned man who had predicted many things to him (for he knew certain secrets), who would rule after him, he learned from him that a certain man from the Ex-Silentiaries would take up his empire and his wife. Having understood this, he seized **Pelagius** the Patrician, who had served as a Silentiary and had thence arrived at the dignity of Patrician, a wise man; and after his goods were made public, Zeno ordered him to be guarded. Then the Excubitors, by the order of Emperor Zeno himself, strangled him with a rope. When **Arcadius**, the Praetorian Prefect, received news of this, he pursued Emperor Zeno with insults because he had killed Pelagius the Patrician. Zeno, having had the accusation against Pelagius brought to him <note>The Latin here likely implies the news of Arcadius's criticism reached Zeno.</note>, ordered that as soon as he entered the Palace, he should be killed. But Arcadius the Praetorian Prefect, when he had found this out and saw himself being summoned by the emperor, while passing toward the Great Church, feigned that he wished to pray; and having climbed out of his chariot, he entered the Great Church of Constantinople, and staying within there, he was delivered from a bitter death.

**Anastasius** <term>Dicorus<note>original: "Δίκορος" (Dikoros). Meaning "Two-Pupiled." He was from the province of New Epirus and had served as a <term>silentiary<note>original: "σιλεντιαρίων" (silentiariōn). Literally the "Great Week," the period before Easter Sunday.</note></term>, in the 14th Indiction, in the year 537 according to the era of Great Antioch. He married the Lady **Ariadne**, who had been the wife of the previous emperor, **Zeno**. This same **Anastasius** reigned for twenty-seven years. Total years from creation: 6,027.

# CHRONICLE

...the <term>Grand Chamberlain<note>original: "κουβικουλάριον" (implied by the suffix -σιακὸν). The high-ranking eunuch in charge of the imperial bedchamber.</note></term> and **Theocritus** the Count, who was the <term>domestic<note>original: "δομέστικον". A high-ranking assistant or deputy to a commander or official.</note></term> of the aforementioned **Amantius**. This Amantius had intended to make Theocritus emperor, having given money to **Justin** to distribute as a donative <note>original: "ῥογεῦσαι". A formal distribution of cash, often used by imperial candidates to secure the loyalty of the army and the public.</note> so that Theocritus would be chosen as ruler. Justin did indeed distribute the money; however, the army and the people, once they had received it, did not choose to make Theocritus emperor. Instead, they proclaimed **Justin** himself as emperor. Therefore, after he had taken the throne, he executed them on the grounds that they were usurpers who had plotted against his sovereignty. They were put to death inside the palace.

<margin>R 766 D</margin>
The same emperor recalled the <term>Patrician<note>A title of the highest nobility in the later Roman Empire.</note></term> **Apion**, as well as **Diogenian** (a former Master of Soldiers) and **Philoxenus** (also a former Master of Soldiers), who had been sent into exile by the previous emperor. He appointed Apion as **Praetorian Prefect** <note>The highest administrative official in the empire, second only to the emperor.</note>, Diogenian as **Master of Soldiers of the East**, and after some time, he named Philoxenus as **Consul**.

In the same year, a terrifying star appeared in the sky in the East, called a **comet**, which had a ray pointing downwards.
<margin>P 332</margin>
Some said it was a <term>pogonias<note>original: "πωγωνίαν". Meaning "bearded," referring to the tail of the comet looking like a beard.</note></term>, and the people were filled with fear.

# CHRONICLE

In the same year, the Persians made war against **Tzathius**, the King of the **Lazi** <note>The Lazi were a people inhabiting the eastern coast of the Black Sea, in modern-day Georgia; they were a crucial buffer state between the Roman and Persian empires</note>, because he had allied himself with the **Romans**. Consequently, this same **Tzathius** sent word and pleaded for help from the Emperor **Justinian** and the Roman forces. The Emperor **Justinian** sent him a multitude of soldiers and three generals: **Belisarius** <note>This is one of the earliest mentions of Belisarius, who would become Justinian's most famous military commander</note>, **Cerycus**, and **Irenaeus** the son of Pentadia. They joined in battle, and many of the Roman army fell.

<margin>B</margin>
And the Emperor **Justinian** was indignant with the generals, because they envied one another and were betraying each other, making reports against one another to the 

<margin>R 774</margin>
Emperor. He replaced them, and **Peter** the general—formerly one of the Emperor's notaries <note>A 'notarius' was a high-ranking imperial secretary or administrative official</note>—went down, removed them from command, and took over the military campaigns <note>original: "ἐξπέδιτα" (expedita), a Latin military term for expeditions or baggage trains</note> from them. Having joined battle with the Persians alongside the **Lazi**, they cut down many Persians.

During this time, the Emperor **Justinian** renewed the suburb formerly called **Sycae** <note>Sycae, meaning "The Fig Trees," was the district across the Golden Horn from Constantinople, known today as Galata or Pera in Istanbul</note>, situated opposite **Constantinople**, as well as the theater of **Sycae** and the walls. He granted it the rights of a city and renamed it **Justinianopolis**.

<margin>C</margin>
He also built the bridge through which one can travel from the opposite side into the "All-Blessed" city <note>original: "πανευδαίμονα" (paneudaimona), a common honorific title for Constantinople, emphasizing its prosperity and divine favor</note>.

The same Emperor also completed the public bath in **Constantinople** which the Emperor **Anastasius** had previously begun to build in the district of **Dagisthaeus**.

# CHRONICLE

After a few days, the Emperor ordered his <note>Justinian's</note> relatives to take up his <note>Hypatius'</note> remains and bury them. <margin>R 786 D</margin> The other **patricians** <term>patrikioi; the highest rank of the Byzantine nobility</term> who were found with them fled, some <margin>5</margin> to monasteries and others to houses of prayer <note>churches</note>, and their houses were sealed. After these events, the Emperor learned of the response given by **Thomas the *asecretis*** <term>asecretis; a high-ranking imperial secretary or notary</term> to **Ephraemius the *candidatus*** <term>kandidatos; an elite palace guard distinguished by a white tunic</term>; he had <margin>10</margin> **Thomas** beheaded and exiled **Ephraemius** to the great city of **Alexandria**.

For several days, all business remained at a standstill, and <margin>15</margin> **Constantinople** was without any trade or commerce <note>original: "ἀδοσόληπτος" (adosolēptos). # PASCHAL CHRONICLE

...[under Pontius] Pilate, and was buried, and rose again on the third day. We acknowledge that the miracles and the sufferings, which he voluntarily endured in the flesh, belong to one and the same [person]. For we do not recognize one as God the Word and another as the Christ, but we know one and the same, of one substance <note>original: "homoousion" — the theological concept that the Son shares the exact same essence as God the Father</note> with the Father according to his divinity, and the same being of one substance with us according to his 
<margin>P 343</margin> humanity. We accept and confess the unity according to person <note>original: "hypostasin" — referring to the "hypostatic union" where the divine and human natures are joined in one individual person</note>. For the Trinity remained the Trinity even when one of the Trinity, God the Word, became incarnate; for the Holy Trinity does not admit the addition of a fourth person. Since these things are so, we condemn with anathema <note>original: "anathematizomen" — a formal ecclesiastical curse and expulsion</note> every heresy, and especially Nestorius the man-worshipper <note>original: "anthropolatren" — a derogatory term used by his opponents to suggest he worshipped Jesus as a human being rather than as God</note> and those who held or hold his views. These are the ones who divide our one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our God, and who do not confess properly and in truth that the holy, glorious, ever-virgin Mary is the Mother of God <note>original: "theotokon" — literally "God-bearer"</note>, that is, the Mother of God; instead they claim there are two sons: one being God the Word from the 
<margin>B</margin> Father, and the other from the holy ever-virgin and Mother of God Mary. They deny that he became God himself through grace, relation, and intimacy with God the Word; and they do not confess that our Master Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our God—who was incarnate, became human, and was crucified—is one of the same-substance Trinity. For he alone...

# PASCHAL CHRONICLE

### THE PASCHAL [CHRONICLE]

[He] is the one who is worshipped together with and glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

We also anathematize <note>original: "anathematizomen" — to formally exclude or curse someone from the church</note> Eutyches, the one of unsound mind <note>original: "phrenoblabe" — literally "brain-damaged" or "insane," a common polemical insult in late antiquity</note>, and those who held or hold his opinions, who introduce a "phantasm" <margin>C</margin> <note>original: "phantasian" — the Docetic belief that Christ’s physical body and sufferings were only an illusion or appearance rather than physical reality</note>, and who deny the true <margin>R 792</margin> incarnation <note>original: "sarkosin" — the taking on of flesh</note> of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ from the holy, ever-virgin, and Mother of God <note>original: "Theotokou" — God-bearer</note> Mary—which is to say, they deny our salvation—and who do not confess him to be of one substance <note>original: "homoousion" — sharing the same divine essence</note> with the Father according to his divinity. In the same way, we condemn Apollinarius, the destroyer of souls <note>original: "psychophthoron"</note>, and those who held or hold his opinions, who say our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God and our God, was a man only <note>Apollinarius taught that Christ had a human body but a divine mind, rather than a human soul</note>, and who introduce a confusion or a mixing into the "becoming-human" <note>the Incarnation</note> of the only-begotten Son of God, and all those who held <margin>D</margin> or hold their opinions.

All the bishops received a copy of this [edict] in their own cities and posted it in the churches.

# CHRONICLE

<margin>B</margin> The Emperor, Caesar, Flavius Justinian, Alamanicus, Gotthicus, Francicus, Germanicus, Anticus, Alanicus, Vandalicus, Africanus <note>These are Justinian’s "victory titles," named after the various Germanic and barbarian tribes his generals (like Belisarius) had defeated to reclaim Roman territory</note>, pious, blessed, glorious, victor, triumph-bearer, ever-venerable, <margin>5</margin> Augustus, to the whole fullness of the catholic and apostolic church.

Knowing that nothing so serves the God who loves mankind as for all Christians to think one and the same thing regarding the right and blameless faith, and for there to be no schisms in the holy <margin>R 796 C</margin> church of God, we have deemed it necessary—removing every pretext from those who are offended or who cause offense—to make the confession of the right <margin>10</margin> faith, which is preached in the holy church of God, manifest through the present edict. This is so that those who confess the right faith may keep it in a firm state, and those who strive against it may learn the truth <margin>15</margin> and hasten to be united with the holy church of God.

We confess, therefore, that we believe in Father and Son and Holy Spirit, a consubstantial <note>original: "homoousion" — meaning "of the same substance," the key term from the Council of Nicaea</note> Trinity; glorifying one deity, or rather nature and essence <margin>D</margin> and power and authority, in three subsistences <note>original: "hypostases" — the distinct "persons" of the Trinity</note>, or rather persons, into whom we have been baptized, in whom we have believed, and to whom <margin>20</margin> we have been joined; distinguishing the individual properties <note>the unique characteristics of the Father, Son, and Spirit</note>, but uniting the deity. For we worship a Unity in Trinity and a Trinity in Unity, possessing a paradox in both its division and its union.

<meta>This page continues the theological declaration of Emperor Justinian I, shifting from a general call for unity to a specific, technical definition of the Trinity. It aims to strike a middle path between the "confusion" of Sabellianism and the "division" of Arianism, which were the two primary theological errors the imperial government sought to suppress to ensure social and religious stability.</meta>

# PASCHAL [CHRONICLE]

...unity indeed according to the principle of essence—that is, of deity—but a Trinity according to the properties—that is, the <term>subsistences</term> <note>original: "hypostases" — the distinct "persons" of the Trinity who share one nature</note> or persons. For it is divided without division, so to speak, and joined together while yet distinct. For the deity is one in three, and the three are one, in whom <margin>P 346</margin> the deity is—or to speak more accurately—which the deity is. Each person, if viewed alone, is God, with the mind separating the inseparable; but the three are understood together as God by the same movement and nature. Since it is necessary both to confess the one God and to preach the three subsistences—that is, three persons—each with its own property. And we do not make the union a "confusion" according to <margin>V 276</margin> **Sabellius** <note>Sabellius was a 3rd-century teacher who claimed Father, Son, and Spirit were just three "roles" or masks worn by one person, rather than three distinct persons</note>, who says the Trinity is one person with three names, the same being Father and Son and Holy Spirit. Nor in dividing do we alienate the Son or the Holy Spirit from the essence of God the Father, according to the **madness of Arius** <note>Arius taught that Jesus was a created being, lower than God the Father, thus "cutting" the divine essence into different levels</note>, cutting the deity into three different essences.

Therefore, there is one God the Father, from whom are all things; and one only-begotten Son, through whom are all things; and one Holy Spirit, in whom are all things. And we confess that this same only-begotten Son of God, God the Word, who was begotten before the ages and timelessly from the Father, <margin>R 798</margin> was not made; and that in the last days for us and for our salvation He came down from heaven and was incarnate by the Holy Spirit and the holy, glorious <term>Mother of God</term> <note>original: "Theotokos" — a title emphasizing that Mary gave birth to God in human form, not just a human man</note> and ever-virgin... <margin>C</margin>

# CHRONICON PASCHALE

<header>PASCHAL</header>

To the same Successus, instructing him in similar matters, he writes as follows: <margin>D</margin> "For if, while saying 'one nature of the Word,' we had remained silent and had not added 'incarnate'—as if setting aside the <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: "oikonomian" — the divine plan of the Incarnation, where God takes on human form</note>—their argument might perhaps have been not unconvincing when they pretended to ask: 'Where is the perfection in his humanity?' or 'How does our own substance <margin>R 808</margin> subsist in him?' But since the perfection in his humanity and the manifestation of our own substance have been introduced by the word 'incarnate,' let them cease propping themselves up with a reed staff <note>A biblical metaphor for a weak or broken support that pierces the hand of the one leaning on it; see Isaiah 36:6</note>. For it would be right to accuse one who rejects the <term>dispensation</term> and denies the incarnation of stripping the Son of his perfect humanity. But if, as I said, by saying he is 'incarnate' there is a clear <margin>P 351</margin> and unambiguous confession that he became man, then nothing prevents us from understanding that since Christ is the one and only Son, the same is both God and man—just as he is perfect in divinity, so he is also perfect in humanity. And your Perfection <note>A formal honorific title used when addressing a high-ranking cleric like Successus</note> sets forth the argument regarding the saving passion most rightly and very wisely: you assert that the Only-begotten Son of God—insofar as he is understood to be and is God—did not suffer in his own nature the things belonging to the body, but rather suffered in his earthly nature. For it is necessary that both be preserved in the one and true Son: both the fact that he did not suffer divinely, and the fact that he is said to have suffered humanly; for his flesh suffered."

...the letter teaching similar things, writes thus: "For indeed if, while saying 'one nature of the Word,' we had been silent, not introducing 'Incarnate,' but as it were putting the <term>dispensation</term> aside; there would perhaps be a likely reason for them to happen to ask, 'where is the perfection in his humanity, or how does <margin>subsisted</margin> our human substance subsist?' But since both the perfection in humanity and the demonstration of our substance is introduced by saying 'Incarnate,' let them cease placing a reed staff beneath themselves. For it was right that the one casting out the <term>dispensation</term> and denying the incarnation be justly accused of taking away perfect humanity from the Son. But if (as I said), by saying he is incarnate, there is a clear and indubitable confession that he was made man; nothing now prevents us from understanding that, since there is one and only Son Christ, the same himself is God and man; just as he is perfect in Deity, so also is he perfect in humanity. Most rightly and exceedingly prudently does your Perfection set out the reason concerning the saving passion, affirming that the unbegotten Son of God himself—according to which he is understood and is God—did not suffer in his own nature those things which belong to the body, but rather suffered in his earthly nature. For it is necessary that both be preserved for the one and true Son: both to not suffer according to his Deity, and to be said to have suffered that same thing according to [his humanity]..."

# PASCHAL CHRONICLE

<page-num>651</page-num>
<header>PASCHALE.</header>

...signifying [the difference], but in no way making a division into separate parts. <margin>B</margin> For just as the nature of the soul is one thing and that of the body another, and yet one human is completed through their composition and not two, <margin>5</margin> so also in Christ—even if two natures are perceived, one of divinity and one of humanity—nevertheless, two Christs or two Sons are not introduced because of this. <margin>R 816</margin> Therefore, those who refuse to speak of the number of natures in Christ in the manner described are clearly denying the difference between them and introducing "confusion" <note>original: σύγχυσιν (synchysis). In early church debates, this referred to the "mixing" of divinity and humanity into a single new substance, which was considered a heresy because it would mean Christ was neither truly God nor truly man.</note> <margin>10</margin> into the divine plan <note>original: οἰκονομίᾳ (oikonomia). Often translated as "economy," this term refers to God’s management or arrangement of the world, specifically the plan for human salvation through Christ.</note>. If they acknowledge the difference, it is absolutely necessary for them to also state the number of natures which have come together without confusion <margin>C</margin> into one individual existence <note>original: ὑπόστασιν (hypostasis). This technical term refers to a distinct, concrete person or individual reality. The Church taught that Christ had one "hypostasis" (one person) but two "physeis" (two natures).</note>. For where a difference is preserved, a number necessarily follows. To confirm what we have said, we shall use the testimony of the holy Fathers <margin>15</margin> to show them saying that, regarding the mystery of Christ, the definitions are divided according to the difference of the natures—the divinity and humanity from which he was composed—and they accept the use of number in this regard. However, they do not actually make a division of the natures into two individual existences <note>original: ὑποστάσεις (hypostases)</note> or two <margin>20</margin> persons. For the saintly Cyril <note>Cyril of Alexandria (c. 376–444 AD), a central figure in the Christological debates of the 5th century.</note> speaks thus in his interpretation of the book of Leviticus: <margin>D</margin> "Look again clearly at the mystery of our Savior in these things, and the cleansing that comes through holy baptism. For [it is written] that two small birds are to be taken..."

...of the things which came together, by this signifying: but in no way making a division by parts. Therefore, those who refuse to state the number of natures that are in Christ according to the aforesaid manner, are clearly denying the difference of the natures and introducing confusion into the divine plan. If they confess the difference, it is necessary in every way to signify it, and also to state the number of the natures which have come together without confusion into one individual existence <note>original: subsistentiam</note>. For where a difference is preserved, there in every way a number follows. To confirm those things which we have said, using the testimony of the holy Fathers, we shall show them saying that in our one Lord Jesus Christ, the reasons are indeed divided according to the difference of the natures of Deity and humanity from which he was composed, and they assume the number in this, yet they do not make a division into two individual existences <note>original: subsistentias</note> or persons by the thing itself or by parts of the natures. # PASCHALE

[...the Father of] glory. For even if both together are one, they are not so by nature, but by their union.

And the one among the saints, Gregory, Bishop of Nyssa, in the fourth book of his work *Against Eunomius* <note>Gregory of Nyssa (c. 335–394 AD) was a prominent theologian; his work *Against Eunomius* defended the divinity of the Son and the Holy Spirit against Arian-leaning thinkers.</note>, teaching us these same things, writes as follows:

<margin>C</margin> “And so that no one should attribute the suffering of the cross to the undefiled nature <note>The "undefiled nature" refers to Christ's divinity, which the Church Fathers argued could not suffer or change.</note>, he corrects such an error more clearly through other words, naming him the mediator of God and men, and both man and God himself—so that by two things being said of the one person, that which is appropriate to each might be understood: regarding the divine, <term>impassibility</term> <note>original: ἀπάθεια (apatheia); the theological concept that God is not subject to suffering, pain, or change.</note>, and regarding the human, the <term>dispensation</term> <note>original: οἰκονομία (oikonomia); often translated as "economy," this refers to the way God manages or arranges the plan of salvation through the human life of Jesus.</note> of suffering. Therefore, while the distinction is made in the mind—the person being united according to his love for mankind, but distinguished by reason—whenever he proclaims that which is above and exceeds all understanding, he uses the loftier names, calling him 'God over all,' and 'Great God,' and 'Power of God,' and 'Wisdom,' and the like. <margin>D</margin> But whenever he describes with words the experience of sufferings, which was necessarily taken up because of our weakness, he names the composite whole <note>original: τὸ συναμφότερον (to sunamphoteron); literally "the both together," referring to Christ being one person who is both God and man.</note> from our side, addressing him as 'man'—not to make him common with the rest of [human] nature by that title, but so that the pious truth regarding each nature might be preserved.”

With these things thus demonstrated through the teaching of the fathers, let those who make the number of the natures in Christ an occasion for their error cease [their complaints]...

***

<margin>At Nyssa.</margin> God, and Father of glory. For although both are one, yet it is not by nature, but by coming together.

“And the Saint Gregory of Nyssa in the fourth book against Eunomius, teaching us the same, writes thus: ‘And lest anyone should apply the suffering of the cross to the incorruptible nature, he corrects such an error more clearly through other things, naming him the mediator of God and men, and both man and God himself: so that when two things are said of one, they may be understood as fitting for each—regarding the Deity, indeed, impassibility, but regarding the humanity, the dispensation of suffering. With the intellect therefore dividing that which is indeed united through mercy, but discerned by reason; when it preaches that which is placed above and surpassing all sense, it uses higher names, calling him God over all, and Great God, and the Power of God, and Wisdom, and such things: but when it signifies in words the trial of sufferings, necessarily accepted because of our infirmity, naming both from our side, it calls him man—not communicating by that voice the one signified to the rest of nature, but so that piety may be preserved regarding both.’

“These things having been so demonstrated through the doctrine of the holy Fathers, let those cease who make the number of natures which are in Christ the occasion of their error...”

# CHRONICON

...making [this] a pretext for their own error, and by this rejection of number, attempting to introduce confusion by denying the difference <note>The author argues that "counting" two natures in Christ is not the same as "dividing" Christ into two people; the opposition feared that any "number" implied a split.</note>. <margin>P 356</margin> Therefore, since it has been demonstrated from every side that it is impious to speak of "one nature" or "substance" of the divinity and the flesh of Christ, we shall also state this: just as we speak of one <term>hypostasis</term> of the divinity and humanity of Christ, it is not possible to also speak of "one nature" of Christ, since nature and <term>hypostasis</term> are not the same thing. 

<margin>R 820</margin> <margin>B</margin> For all the Holy Fathers teach us harmoniously that <term>nature</term> <note>original: φύσιν (physin)</note>—that is, <term>substance</term> <note>original: οὐσίαν (ousian)</note> and form—is one thing, and <term>hypostasis</term>—that is, person—is another. # PASCHALE

...three persons <note>original: ὑποστάσεις (hypostaseis)</note>, so also there would be three natures in the Holy Trinity, such that one could even say that a single nature was composed out of three natures for the purpose of the Incarnation. However, Arius was the only one who dared to speak of "three natures" in the Holy Trinity, and he was condemned as a blasphemer for it. 

<margin>D</margin> Therefore, according to right reason, we speak of a union of two natures and a single <term>hypostasis</term> <note>often translated as "person" or "individual existence."</note>. This is because the Son of God—while being a distinct person from the Father in terms of his <term>hypostasis</term>, yet being of the same nature as the Father—fashioned for himself in his own person a flesh animated by a rational and intellectual soul. This signifies that the Word of God was united to human nature itself, and not merely to a [pre-existing] person or to some specific individual. 

The Word of God, even when incarnate, is therefore a single <term>hypostasis</term> recognized in two distinct natures: in the divine nature, in which he existed according to the scripture: *Who, being in the form of God* <note>A reference to Philippians 2:6.</note>, and in the human nature, according to the phrase: *Being made in the likeness of men* <note>Philippians 2:7.</note>. 

<margin>P 357</margin> Because of this, one might piously speak of the "one composite person" <note>original: μίαν ὑπόστασιν... σύνθετον (mian hypostasin... syntheton)</note> of the Word of God, rather than "one composite nature." This is because when "nature" is spoken of simply by itself, without a specific person being attached to it, it signifies something indefinite and non-subsistent <note>i.e., "human nature" is an abstract concept until it exists in a specific person like Peter or Paul.</note>. That which is indefinite cannot be "composed" or combined with anything. But if anyone, even after such rational arguments, should attempt to oppose this out of mere love for conflict...

<summary>This page argues that Christ is one "person" (hypostasis) existing in two "natures" (divine and human). It warns that calling Christ's nature "composite" is a theological error, as it would imply that the Trinity itself has multiple natures, a heresy attributed to Arius.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical theological debate regarding the nature of Christ. The previous page concluded that the Word of God was united to human nature in a single "composite person," rather than being two separate individuals joined together. This page now addresses the logical errors of those who claim Christ's human nature must have its own independent "personhood."</meta>

# CHRONICON

If someone says that, according to the definition given for "nature," Christ’s human nature must also have its own <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: ὑπόστασιν (hypostasin); refers to a distinct, individual existence or "person."</note> or its own person, such a man clearly suggests that the Word was united to a human being who already existed, and that this union was merely "relative" <note>original: σχετικήν (schetikēn); a "loose association" or a moral union rather than a physical or essential one.</note>. 
<margin>B</margin> Indeed, it is impossible for a union "according to <term>hypostasis</term>" to occur between two pre-existing <term>hypostases</term> or persons. Therefore, anyone who says these things—striving to empty the power of God through the arguments of human wisdom—ignores the "great mystery of godliness" <note>A reference to 1 Timothy 3:16.</note>, which is believed in the heart leading to righteousness and confessed with the mouth leading to salvation <note>A reference to Romans 10:10.</note>. For Christ's human nature is never said to exist simply on its own, nor did it ever possess its own <term>hypostasis</term> or person; rather, it received its very beginning of existence within the <term>hypostasis</term> of the Word. Because of this, we confess that God the Word Himself became man without undergoing change, 
<margin>C</margin> and that He did not merely enter into some [pre-existing] man. We confess that the birth from the Virgin was the birth of that same Word of God made flesh, and for this reason, the holy, glorious, and ever-virgin Mary is the <term>Theotokos</term> <note>original: Θεοτόκον; literally "God-bearer." This title confirms that Jesus is truly God from the moment of conception.</note>. For this reason, 
<margin>V 285</margin> both before the incarnation of God the Word and after His incarnation, we speak of only three <term>hypostases</term>—the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit—as the Holy Trinity does not admit the addition of a fourth <term>hypostasis</term> or person. Based on all these points, those who claim there were "two natures before the union" are proven wrong, 
<margin>D</margin> as they are essentially saying that the man existed beforehand as a distinct person and was only then united to God.

# THE EASTER CHRONICLE

Since those who support Theodore and his impiety act impiously and in vain, they flee to another empty excuse, <margin>P 368</margin> saying that he ought not to be anathematized <note>original: "ἀναθεματισθῆναι"</note> because he died in the communion of the churches. But they should know that those who die in the communion of the churches are those who preserved the common dogma of piety, which is preached in the universal <note>original: "καθολικῆς" (catholic)</note> church, until the end. But this man, having died in his own impiety, was cast out from every church. Indeed, even the entire congregation of the church in Mopsuestia <note>A city in ancient Cilicia, modern-day Turkey, where Theodore served as bishop.</note>, in which he is said to have been bishop, because of the blasphemies for which he was numbered among the Pagans <note>original: "Ἕλλησί" (Greeks); in this context, it refers to non-Christians or polytheists.</note>, Jews, and Sodomites by the holy fathers, <margin>B</margin> erased his name from the sacred diptychs <term>diptychs<gloss>List of names of bishops and benefactors read aloud during the liturgy to indicate they are in good standing with the Church.</gloss></term> of the church. This is shown by the records regarding him that were established in that same city by the provincial council.

We wonder, therefore, at those who defend Theodore, making him and his impiety their own, when even the church in which he was bishop has cast him out as a heretic for many years. That his defenders put forward such an excuse to their own condemnation can be known from the terrible judgment that fell upon Judas. For he, thinking to hide from the One who knows the secrets of men, <margin>C</margin> shared in the sacraments with the Apostles; yet it did him no good that he shared in them through deceit...

### CHRONICLE

...of the synod, just as the one among the saints, Athanasius, <note>St. Athanasius (c. 296–373), the Bishop of Alexandria and a staunch defender of Nicene orthodoxy against Arianism.</note> testifies. Since the heretical defenders of Theodore <note>Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428), whose writings were a focal point of the "Three Chapters" controversy.</note>—having failed in every argument and attempt—have tried to claim, in order to deceive the ignorant, that Cyril of holy memory had praised Theodore in some part of a letter, it is demonstrated by many proofs that their attempt does not agree with what was said by Saint Cyril in his various discourses against the impious Theodore. In those works, Cyril showed Theodore to be more impious than all other heretics; then, unable to bear the number and magnitude of Theodore’s <margin>P 370</margin> blasphemies spoken against our great God and Savior Jesus Christ, Cyril cried out, saying: *“Heaven was amazed at this and shuddered very greatly, says the Lord.”* <note original="Ἐξέστη ὁ οὐρανὸς ἐπὶ τούτῳ καὶ ἔφριξεν ἐπὶ πλείω σφόδρα, λέγει κύριος">A quotation of Jeremiah 2:12, used here to express Cyril's shock at Theodore's theology.</note> O, the unspeakable perversity! How long will you leap upon the long-suffering Christ? Keep in mind what was written by the divine Paul: <margin>B</margin> *‘But thus sinning against the brothers and striking their weak conscience, [you sin] against Christ.’*” <note original="Οὕτω δὲ ἁμαρτάνοντες εἰς τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς καὶ πλήττοντες αὐτῶν ἀσθενοῦσαν τὴν συνείδησιν εἰς Χριστὸν">1 Corinthians 8:12</note>

# CHRONICON

<page-num>680</page-num>

...of Mopsuestia he wrote, but rather to Theodore, the Bishop of Tyana, which is the <term>metropolis</term> <note>The capital city of a Roman province and the seat of its highest-ranking bishop.</note> of the province of Second Cappadocia. From this same region comes Nazianzus, where the same Gregory—now among the saints—served as Bishop, as well as the village of Arianzus, where he originated. For the letters themselves clearly demonstrate this, making mention of local customs, <margin>P 371</margin> church assemblies, the village of Arianzus itself, and other locales within the same province. They even mention the names of months in the local Cappadocian dialect, and speak of Bishop Bosphorius of the city of Colonia—who served under him—as well as other bishops, <term>chorepiscopi</term>, <note>Greek: χωρεπισκόπων; "country bishops" who oversaw rural areas under the jurisdiction of a city bishop.</note> and monasteries under the authority of the same Theodore [of Tyana]. These places still retain the same names even to this day. Indeed, what shared community could the Cappadocians have with the people of Second Cilicia, <margin>B</margin> <margin>R 852</margin> since the administration of these provinces was—and remains—entirely separate? Furthermore, what bishops could the Bishop of Mopsuestia have had under his own authority, seeing as he himself was subject to the <term>metropolitan</term> <note>The presiding bishop of a province who oversees other bishops.</note> of Second Cilicia?

It is true that John [Chrysostom] of Constantinople wrote a letter to Theodore of Mopsuestia, but it was a letter filled not with praise, but with reproaches and rebukes, as he had fallen away from true godliness. John reminds him of their shared life, for they practiced the monastic life together in one and the same monastery during their time there; this is further attested by Sozomen and Hesychius. <note>Historical writers of the 5th century who recorded the early lives of these church figures.</note>

<margin>Tyana. So also Leuncl. Nazianzus</margin> It is said that he did not write to Theodore of Mopsuestia, but to Theodore, Bishop of Tyana, which is the metropolis of Second Cappadocia. Within the same province are the city of Nazianzus, where the same Gregory of holy memory was Bishop, and the estate of Arianzus, where he was born. This is clearly indicated by the letters themselves, which mention customs, gatherings, and the estate of Arianzus, as well as other estates in the same province, and a month named in the native tongue of the Cappadocians. They also mention Bishop Bosphorius, who was established under the same Theodore and was at that time the Bishop of the city of Colonia in the same province, along with other Bishops, Country-Bishops, and Monasteries under Theodore’s jurisdiction, which keep the same names to this day. Furthermore, what fellowship is there between the Cappadocians and Second Cilicia, given that the governance of those provinces was then, as it is now, divided? And what Bishops could the Bishop of Mopsuestia have had under him, when he was himself established under the Metropolitan of Second Cilicia? However, John of Constantinople did write a letter to Theodore of Mopsuestia—one not of praise, but full of complaints and rebukes, since he had lapsed from a good way of life. Because he had practiced the monastic life with him in one and the same Monastery, he reminds him of the life they led there...

<meta>This page continues the argument for the legitimacy of posthumous condemnation, a central issue in the "Three Chapters" controversy. The previous page discussed the authority of various historical figures; this page provides specific legal and historical precedents for condemning individuals after their death, specifically to justify the condemnation of Theodore of Mopsuestia.</meta>

# CHRONICON

<page-num>682</page-num>

Moreover, even a canon of the holy synod in Africa <note>Likely referring to the Council of Carthage (419 AD), which established rules for the conduct and legacies of bishops.</note> declares that bishops who bequeath their own property—whether by a will or through an heir-at-law—to a heretic <note>original: αἱρετικῷ (hairetikō)</note> must be anathematized <note>Anathema: a formal curse by a church leader or council excommunicating a person or denouncing a doctrine.</note> even after death. In addition to all this, who is ignorant of the events that occurred in our times in the Church of Elder Rome regarding Dioscorus <note>This refers to the Roman deacon Dioscorus, who was briefly elected as a rival Pope in 530 and was posthumously condemned by Pope Boniface II to ensure he would not be listed in the official records (diptychs).</note>, who, though he had committed no error regarding the faith, was anathematized after death by the same most holy Church of Rome <margin>R 854</margin> solely for the sake of ecclesiastical order. If, therefore, bishops who have not stumbled in the faith are subjected to anathema even after death for the sake of ecclesiastical order <margin>B</margin> and for financial reasons, how much more should Theodore be condemned, who acted impiously against God himself?

As for the senselessness of those who say that those who die in their own impiety should not be anathematized after death, it would then also be necessary that the fathers who were unjustly condemned should not be restored <note>original: ἀνακαλεῖσθαι (anakaleisthai); literally "to be called back" or "recalled" from condemnation.</note> after death—which is exactly what happened in the case of John <note>John Chrysostom, the famed preacher and Archbishop of Constantinople who was deposed and died in exile but was later vindicated.</note> of holy memory, who was the bishop of Constantinople and was restored after death by the universal <note>original: καθολικῆς (katholikēs)</note> church, and also in the case of Flavian <note>Flavian of Constantinople was deposed and physically mistreated at the "Robber Synod" of 449 but was declared a martyr and restored at the Council of Chalcedon.</note> of holy memory, who also became bishop of Constantinople. The latter was unjustly condemned during his life, but was justly restored after death <margin>C</margin> by both Pope Leo of holy memory and by the holy Synod of Chalcedon. Furthermore, it follows from the arguments of those people that heretics would be numbered among the holy fathers, as they would be...

-> P. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; 21. *but/and* is *and* in manuscript V. <-

<margin>...let us omit...</margin> ...of the holy African Synod established that Bishops, who leave their assets in a will, or by intestacy, to a heretic, ought to be anathematized even after death. Above all these things, who is ignorant of those things which in our times were done in the Church of Elder Rome against Dioscorus? Who, although he had sinned in nothing regarding the faith, was nevertheless anathematized after death by that same holy Roman Church solely for the sake of ecclesiastical order? If therefore Bishops who sin in nothing regarding the faith are subjected to anathema even after death for the sake of ecclesiastical order alone, and for a financial cause: how much more Theodore, who sinned against God himself? As for the foolishness of those saying that those who died in their own impiety ought not to be anathematized after death: it would follow that those Fathers who were unjustly condemned ought not to be restored after death, as happened in the case of John of holy record, Bishop of the city of Constantinople, restored by the universal Church after death, and in the case of Flavian of holy memory, also Bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned unjustly indeed in life, but justly restored after death both by Pope Leo of holy memory and by the holy Synod of Chalcedon. From this it follows, according to their words, that heretics are indeed numbered among the holy Fathers, as if they were freed from the condemnation due to them...

...preached to you, let him be accursed, as we have said before. If anyone, then, after such a righteous confession and the condemnation of the heretics, while the pious meaning is preserved, should separate himself from the <margin>10</margin> holy church of God by fighting over names, syllables, or words—as if our piety resided only in names and words and not in deeds—such a person, as one who delights in schisms, shall render an account for himself and for those who have been or will be deceived by him to the great God and our <margin>C</margin> <margin>15</margin> Savior Jesus Christ on the day of judgment.

In this 35th year of Justinian’s reign, and in the 21st year after the consulship of Basil, on the 20th day of the month of March, in the 10th Indiction, and in the 3rd year of the 335th Olympiad, the 532 years of the feast cycle <note>The "Paschal Cycle" of 532 years is a period after which the dates of Easter repeat in the same order. It is calculated by multiplying the 19-year lunar cycle by the 28-year solar cycle.</note> of the holy and life-giving Cross were completed—measuring from the time when Christ our true God accepted a voluntary and life-giving death for our sake, and we Christians began to celebrate His holy resurrection. And the second period of the 532-year feast cycle begins from the twenty-first day of that same month of March in the present indiction, which is the day on which the equinox <note>The spring equinox (around March 21) is the astronomical anchor for calculating Easter, which falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon following the equinox.</note> is recognized.

# PASCHAL [CHRONICLE]

The nineteenth year of Tiberius Caesar—which is the 4th year of the 202nd Olympiad <note>original: Ὀλυμπιάδος. A four-year period used by the Greeks for dating, starting from 776 BC.</note>—in which the salvific passion of our Lord Jesus Christ occurred, will be found to be a period of 218 years <note>The chronicler is calculating backward from a later point to show the passage of time.</note>. Moving down to the 8th year of Constantine the Great, the emperor, during which the first indiction <term>indiction: a 15-year tax cycle used as a standard dating method in the later Roman Empire</term> was established <margin>P 375</margin> in the consulship of Volusianus and Anianus, it totals 65 years. From the 9th year <margin>R 860</margin> of Constantine until the present 10th indiction, which is the 35th year of the reign of Justinian, in the 21st year after the consulship of Basilius alone, it will total a time of 249 years; so that together, from the salvific Passover <note>original: πάσχα (Pascha). This refers to the date of the Resurrection.</note> until the present 35th year of Justinian’s reign and the 3rd year of the 335th Olympiad, there are 532 years.

**4th Indiction. 19th year. After the 17th consulship of Maurice Tiberius.**
<margin>C</margin>
**5th Indiction. 20th year. After the 18th consulship of Maurice Tiberius.**
In this year, in the month of February, the marriage of Theodosius, <note>Theodosius was the eldest son of Emperor Maurice, who had been crowned co-emperor in 590 AD.</note> the son of Maurice, took place. The festivities lasted for seven days, from the 9th until the 15th of the same month of February. And on the 6th day of the month of July, in the same 5th Indiction, an edict was posted. It was written for the remainder of the year—specifically until January of the 6th Indiction—as follows: <note>original: "καὶ ὑπατείας τοῦ αὐτοῦ εὐσεβεστάτου ἡμῶν δεσπότου τὸ δεύτερον"</note> "And the second consulship of our same most pious lord." <note>This marks a change in official dating, likely to honor the young co-emperor Theodosius.</note>

And in the month of November of the same 6th Indiction, a rebellion against Maurice broke out, led by Phocas, <margin>D</margin> a soldier, along with the army. Maurice Tiberius, together with his wife Constantina and nine children—namely six males: Theodosius, Tiberius, Peter, Paul, Justin, and Justinian; and three daughters: Anastasia, Theoctiste, and Cleopatra—fled on the 22nd day of the month of Dius, <note>Dius was the Macedonian name for the month; the text clarifies it was November.</note> which according to the Romans is November, during the night leading into Friday the 23rd.

Phocas, on the 23rd of the same month, on a Friday, was crowned by Cyriacus, the Patriarch of Constantinople, in the venerable house of Saint John at the Hebdomon. <note>The Hebdomon was a famous suburb and military parade ground located seven miles from the center of Constantinople.</note> On the 25th of the stated month, a Sunday, he entered Constantinople seated in a chariot. He traveled from the <margin>P 379</margin> Hebdomon, entering through the Golden Gate <note>The main ceremonial entrance to the city, used for imperial triumphs.</note> and through the Troadensian Porticoes and the entire Middle Street <term>Mese: the main central thoroughfare of Constantinople</term> as far as the palace, with no one resisting at all, but everyone cheering.

<margin>P 380 R 870</margin>
Indiction 6. Year 1 of the Consulship of Phocas Augustus alone. <note>603 AD. The Indiction was a 15-year tax cycle used for dating in the Byzantine Empire.</note>

In this year, Constantina, the former Empress <note>The widow of the recently executed Emperor Maurice.</note>, was forced into a monastery. Also, Philippicus the Patrician and Count of the Excubitors <note>term: Excubitors; the elite imperial bodyguard unit of Constantinople.</note>, and Germanus the Patrician—who was the father-in-law of Theodosius, the son of Maurice—were both tonsured as clerics <note>Forced tonsure was a common way to remove political rivals by making them ineligible for the throne.</note>. Later, a popular riot broke out, and the Middle Street <note>original: "ἡ μέση" (Mese); the main ceremonial thoroughfare of Constantinople.</note> was burned, from the Palace of Lausus and the Praetorium <note>term: Praetorium; the headquarters and residence of the City Prefect, similar to a city hall or high court.</note> of the City Prefect as far as the Arch opposite the Forum of Constantine of divine memory. <margin>B</margin> At that time, the City Prefect was Leontius, the former curator of the estates of Antiochus. > ...gymnasium. Because [the Emperor Maurice] had ordered them to wear iron armor, they armed themselves not for battle as they should have, but for other reasons. Consequently, when day broke, a tumult and panic seized the army. The barbarians <note>Refers to the Avars, a nomadic confederation threatening the northern borders.</note>, seeing the ranks in disorder and the people without a leader, cruelly slaughtered some and took many others from Thrace into slavery as captives. Afterward, the barbarian Khagan <note>term: Khagan; the title of the supreme ruler of the Avars.</note>, having taken these captives, offered to return them to the Emperor, asking for a ransom of one gold coin <note>original: "νόμισμα" (nomisma); the standard Byzantine gold coin.</note> per soul. But the Emperor [Maurice], harboring a grudge against his own army, would not agree to pay. Again, the Khagan asked him to take only half a gold coin <insert>P adds: "half"</insert> for each soul. When the Emperor responded that he would not pay even four *keratia* <note>term: keratia; a small unit of currency, 1/24th of a gold nomisma.</note> to get the captives back, the Khagan became enraged and slaughtered them all. He then imposed a tribute of fifty thousand gold coins on the Romans. Because of this unholy deed, the Emperor Maurice suffered the penalty of slaughter, being torn apart along with his wife, his children, and his relatives. <margin>6. Praetorium. 10. "between" - P reads "rank/order".</margin>

Then, a popular sedition having been stirred up, the Middle Street of the city caught fire, from the Palace of Lausus and the Praetorium of the City Prefect as far as the Arch, in the region of the Forum of Constantine of divine memory, while Leontius, former curator of the Palace of Antiochus, was City Prefect. The fire also consumed the area between the Praetorium of the City Prefect and...

> ...the reason armor was ordered was not for entering battle, so they did not arm themselves as the situation required. Thus, as day approached, tumult and fear seized the army. The Barbarians, finding the soldiers in disordered ranks and without a leader, cruelly butchered some, and led others into servitude—many from Thrace—into captivity. The barbarian Khagan, having received the captives, offered to return them to the Emperor if he would pay one gold coin per head. But the Emperor, angry with his soldiers, refused. Again, the Khagan demanded only half a gold coin per head. When the Emperor replied that he would not redeem the captives for even four *keratia*, the Khagan, inflamed with rage, killed them all and imposed a tribute of fifty thousand gold coins upon the Romans. Therefore, on account of this inhuman and impious deed, the Emperor paid the penalty, being killed along with his wife, children, and kinsmen.

### 6th Indiction. Year 1 of the reign of Phocas Augustus. <margin>3. Year of the World 6111.</margin>

In this year, **Constantina**, the former Empress <note>The widow of the recently executed Emperor Maurice.</note>, was cast into a monastery. **Philippicus** the patrician and **Count of the Excubitors** <note>term: Count of the Excubitors; the commander of the elite imperial guard units in Constantinople.</note> and **Germanus** the patrician—who was the father-in-law of **Theodosius**, the son of **Maurice**—were both forced to become clerics <note>Forced tonsure (cutting the hair and entering the priesthood) was a common Byzantine method of neutralizing political rivals without killing them, as it made them ineligible for the throne.</note>.

...gymnasium. The barbarians <note>The Avars, a nomadic confederation threatening the northern borders.</note> attacked the disorganized ranks; finding the people without a leader, they slaughtered some mercilessly and took many others from **Thrace** into captivity.

When the Emperor replied that he would not even pay four **keratia** <note>term: Keration; a small weight of gold, 1/24th of a gold coin (nomisma/aureus).</note> to redeem the captives, the **Chagan** became enraged and slaughtered them all. He then imposed a tribute of fifty thousand gold pieces upon the Romans. For this unholy and wicked deed, the Emperor paid the penalty of being slaughtered himself, along with his wife, children, and relatives.

## 346th Olympiad

<margin>V 303</margin> **7th Indiction. Year 2 after the consulship of Phocas Augustus.** <note>The Indiction was a 15-year cycle used for tax and dating purposes. Phocas had seized the throne in 602 AD.</note> <margin>4</margin>
**8th Indiction. Year 3 after the consulship of Phocas Augustus, 1st year.** <margin>5</margin>

<margin>C</margin> In this year, in the month of Daesius—which according to the Romans is June—on the 7th day, the following were beheaded: **Theodore**, the **Praetorian Prefect** <note>term: Praetorian Prefect; the highest-ranking civil administrator in the Empire, responsible for taxes, justice, and the army's logistics.</note>, **John** the secretary, **Romanus** the lawyer, **Theodosius** the deputy-assistant <note>original: "σουβαδιουβᾶ" (subadjuva); a Latin-derived title for a middle-ranking bureaucratic official.</note> of the Master of Offices, **Patricius** the Illustrious—who was the cousin of **Domniziolus**, the former manager of the **Palace of Hormisdas**—**John** and **Tzittas**, who were **spatharioi** <note>term: spatharios; literally a "sword-bearer," a high-ranking imperial bodyguard and court title.</note> and **candidati**, **Athanasius**, **Count of the Sacred Largesses** <note>The empire's chief financial officer.</note>, **Andrew** the Illustrious, surnamed **"The Mackerel"** <note>original: "τοῦ Σκόμβρου" (Scombrus).</note>, and **Elpidius** the Illustrious.

<margin>C</margin> ...of the month of **May**, in the **12th Indiction** <note>An "Indiction" was a 15-year cycle used in the Roman Empire for tax and dating purposes.</note>. For if **Pentecost** <note>The Christian feast occurring 50 days after Easter.</note> occurred on the 22nd of the month of May in that year, then without controversy the day of the **Resurrection** <note>Easter Sunday.</note> occurred on the 3rd of the month of **April**, so that the 1st of that April fell on **Friday** <note>original: "Parasceve," the Day of Preparation.</note>. 

Add, therefore, a fourth part to 272—which is 68—and it makes 340. Divide these by 7 <note>The author is calculating the "day of the week" shift by accounting for leap years (the fourth part).</note>, and there is a remainder of 4. Since April then began on a Friday, count Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday; consequently, the year 273 begins on <margin>V 304</margin> **Tuesday**. Therefore, April is found in the current **19th Solar Indiction** <note>The solar cycle of 28 years used to track the days of the week.</note> and the **19th Lunar cycle**, beginning on the third day of the week <note>Tuesday.</note>, which is indeed the case. 

Furthermore, having consulted both the **Paschal tables** and the **Consular lists** <margin>D</margin>, I found this calculation to be in agreement. There are, therefore, 272 years from the death of **Constantine** <note>Constantine the Great, who died in 337 AD.</note> until now, and 281 full years from his **Vicennalia** <note>original: "eikosacteridos," the 20th-anniversary celebration of an emperor's reign.</note>.

And **Easter** also occurred 272 years ago in the 13th year of the Moon's indiction, in the second year of the **279th Olympiad** <note>The ancient Greek system of dating in four-year blocks.</note>, on the 3rd of April.

<margin>B</margin>
In this year <note>615 AD</note>, a silver coin of six grams <term>hexagrammon: a large silver coin introduced by Heraclius to help finance the war against the Persians</term> was created by law, and the imperial stipends <note>original: "ῥόγαι" (rogai); the annual salaries paid to officials and soldiers</note> were paid with it, and at half the ancient rate <note>This indicates a major economic crisis; the state was halving the pay of its officials and using a new, potentially overvalued currency.</note>. God, who created all things and holds them together by His own power, has bestowed a gift worthy of His goodness upon the human race: the providence of imperial rule. Through this, we are deemed worthy to live without disturbance, or, if we fall into certain difficulties, we find a remedy. Looking toward this divine gift—we mean the imperial providence—and before all other things, toward your immense Mildness <note>The Greek term *hemerotēta* and Latin *Clementiam* are formal honorifics used to address the Persian King, intended to flatter him during a time of military crisis.</note>, we implore you to grant us forgiveness for daring to use this present report to your Might, contrary to the former established state of affairs.

Having corrupted the Roman army in **Thrace** <note>original: "ΘρἽκῃ" (Thrakē); a region in the southeast Balkans.</note>, he suddenly fell upon our imperial city, and he killed **Maurice**, who had reigned over us piously, along with his wife, and even his children and relatives, and not a few of the officials.

> “God, who created all things and contains them by His power, bestowed a gift worthy of His goodness upon the human race: namely, the providence of empire, by which security of life is provided for us, and if it happens that we fall into some difficulties, a remedy is procured. ### PASCHAL CHRONICLE

...your benevolence <note>original: "φιλανθρωπίας" (philanthrōpias); a standard diplomatic honorific for the King’s kindness.</note>. Now he [Shahin] has also sent a response to us through **Spadadouar** <note>A Persian official or envoy.</note>, promising under oath that your immense Power will receive those sent by us as is fitting, and will release them to return to us unharmed, and that he was commanded by your benevolence to do this. We, in turn, having gained confidence from these developments, and above all trusting in God and your Majesty, have sent your servants: **Olympius**, the most glorious ex-consul, patrician, and Praetorian Prefect; **Leontius**, the most glorious ex-consul, patrician, and Prefect of the City <note>The Prefect of the City (Praefectus Urbi) was one of the highest-ranking administrative officials in Constantinople.</note>; and **Anastasius**, the most God-beloved priest and **Syncellus** <note>original: "σύγκελλον" (synkellon); a high-ranking ecclesiastical advisor who often lived in the same cell as a Patriarch.</note>.

<margin>D</margin> We entreat you that they be received as is fitting for your immense Power and that you quickly send them back to us, bringing that peace which is pleasing to God and appropriate to your peace-loving Power. 

<margin>P 388</margin> We also beg your Clemency to hold **Heraclius**, our most pious Emperor, as your own true son <note>In the diplomatic language of the time, for one ruler to call another "son" or "brother" established a formal hierarchy or alliance between the two empires.</note>, as he is eager in all things to provide service to your Serenity <note>original: "γαλήνης" (galēnēs); literally 'calmness,' a title used for imperial majesty.</note>.

<margin>D</margin> <margin>10</margin> In this year, in the month of Artemisios—which according to the Romans is May—of the 12th <term>indiction; a 15-year tax cycle used for dating</term>, during the time of Sergius, Patriarch of Constantinople, it was devised that a chant should be sung after everyone has partaken of the holy mysteries <note>The Eucharist or Holy Communion</note>. Alexander, the Praetorian Prefect <note>The highest-ranking civil administrator in the empire</note>, addressed the people, saying: "From this moment, you have me to thank for your bread, and I hope to quickly bring about a correction in this matter." For the aforementioned John "the Earthquake," although bread was being sold for 3 <term>folles; small copper coins used for everyday transactions</term>, had intended to make it 8 *folles*; but God overthrew his plan.

<margin>P 392 R 896</margin> It is fitting to recount how now also the only most-merciful and compassionate God—through the acceptable intercession of his immaculate Mother and truly our Lady, the <term>Theotokos; the Mother of God</term> and ever-virgin Mary—saved this, His humble city, from the godless enemies who had surrounded it by mutual agreement. By His mighty hand, He rescued the people found within from the expected sword, from captivity, and from the most bitter slavery, which no one would be able to fully describe. For the cursed Salbaras <note>Shahrbaraz, a famous Persian general under King Khosrow II</note>, the leader of the Persian army, was waiting—as it seems and as was later proven by his actions—for the arrival of the godless Chagan <note>The title of the supreme ruler of the Avars</note> of the Avars. Having arrived many days earlier at Chalcedon <note>A city located directly across the Bosporus from Constantinople</note>, he godlessly burned all the suburbs, the palaces, and the houses of prayer,

Since a "Seismos" <note>original: "Sismo"; referring to the riot or the man's nickname</note> was stirred up by the people so that he might be removed from the administration of public affairs, he was stripped of his rank, and his statues were immediately thrown down. Alexander, the Praetorian Prefect, addressed the multitude in this way: *From now on, you shall receive your loaves of bread from me, and I hope it will happen that the matter is restored to its former state in a short time.* Indeed, that man John "the Earthquake," although bread was being sold for only three <term>folles; copper coins</term>, was attempting to lead the matter to such a point that eight *folles* would be demanded: but God overturned his counsel.

Furthermore, it seems a worthy task to set forth how even now the only merciful God, full of clemency, through the most acceptable intercession of His own unstained mother—the truly our Lady, the Mother of God, and ever-Virgin Mary—delivered this, His humble city, from the impious enemies who had besieged and surrounded it by a mutual conspiracy. By His powerful hand, He freed the people then within the city from the imminent sword, from captivity, and from the most bitter servitude; indeed, no one will be able to sufficiently explain all these things. For that accursed Salbaras, the Leader and Exarch of the Persian army, while he was waiting—as is likely and as finally appeared from his deeds—for the arrival of the Chagan of the Avars, who is hated by God, had in the meantime, many days before, placed his camp at Chalcedon and sacrilegiously consumed all the suburbs and sacred buildings with fire; and he remained there, waiting for the Chagan's arrival.

### 352nd Olympiad

**1st Indiction. 18th Year [of the reign of Heraclius]. 17th year after the consulship of Heraclius Augustus.**

**In the 18th year of the reign of Heraclius, and the 17th year after his consulship, and the 16th year of the reign of his son, Heraclius the New Constantine, on the 15th day of the month of May, in the 1st Indiction, on the first day [of the week], <margin>10</margin> on the holy day of Pentecost itself, dispatches were read from the <term>ambon</term> <note>A raised pulpit or platform in the center of the church used for readings and announcements</note> in the most holy Great Church <note>Hagia Sophia, the cathedral of Constantinople</note>. <margin>15</margin> **"Shout for joy to God, all the earth! Serve the Lord <margin>B</margin> with gladness; enter into His presence with exceeding joy! Know that the Lord Himself is God. He made us, and not we ourselves; we are His people and the sheep of His pasture. Enter into His courts with hymns and give thanks to Him. Praise <margin>20</margin> His name, for Christ is Lord! <note>The Emperor adds "Christ" to the traditional text of Psalm 100 (LXX 99) to emphasize the Christian victory over the Zoroastrian Persians</note> His mercy endures forever; His truth from generation to generation. Let the heavens rejoice!"**

### CHRONICON

...to reach the regions of Zara, and then for winter to have set in [there]; since such supplies were not to be found in those places, our most fortunate expeditionary forces would have suffered a great disaster. For from the time we moved from Siarsouron <note>Modern Sharizor in Iraqi Kurdistan</note>—that is, from the 24th of the month of February—until the 30th of the month of March, the snow did not let up. But by the grace of God, arriving at <margin>V 319</margin> the regions of Ganzak <note>A major city in Atropatene, modern Iranian Azerbaijan, and home to a great fire temple</note>, we found plenty of provisions for both <margin>D</margin> men and horses. We remained in the city of Ganzak itself, which is a substantial place containing about three thousand houses, and in the surrounding villages, which allowed us to spend so many days in a single location. We ordered the members of our Christ-loving expeditionary forces to stable their horses in the houses of the city because of the winter that had set in, and so that each man might keep one horse at our <term>encampment</term> <note>original: ἄπληκτον (*aplēkton*); a term for a fortified imperial military camp</note>; for our <term>army</term> <note>original: φωσᾶτον (*phosaton*); derived from the Latin *fossatum*, referring here to the entrenched camp or the troops themselves</note> is located near this city. For the <term>governor</term> <note>original: βαρισμάνας (*barismanas*); a Greek rendering of the Persian title *Marzban*, meaning a provincial military governor or warden of the marches</note> of the city of Ganzak and all its inhabitants, when they learned that we had crossed over the mountain of Zara, withdrew and <margin>P 401</margin> fled into the mountain regions to more secure fortresses. When we received the two men sent by Siroes, the King of the Persians, we released <margin>R 916</margin> one of them—namely, the Persian—along with other men to the governor of Ganzak, who was forty miles away in a secure fortress, and [sent letters to him]...

### PASCHAL CHRONICLE

We sent a <term>memorandum</term> <note>original: ὑπομνηστικόν (*hypomnēstikon*); an official written instruction or reminder</note> to him so that he might prepare at least seven <term>mounts</term> <note>original: ἄλογα (*aloga*); literally "unreasoning animals," the standard term in this period for horses or pack-animals</note> for the ambassadors, in order for them to depart quickly and without hindrance to Siroes, the King of the Persians. When the <term>governor</term> <note>original: βαρισμανᾶς (*barismanas*); the Greek rendering of the Persian title *Marzban*</note> received those sent by us along with this memorandum, <margin>5</margin> both he and all those found there offered cheers of acclaim for many hours, honoring both us and Siroes, the King of the Persians. <margin>B</margin> For they had been fully informed by the Persian who had been sent from the ambassador that the God-fighting Chosroes <note>Chosroes II, who had ruled for decades and nearly destroyed the Roman Empire; the epithet "God-fighting" reflects his role as the great persecutor and enemy of the Christian empire</note> had perished, and that Siroes had become King of the Persians. The same governor wrote back to us <margin>10</margin> that, according to the instructions given to him by us, he was readying the horses for the ambassadors; and whenever he receives a second order from us containing the instructions for the ambassadors to arrive, the governor will come to us in person, bringing these horses and being bound to perform every service and duty.

While we <margin>15</margin> were staying in that same <term>encampment</term> <note>original: ἀπλήκτῳ (*aplēktō*); a fortified military camp</note> near Ganzak until the third day of the month of April, <margin>C</margin> Phaiacus the <term>imperial secretary</term> <note>original: ἀσηκρῆτις (*asēkrētis*); from the Latin *a secretis*, a high-ranking official in the imperial chancery</note>—who is also called Rasnan—arrived around the second hour, it being Sunday. We received him at that very hour, and he delivered to us a memorandum from Cabates—who is also <margin>20</margin> called Siroes <note>Kavad II, the son of Chosroes II, who took the throne after his father's overthrow</note>—the most mild King of the Persians, which contained the announcement of his proclamation as king and stated that he wishes to have peace with us and with every person. We therefore reviewed the copy of the memorandum of the most mild Cabates, also known as Siroes...

...to join, as well as what we then wrote back to them. Therefore, from the seventh day of the month of April, we spent twenty-seven days in our same camp at Ganzak: and on the eighth of the same month, we dismissed Pheacus the *A Secretis*, called Rharnan, having received him with as much honor as was permitted, as well as those who were with him; for he had a distinguished retinue with him. ### Scholarly Annotations

**2.** These sections are to be restored by comparing them with pages 735 and 736. **In the same place.** *semainomen* <note>original: σημαίνωμεν; a variant spelling of 'we signify'</note> in manuscript **V.** **3. [phthen]** The phrase "the memorandum which was sent" should be supplied, and soon after, "your Brotherhood." **Regarding [dae]**, see whether *Chosdae* <note>original: Χοσδάη</note> on page 730 is related. **5. of the]** *ton* <note>original: τον</note> in manuscript **V.** **In the same place.** "and Rasnan"] In the copy, this reads *nan*, which is missing about six letters at the beginning. **6. dia]** To be supplied as "diadem." **7. [thentes]** To be supplied as "having been adorned" <note>original: κοσμηθέντες (*kosmethentes*)</note>. **10. prosperity]** in manuscript **V.** **11. may He deem worthy]** This should be written as *axiose* <note>original: ἀξιώσῃ; the subjunctive form</note>. But the genitive case is correct here. Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* Book 1, Chapter 1: "so that no one, through ignorance of the facts, may condemn the work as a falsehood" <note>original: ἵνα δὲ μή τις ἀγνοίᾳ τῶν ὄντων καταψηφίσηται ψεύδους τῆς πραγματείας</note>.
